To repeated applications for permission to hold public installations, I r epliecl,
that there is no law against a public installation. yet, in my opinion . t!1e net would
be contrary to the spirit of Ma.sonry. In our workings we seek retirement, and
refrain from obtruding our practice upon the public notice, nor leave our own quiet
ways to please or win the favor of the multitude; and, saving the performance of a
required ceremony, which must occur in pub;io, there is no good reason for a
departure from tho original intention of the F1·aternity. Again, na in this jurisdiction the Grand Lodge holds no public in~t:.1llatlo11 , it seems proper for subordinate
J,.odges to follow the example. Youi· attention is inYited to the subject, that you
may definitely determine the f uture action of Lodges in this particular. '

Repeated inquiries have been made regarding the right or feasibility of Lodges
to incorporate, in view of the pnrchase nnd holcling of property, and aa to the manner of election and power of trnstees for the same purpose. 1 had only to reply that
if trustees were elected merely to hold property about to be purchsaed, in tmst, the
act would be in accordance with the common p1·actice; but if the trustees were
elected in view of actual incorporation of the Lodge-i. e., articles of incorporation
to be filed with the County Clerk nnd Aecretary of State, in conformity with Sec.
290, Civil Code-then the action would be wit110nt prMedent in this jurisdiction.
To make valid the election of trustees it would be necessary for a majority of the
members of the Lodge. tluly conver.ed for the purpose, to be present ancl vote for
said trustees, which facts must be verified by the officers of the Lodge. (Bee Sec;
594, Civil Code.) That a Lodge can obtain a title to purchsaed property by the
agency of trustees, though true that if it became necessary or desirable to sell the
same, and the original trnstees were succeeded by others, the purcl1asing party might
not be satisfied with the title, which, however, could be mrule good by an enabling
act of the legislature. That I knew of no law to prevent the incorporation of a
Lodge, yet as the Uivil Code recognizes certain rules, regulations, or di6cipline of 11n
association incorporating, epd as such rules, regulations, or discipline do not exist
in our institution, I considered the a~t of iucorpol'ation inexpedilmt until the matter
bad been settled by the Grand Lodge. I submit for your consideration, if, by the
act of incorporation, a Lodge may acquire a legal existence, in a degree, independent
and beyond the control of the <;rand Lodge, which would not terminate with an
arrest or surrender of its charter, or if, by a recent special legislative act, psased for
the benefit of Masonic and kindred organizations, incorporation can occur without
weakening the allegiance to the Grand Lodge. To determine then the expediency of
permitting Lodges to become bodies corporate and politic, and to define the manner
of electic1n, the duties, powers, and succession of trustee•, aro points which merit
attention, and should evoke your deliberate disposition:
A Lodge in Missouri elected a candidate to receive the degrees, but, before taking
the third, the brother removed to California. The Lodge in l\Iidsouri reported him as
a Fellow Craft in good standing, and, in consequence of his removal from its jurisdiction, granted a dismissal, with permission to apply to another Lodge for the remaining degree. The brother petitioned a Lodge in this juril!Cliction for the third degree,
which had the usual course, but received an objection. His case was then referred
to a committee, in accordance with Sec. 6, Art. III, Part III. of our Constitution,
and my opinion was asked.
I replied that Sec. 6, Art. III, Pan III, applies to Entered Apprentices nnd Fellow
Crafts who have received their degi·ees in this jurisdiction. In the case cited, CO!ll·
ing from another jurisdiction, with no request, but only a permission from the Lodge
conferring the first and second degrees, the petitioner is subject to the same careful
scrutiny thnt our laws provide in the application of a Master Mason for affiliation;
consequently, the petition of the brother should be referred, reported on, and balloted for, as if ho were a Master ~saon applying for affiliation, or a candidate for
the degrees.
·
I decided : That, because an Entered Apprentice is. dropped from the report of bis
Lodge to the Grand Lodge, it does not follow that the Lodge relinquish61! its claim
to him. The statutes assert no specified time when an Entered Apprentice may be
deprived of tho privilege of seeking advancement. He c~n apply for the other degrees, and it will rest with his Lodge to determine if his conduct aa an Entered
Apprentice entitles him to advance:
That a brot!Jer duly summoned to appear for trial cannot " remain away and put
in a plell. of guilty through a brother;" in such absence the trial will proceed e:i:
parte, and the finding of the Commissioners will be in accordance with the evidence

adduced. If the brother disobeys the summons, without good resaon therefor, such
disobedience is an offense and may constitute a charge for a subsequent trial:
'.!.'hat the act of preferring charges against a brother elected to office wonl.1 not
debar him from being installed, as he cannot thereby be deprived of any of his
Masonic privileges, it being unclei·stood that a valid objection to the inetallation of

A case happened where a member of a Lodge was in prison awaiting trial on the
charge of murder. I wsa asked if the Lodge should at once p1 oceed to have charges
preferred against· the prisoner. I answered that there was no necessity for u Masonic
trial until nfter a trial wsa hacl in a civil court, sin!)e, with a charge so grave, the
former could not have the facilities in procuring witnesses as would pertain to the
latter, and there was no occa;oion fol' an undue haste. If the civil court convicted,
then the accused could be tried e:i: pcrrte, represented, if desired, by his counsel, na
conviction in a civil court does not lessen the necesaity of a lll.saonic trial ; if
acquitted, he could be brought before the Lodge for tri111.
In respect to the question, "Would the Secretary of a Lodge be justified in refusing the clues of a suspended member, from persons who might be deemed having
personal interests in collecting and paying the same, even without the knowledge or
consent of the suspended member?" I answered: The Lodge has a ri~ht to expect
that a brother in arrears will, in event of an inability to pay, either directly or indirectly set forth his condition, and seek remission or further time. Any failure to do
so implies an indifference as to his position as a Master MnKon in "good standing,"
and such inaction may well be reg11rded ns culpable. 'l'he Lodge is always supposed
to act charitably towards delinquents, and prevent suspension whenever the benefit
of the doubt can be given. The reading of the law enforces the opinion that the

I also accompanied the Grand Master aud exemplified the work in the following
districts, namely: the Orst, where the brethren assembled at Eureka, Humboldt
oounty; the fourteenth , where the meeting was htlld at Petaluma, Sonoma county;
and the eighteenth, where the meeting was held at Jackson, Amador county, These
districts comprise twenty·seven Lodges, the most of which were represented, and
the degrees were conferred by the several officers in an impressive manner and in
strict conformity with our ritual.
Inspector JOHN A. WATBON, of the first district, reports that, owing to tl1e unusu11l depression in all kinds of bu!ln~~s, tho Lodges in his district have done but
little work during the past year, btit that what has been done has been well done.
Inspector JOHN OLEMENTe reports the seven Lodges comprising the third district
as in a prosperous condition, the brethren being all anxious to comply with the requirements of the Grand Lodge. He had visited them all, and claims for them the
·
highest state of proOcienoy in the work .
Inspector WILLIAM O. LEMMON was able to visit but two of the four Lodges comprising the fifth district. He reporta them as doing good work and as being in a
prosperous condition.
Inspector BENJAMIN W. BARNES reports the three Lodges of the sixth district as
doing their work in strict conformity with the established work of the Grand Lodge,
and a8 being in a healthy condition.
Inspector JosIAH P. BROWN, or the seventh district, had visit.ed every Lodge
therein and witnessed the conferring of the degrees in each He bad also devoted
considerable time in lecturing the officers, and had found them ready and anxious to
perfect themselves in the ritual·. He has noticed a steady 'improvement in the work
from year to year, and thinks that they are nearly perfect.
Inspector !ANTHIS J, ROLFE reports having visited all the Lodges in the eighth
district, except one, .Dibble, No.109, the members of which are so scattered that it
was impossible to get enough together to have made the visit an object. He, how·
ever, having a knowledge of the proficiency of the officers, could vouch that they
conferred the degrees in a proper manner. He had instruct.ed a number of the
Masters in his district and pronounced them well qualified.
Inspeot~r ORRIN W, HOLLENBECK reports having visited six of the ten Lodges in
the ninth district. He did not deem it necessary to visit the other four, as they were
presided over by Masters of whose competency he was fully sati•fied, He rePorts
the work in the district as up to the average standard, and the Lodges as severally
prosperous.
Inspector ROBERT E. WARREN reports th11t the Lodges in the tenth district have
done but little work, but that they are in a healthy and prosperous condition financially, and that their affairs are administered by :Masters noted for their Masonic
knowledge, zeal, and :fidelity. ·
Jnsi>ector FRANCJ8 E. WARREN comPlains of the lack of interest manifested by
the members of the two Lodges comprising the twelfth district, but attributes it to

however, endeavor to do their work in an efficient manner.
Inspector BENJAMIN F. TUTTLE reports the eleven Lodges comprising the fourteenth district ns beii1g in a healthy and prosperous condition. Convocations had

It is now seven years pince the present system of inspection was adopted by this
Grand Lodge, and it affords me great pleasure to be able to report that it has ~cco~­

the conferring of the degrees have been corrPcted, and the Lodges now, with very
few exceptions, confer the degrees in .accordance with the ritue.l prescribed by this
Grand Lodge. I have exemplified the work in nearly all the distriota under the jn?s- .
diction , and have, more tban nn hundred times, seen the degrees conferred therein;
and I am pleased to say that the r,odgee have gained ns high 11 state of proficiency in
the work and lectures as they will (in my opinion) ever attain. Jt is tn10 tbat the
brethren sometimes make a mistake in the selection of their officers (especially of
the Maete1·), who take but little interest in the work, seeking the positions only for
the honors they confer. Of course, during such an aclminietration, poor work is
done· but their shortcomings are genere.Jly corrected !l.t the ensuing election, when
more' vigorous Masters soon bring the Lodge back to its former standard and position. But in order to keep up the present slate of proficiency, the Inspectors must
eiercise proper vigilance over the Lodges in their respective districts, and not suffer

them to relapse into their former condition. They should also frequently compare
their .work with the Grand Lecturer, and endeavor to become so perfect as not to

by this Grand Lodge, in 1875, requiring "that the Grand Master issue Inspector's
commissions to such brethren only as have a certificate from the Grand Lecturer as
to qualification· and proficiency in the work and lectures adopted by this Grand
Lodge," was Intended to remedy the evil and make the Inspectors letter-perfect. I
am sorry to say that in many cases it has proved a dead letter, and could not be enforced. The In~pectors are usually appointed after the close of the Annual Communication, at which they have attended a week or more. At its close, they are all
anxious to return to their homes and resume their usual avocations, and it is a rare
instance i! one remains to review his work with the Grand Lecturer.
Some months, ago I suggested to the Grand Master that. taking into conRideration
the fact that the Lodges are now working as well as perhaps they ever will, the salary
of the Grand Lecturer mip:ht with propriety be dispensed with, and that his offica be
made a position of honor alone, without any actual or imagined source of profit.
Should he be called upon to visit districts and exemplify the work, the Grand Lodge
ought 10 reimburse him for his traveling expenses.

by all the Fraternity in Knnsos.
;
At the Annual Communication Grand 1r!aster SHARP delivered an Address which
tills some twenty pages of the proceedings, bnt is none too long. · He congr~tulates
the Fraternity on the unanimity and harmony that have prevailed, there having been
only one distressing event daring tile year. He had granted djspensations for the
formation of seven new Lodges, but had persistently refused all applications for e.
shortening of the time in the conferring of degrees,
The "disturbing element" alluded. to by the Grand Master, resnlted lo the su'~pen­
sion and final revocation of the charter of Frankfort Lodge, No. 67. A member of
that Lodge was habitually guilty of one of the lowest a1Jd most debasing of crimes,
and yet had such influence in the Lodge that itwa.q impossible to discipline him, when
found guilty. Even the edict of the Grand Lodge was disregarded. The offending
brother boasted of his power, and habitually indulged in abuse of all who attempted
to deal with him as he deserved. The Grand Lodge approvea of the action of the
Grand Master and expelled the brother from e.11 the rights and privileges of Masonry.

JosKPH WEDD was the first Grand Master of the Independent Grand Lodge of Maesachnsette, and this Lodge, taking his name at the close of the century from nie incumbency, wns thus specially honored by the Grand Lodge. From the address made to
the oftlcere by the R.'. W.-. CRADLES L. WOODBURY, we cull the following extracts,
full of good words and sound Masonic sense:·
MaPonry is a social institution, and its bnsie is the good sense, honesty, and truth
of Its craftsmen. 'l'he virtues we chel'ish nre plain and homespun, those which the
experience of life shows are the safeguard of the practical middle interests of society.
We neither seek the very rich nor the very poor, neither the erratic scintillations of
genius nor the unimpressible apathy of ignorance.
"The rank is but the guinea's stamp;
The man is the gold for a' thnt."
The Masons, as n class, represent, more than any other I know of, the practical
common •ense 01· the whole community in its most liberal aspect, solid men of judgment, Pelected from •very interest in society for the good ot· society. She seeks no
political distinction, nor does she ostracise any one for hie politics. We welcome
good men or all parties. and think the more they meet here on the level the better
thev all will be for it. We welcome varieties In creeds as we do in politics; an equal
consideration for all good men. Every Mason hne his own politics, his own creed ;
that is his private right. To our Fraternity the solid charactel' is the test 'of the
man,-his equity, his prudence, his energy, his Rocial worth. Has he, in the common

Our fraters are familiar with the fact, often stated in our ritual, that once the
brethren were acc ustomed to "meet upon the highest hills and in the lowest vales."
After our Nevada Fraternity had been burned out of house and home, the Grand
Master convened" Virginia Lodge, No. 3," on the summit of Mount Davidson, the
towering peak that keep~ perpetual guard over the Bonanza City. He gives this
brief account of the occurrence:On t'eptember 8, 5875, soon after the burning of the Odd Fellows' Hall at Virginia
City, I was requested to convene Vb·giflia Lodge;No. 8, on the summit of Mt. Davidson. I readily assented, inasmuch as the brethl'en were without other place of meet·
ing. ~·or the first time in centuries, ns I believe, we met as did our ancient brethren

near Ragiown, where the brethren had come together in that way to raise money

preside; of a similar gathering in 1851, in Eureka, and of another at Auburn, California. But none of these were gatherings like the present, and he again thanked
the brethren that he had been called upon to preside over their deliberations.
Afier the regular business of the Lodge had been transacted, and under the head
of the" Good of Masonry,'' Bro. CHARLES E. DELONG, late United States Minister to
Jap1m (who died October 26th, 1876), was called upon, and responded very happily.
He sketched the surroundings within which they bad erected their altar. Beneath
them was the wealth of Ophir, and around them the tumult of trade, etc., etc. He
told them how in Japan Ile had assisted in welding the link in Masonry which made
the chain complete around the world. Up to that time there had been one land
where the Craft was not known. Now there was none. Masonry belted the globe.
The lights of the altar had been lighted, and now there were six Lodges in tile
Empire, and the institution was rapidly spreading.

TEXAS.
The Grand Lodge of Texas commenced its forty-first Communication in the city
of Houston on the fourteenth day of December,1876,-the M.'. W.'. MARCUS F. MoTT,
Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.'. GF.ORGE B. BRINGHURST being Grand Secretary. Eighty-one Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master is a straight-forward, well written, and able
. document. We are pleased to learn that, on the whole, peace and prosperity have
blessed tbe Fraternity and peopl,e of Texas. He had granted dispensations for seven
new Lodges, and had refused thirteen other applications.
In one respect,' we think the Masons of Texas are somewhat loose in their
way of doing business. The Grand Master states that the signatures of the
applicants for some of the new Lodges were all in one handwriting, and after·
wards many of the apparent signers denied that they had given any one authority
thus to 11Se their names, and still claimed membership in their old Lodges. He bad
therefore required, as an absolute prerequisite, that each petitioner shall sign bis
name. A very common-sense requirement, which is our law.
They· b.ave an edict In Texas that MaAOnic halls shall not be rented or used for
any other purpo•es than for Masonic work. The edict has been in force some four
years. Notwithstanding the prohibition, two Lodges have rented their halls to the
q,rangers. For this the Grand Master arrested their charters ; but upon their humble submission and apology, the same were subsequently restored. We have had our
say on this subject in former reports. While we approve of the rule as a general law,
we do think there are many cases, especially in small country viilages, where an
exception should be made. And If this exception was made to depend upon the consent of the Grand Master, we cannot see bow Masons would be injured thereby. We
note only one of the decisions of the Grand Mast.er:-. Question-Does the loss of the first toe of the right foot disqualify an applicant
from being made a Mason ? Answer-It does.
Foor-toed gentlemen will therefore give Texas Masonry tbe cold shoulder. Sup·
pose the toe"llail only was gone? Is not that a blemish?

WYOMING.
Our young sister of the interior sends us fraternal greeting in the form of the
proceedings of the second Annual Oommunication of her Grand Lodge, held at Cheyenne on the tenth day of October, 1876,- the M.·. W.-. EDGAR P. SNow, Grand
Master, presiding, and the K·. w.· .. JOHN K .•JE~'FREY being Grand Secretary.
Representatives· were present from all the Lodges in the jurisdiction, four in number.
The Address of Grand Master SNOW is well written, and mainly confined to the
Masonic business of the year. He had -granted a dispensation for a new Lodge at
Rawlins. Among the decisions was the following, which commends itself to us as
based on Masonry and common sense :No. 4. When the deformity of the candidate is not such as to prevent bim from
being instructed in the arts and mysteries of Freemasonry, and does not amount to
· an inability honestly to acquire the means of subsist.ence, the admission will not be
an infringement upon the ancient land-marks, but will be perfectly consistent with
the spirit of our institutions.
.
As a guard against impostors, who have much troubled the Wyoming brethren,
the Grand Master recommends that no foreign visitor. be admitted to a Lodge unless
. he first show his diploma. He hoists in the Masonic pillory those brethren from
Eastern and Western homes who had victimized the Fraternity in Wyoming, on
promises to refund the amount advanced immediately npon their arrival at home ..
In no instance had the promise been kept. We have a few ventures in that same
"Ban~ of Faith," and think we are one of a goodly number of victims.

FOREIGN GRAND BODIES.
We make no apology for devoting several pages of this report to a summary of the

of Briti~h, German, etc. Lodges in our midst, that they will be glad to hear from the

Our brotJ1er begins with the Grand Lodge of England, and f'rom his report we clip
the following paragraphs:-ENGLA ND.-The principal PVent of the year culminated at the Quarterly Communication in March last. the Earl of Oarnarvon, Pro-Grand Master, presiding. On his
motion the Grand Lodge un11nimonslv resolv~d to commemmorate the safo return of
His uo'yal Highness, the Prince of Wales, fr?m his visit to India,_ by 8:pproprlitting
$20,000, for the purpose of forming. in pcrpetmt_y, two life-boat ~tat1ons, 1~ such localities on the English coast as might be determmed by a spemal committee and the
National Life-boat Institution.
· Two appeals were passed upon, not of special lmportnnce in themselves, but
tending to show that the practice of our English brethren is substantially the
same as our own. The first was the case of n Master who had invited a Past ~a~ter
to be present at 11 meeting of' his Lodge and confer the Third Degree. To t1!1s the
Senior Warden objected, on the ground that when the Master ?f the Lodge failed to
officiate in person, his prerogatives devolved upon the Immediate Past Master, nnd
from him to the Senior Warden. The Masi er held, very properly, that a brother
(ltficiating in his presence was as if he him~elf conferred the degree, he, (the Master)
being responsible fnr the act of his representative. The Grand Lodge took the same
view, and dismissed the appeal-as would have been done here.
.
The second case 11rose out of' an appeal from the action of the Board of General
Purposes, in r~fusing t~ interl'ere in a lawsuit between two members of a Lodge,
touching a matter ontside of :M11snnry. The President of the Board vel'y properly
remarked that if such ca•es were to be entertained, the Board would have more than
enough to' do. The Grnnd Lodge thought so too, and dismissed the appeal without
dissent. This is entirely in accord with the American doctrine that business disputes
are not to be settled in Masonic courts,

;)'OU. Here in Stockholm are two Symbolic or St.John's Lodges in activity, the 'St.
Eric Lodge' and the' Nordiska Forstn Lodge' (First Northern Lodgo). Ium a member of' St. Erie Lodge,' and we had the fortune to have as Master our beloved King,
OSCAR II, during nearly twenty years, from 1852 until the death of his brother, King
CARL XV, in 1872. He was not Master only b.v the namo, but really the leader of the
Lodge, inasmuch as he conducted nnd presided nt all Lod•e Meetings himself and conferred the degrees, especially in the first ten years of his Mastership, and as he enlightened everything through his fine and amiable spirit. .Now, being King, he is, as
formerly, attached to our Lodge, and visits the same as often as po,sible. A fow weeks
ago he conferred the first degree on two candidates. All the Swedish brethren follow
the development and efficiency of Freemasonry, especially in Germany, with groat inter·
est, but the several systems nnd rites of the Foreign Grand Bodies make us fear that
their working will dissipate the mutual aim and destiny.
"It was several times proposed to change and amend our rite in so far that also non·
Christian candidates could be initi11ted, '!'his could be perhaps effected for the first three
degrees, probably for Borne higher degrees; but a certain limit muRt take place, and

such a change or amendment would be illogical and wrong, because the highest degrees
would be anyhow vei!Pd and closed. We have a very brotherly intercourse with brethren of all foreign jurisdictions, and often such brethren from abroad find (when Uhris·
tians) affiliation and promotion in our Lodges."

UNITED GRAND ORIENT OF BRAZIL.-The struggles against the attacks of the Catholic clergy against Freemasonry in Brazil have not yet ceased. The bishops of
Olinda and Para. however, who were condemned by the higher State Courts to be
imprisoned for their aggressive and unlawful attacks against Freemasonry, have been
pardoned by the Emperor befoi·e he let'! the country for his American and EuropeRn
tour; therefore, and in compensation, the Pope abolished the·' Interdict" which the
two bishops had laid upon all members or the Masonic Fraternity within their
dioceses. Notwithstanding, several Catholic priests refme -the benefits of the Ohurch
to all Masons.
During the first quarter of 1876 four new Symoolic Lodges have been chartered
by the United Grana Orient, (System dos Bencdictinos), two in the Capital and two
in the Province Rio Grande do Sul, so that at present there exist under this united
jurisdiction 189 Symbolic Lodges, 1U7 Chapters, (Rose·Croix), and five Provincial
Grand Bodies.
The subordinate Lodge '' Uniao e Segredo," at Bahia, founded, on the day of the
installation of its newly elected officers; an Orphan Asylum, and bought sixty slaves
to be liberated. Rro. M.A. LoPEB, a member of the Lodge, donated to the liberated
slaves the means for further subsistence.
The Lodge "Zur Eintracht," at Porto Alegre, .in the ProvinceRio Grande do
Sul), with about one hundred members, working in the German tongue, but under
the Biaziljurisdiction. laid the corner-,tone of a Masonic Temple. On this occasion
a Masonic proce>sion through the whole city took place; an event never before
heard of in Brazil. The Master of this Lodge, "Znr Eintracht.. " is Bro. CARL VoN
KosERITZ. editor of a German daily newspaper, and of a Masonic weekly called the
".Acacia." Tho Province of Rio do Sul has a population of 4.50,000 rnhabitants,
among them 60,000 Germans, mostly Pr< testants.
The two Provinces San Panto and llio Grande do Sul distinguish themselves in
the fight against the Roman Oatholic aggression. These provinces have more public
schools than any others; popular scientific lectures are held; they have popular and
circulating libraries, and the Press is in a sound condition. There exist in Brazil
five Masouic periodic!lls.
All Symbolic Lo<lg<s work, so far, under this ·Grand Orient; but it seems there is
a very liberal regime, also a great unity among all brethren of the jurii!d!ction, inasmuch as they have united to stand together against their sole anrl only enemy in the
Empire-the Catholic clergy, beaded by the .Jesuits. The Constitution of the juris·
dict10n forbids the initiation of any individual who is a slave-holder, or who raises or
imports slaves.

And here ends another pleasant waik through the fields and workshops of the
Fraternity. Words of good cheer have generally greeted us. Sometimes matters,
Masonically, were not as bright and cheering as could be wished, but the causes of
embarrassment and stagnation were but temporary, as we believe. The cause of
Freemasonry is onward. Brethren are more and more realizing the n;ioral obligations
of their brotherhood. We care not how strictly Masons are thus held. Numb,ers only
bring weakness, if there be no moral backbone-l)o living up to the principles of the
institution. '.!.'he howlings of the fanatics outside, whether coming from the Vatican
or Blanchard & Co., will hurt no one, if Lodges and members are but faithful to the
inner as well as the outer lire· of Masonry, We therefore hail with joy all steps tend·
Ing to that result, and trust to see t!:te <lay when no such thing as intemperance; profanity, or wrong-doing will be found within or about our Masonic family circle.
With many thanks to our brethren of the reportorial. corps !'or their kind words of
welcome, we bid them all adieu.
For the committee,
WILLIAM H. HILL, Ohafrman.

Your committee, to whom was referi-ed the appeal of Bro . .JAMES REID from
the action of Quumrzn Lodge, No. 88, in acquitting Bro. MICHAEL QUINN on charges
of unmasonic conduct, have carefully examined the evidence in the case and repor•
that they can see no good reason why the verdict of the commis•ion should be interfered with.
·
Bro. REID seems to take it very much to heart that the brethren of his Lodge can·
not be induced to look on the matter in the same light that he does himself; but the
unanimous testimony of every witness called in the case is decidedlv in favor of the
accused, and we are of the opinion that the commissioners were fully justified in
acquitting the brother of the charges brought against him. We therefore off~ the
following resolution and recommend its adoption:Re~olved, That the action of Quitman LoJge, No. 88, in acquitting Bro. MroH~EL
QUINN, be and the same is hereby affirmed.

Bro. SAMUEL G. HILBORN, from the same committee, presented the
following report :To the .M. ·• W. •. (}rand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Bro. G11EEl'II.F~AF CURTIS
from the action of Crescent Lodge, No. 45, in suspending SAMCJEL HARO REA vEs from
all the rights 11nd privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration and
report as follows:In this c~se the accnsed is charged ;vith assault with intent to commit rape upon
two young girls, aged respectively eleven and thirteen yea.rs. There are two specifi·
cations to the charge, each transaction being set forth in a separate specification,
and the accused was found guilty upon both. The only testimony introduced at the
trial in support of the second specification Is wholly hearsay, and therefore insufficient
to sustain the finding; but the proof in support of the first specification is ample, and
consists of a transcript of the record of a trial had in the County Court of the county
of Del Norte, wherein the accused was tried for the offense contained in the first
specification. He was indicted for assault with intent to commit rape, but was finally
convicted of a simple assault.

1877.]

157

. Grand Lodge of California.

The appellant in this case appeals from t hat portion of the judgment of the Lodge
which affixes the penalty of suspension only. An assault is a Ma>onic crime of
greater or le•s gra vity, according to the circumstances under which it is committed.
It may be a very slight Masonic offense or it may be a very grave one. This Grand
Lodge has often thrown the mantle of charity over the violent acts of brethren committed in the heat of passion, engeooered by political strife or the conflicts of busi·
ness. Such occurrences are not taken as evidence of a fixed condition of mental
depravity; but the case before us affords no such apology. The person assaulted was
a young girl, and tbe motive for it. was of the basest kind , and could only spring from
a mind debased and corrupted, and perhaps even diseased, by the contemplation of
filthy things. Such a person is unworthy to remain a Mason. Your committee
therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the action of Crescent Lodge, No. 4.5, in finding SurnEL. HARGREAVES g uilty of the first specification of the charge against him, be approved , but
that the sentence pronounced against him be reversed and set aside, and that the said
accused be expelled from a1t the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All which is reRpectfully submitted by
WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, l
SAMUEL G. HILBORN.
~
Committee.
Lxw1s F. JoNER,
WILLIAM b. CHANE,

Bro. MraHAEL J. KEATING, from the special committee to whom
was referred a memorial from the Masonic Board of Relief of the City
of San Francisco, presented the following report:To the M :. W:. Grand Lodge of Oaliforn..ia :The undersigned, your committee to whom was referred the petition llnd res1,l11tions of the Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco, respectfully pre•en• the following report, recommending the adoption of the following re•olutions :Resolved, That the sum of one dollar is hereby levied annul\IIY upou each and every
Master Mason in this jurisdiction, which amount shall te set apart as a Charity Fund.
Tl1e money so raised shall be collected by the Secretaries of the several Lodges, and
transmitted to the Grand Secretary at the same time as other Grand Lodge dues.
Resolved, That in any place where two or more Lodges have concurrent jurisdiction,
1 the Masters of such Lodges may form a Board of Relief, with articles of agreement to
be a!lproved by the Gri!.nd Master. The moneys raised by the first of these resolutions shall be annually distributed, p1·0 1·ata , umong the Masonic Boards of Relief of
this State, and to the Lodges (where no Board of Relief exists) which have dispensed
charity to brother Mason•, members of Lodges other than their own.
Resolved, That each Board of Relief shall, on the fifteenth day of September of
each year, transmit to the Grand Lodge a plain and comprehensive report of their
operations during the preceding year.
Resolved, That the money raised, as provided by the first of this series of resolutions, shall only be expended for the relief of Master Masons in good standing, hailing from other jurisdictions, their widows and orphans; bnt that the several Board 8
of Relief which may be organized under these regulations shall have power to relieve
the temporary necessities of Master Masons of this jurisdiction, their widows and
orphans-the amount so expended to be refunded to the said Board of Relief by the
Lodge of which the brother relieved may be a member; but. should the said Lodge
be utterly unable to refund the amount, then, on a satisfactory representation of the
faot, this Grand Lodge will as5ume and pay the amount, in its stead, out of the fund
raised by these resolutions, provided that the amount shall not exceed fifty dollars.
Resolved, That any surplus, remaining io the bands of the Committee on Charity
on the first day of November of each year, shall by it be safely invested, with a
view to eventually procure a" home for disabled, indigent Ma~oos," their widows
and orphans. •
All which is respectfully submitted by
MICHAEL J, KEATING, }

Which report was concurred in.
Past Grnnd ;Master LEONIDAS E. PRATT offered the following as a
General Regulation ;At this and at the future Communications of this Grand Lodge the election of
Grand Officers shall be held and conducted in the following manner:The Grand Secretary shall cause to be prepared six ballot•boxes labeled with the
titles of the six elective Grand Officers to be chosen, and he shall also cause to be
prepared a sufficient number of ballots with the titles of the respeotive Grand Officers printed ~hereon.
The Grand Master shall appoint twelve tellers to receive and deposit the ballots to
be cast, being two tellers for each ballot-box.
The Grand Secretary shall call the roll, and ea.ch officer and member of the Grand
Lodge shall, when his name or that of bis Lodge shall be called, deliver to one of the
rollers at each of said ballot-boxes the number of ballots which he is entitled to oast
for the office d esignated on said box.
When all present shall have voted, the tellers shall open each box separately, and
shall call the votes found therein; and the Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand Secretary shall each keep a count and tally thereof.
If there shall be a failure to elect to each and all of the several Grand Offices on
the first ballot, the Grand Lodge shall proceed in like manner to vote again for all
offices to which there bas been such failure to elect.

Which regulation was adopted.

Bro. W1LLIAM A. DAVJE!J, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
to whom had been· referred a resolution relative to the use of Masonic
signs or titles for business purposes, read a report from that committee upon that subject which was presented to the Grand Lodge in 1873,
stating that it was deemed to be a sufficient response to the resolution.
Bro. MORRIS M. ESTEE moved that the committee be instructed to
report some absolute resolution upon the subject, and it was so
ordered.
The hour named for the special order-the delivery of the Annual
Oration-having arrived, it was stated that, the Grand Orator, Bro.
AARON A. SARGENT, having been called away to attend to his duties as
a Senator of the United States at the extra session of Congress about to
be held, the address which he had prepared would be read, at his
request, by the Deputy Grand Master, Bro. CHARLES L. Wwa111; a n +
it was read by that officer, as follows:Mosr WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER
AND IlRETHREN OF TH~; GRAND LODG~ :Amid the exacting tasks of a laborious public position, it has been difficult for
me to find time to discharge the duty imposed upon me by the Grand Lodge, and
impossible to prepare an address entirely worthy of that Grand Body and this occasion. The few ·thoughts which I offer are a partial solution of the problem, interesting
to me ancl to all of us, why Masonry, alone, of all voluntary societies, unaided, as it
has ever been, by extriaJ.sic power, and possessing no military or judiciul force to ex·
ecute its will or enlarge its empire, has preservecl an efficient organization for
ages, and has gradually extended its boundaries until it encircles the tarth.
Masonry seems thus far to have been exempt from the decay that is t11e condition
of all material existence, however enduring. The bills, which are types of the everlasting, are perishable after their kind, as is the snowflake. "The glacier streams,"
says HUSKIN, "weary t11e mountain heart as the crimson pulse does ours." The natural foi·ce of the monntain crag is abated fn its appointed time, like the strength of
the sinews in human old age; and it is but the lapse of the longer years of decay
which, in the sight of the Creat01", distinguishes the monntain range from the moth
and the worm. The shores of time ai·e strewn with wrecked empires and the
debi·is of creeds, associations, and enterprises. As the worn grains of sand contin·
ually roll to the ocenn bed and leave monotonous levels where once were proud voJ.
canic peaks, so dissolves into the abyss of time the strongest work of men's hands,
whether fortress, temple, or dynasty. By what means, then, has Masnory escaped
the operation of these grea.t, depressing Jaws of change?
·
In a repub lio, where all forms of government and habits of society are based on
freedom of thought, Masonry has its most fertile soil and luxuriant growth. Dut ·
such surroundings ere not calculated to give it toughness of fibre, or develop iU!
fruit to the liighest perfeolion. The original purpose of Masonry was to give to its
votaries the very liberty of thought which time and progress !Jave since granted to
vast communities, but which was difficult to assert in the infancy of our society, because it was stampe<l. out by the bigotry of an unenl'ghtened age wl1erever it appeared. The essential distinction of Masonry '.for generations wns that it was the
oppon~nt of tyranny and priestcraft, acting, it is true, by, quiet processes, as the

Following down the record of Maaonry I find that another element of its growth is
that it has never assumed to be a system of, or a substitute for, religion. It dcies not
purport to be a guide to faith. It nowhere seeks to interfere between the creature
and the Creator, or assumes to do more than inculcate reverence to the Supreme and
faithfulness to man. Nowhere in Maaonry is the idea taught or implied that the path
to Heaven runs through the Lodge. We have hever invaded the province of any sect
or creed. The Hebrew who believes in the old dispensation, and the Christian who
trusts in the new, alike kneel at our altars. It is a mistake of some well-disposed
people to think that Masonry aasumes to do more than prescribe the general moralities, without which any faith is dead. But to adopt any creed , to indulge in speculations upon articles of fe.ith, would lead to controversy and disunion. Men's opinione
cannot be caat in the same mculd of religious belief, even by authority; else persecution would have stamped out dissent, which it has never done; or persuasion would
have brought uniformity, which it haa as little accomplished. Religious beliefs are
compounded not only of reason but of emotions, temperaments, dispositions. While
moral trut]j is immutable, religious belief!! may vary with each generation. Many
dogmaa, revered of the peat, excite the derision of the present. Into this domain
.Masonry, wisely, has never intruded. There is not a tenet which it _taught in the
fifteenth century that is not received in this age with reverence. The hot breath of
ridicule haa never attainted it. It is not committed by a record of puerilities in the
past to inevitable pr~.-ent contempt. All that is known of' it excites respect and
admiration. It has escaped the danger of the divisions which gl'OW from polemical controversy because it haa not assumed to dictate opinions, or possess them, on
any subject within the reach ot' such cpntroversy. It has always held whatever it has
gained of members or influence, becauFe there could be no schism from its teachings
without denial of fundamental truths, which are the security of manhood, home, and
~ociety. By aYoiding speculation or dogmatism on .1·eligious topics it has avoided
inconsistency, passion, and disunion. Yet Masonry would have been a failure had it
been l iable to the charge of impiety. It is true that Masons have been ranked with
infidels in persecuting fulminations; and, had the charge been true, the Craft would
have had but a limited following, for the tendency of the human mind is reverential.
But its votaries knew the charge to he unjust, and clung the more strongly to it
from the sense of the injustice.
Masonry has had vast growth because it inculcates a pure morality. No worthy
:M.ason can be a dishonest qr impure man. The first lesson which he is taught is that
truth is a divine attribute and the foundation of every virtue. He is instructed to put
a due restraint upon his aftections and passions; to preserve a nc;>ble and steaqy purpose of mind, equally distant from cowardice and rashness; to regulate his life by the
dictates of reason ; and to r~nder to every man his just due, without distinction. In
short, the three great duties of life are impressed upon his mind and consciencereverence to God, the chief good; kindness to his neighbor, as prescribed by the
golden rule; and respect for himself, by avoiding irreglfiarities and intempe1'a.nce,
which impair the faculties and debaae the-dignity of his profession. While thfl!le are
the familiar lessons of the Craft, it is not assumed that every Mason lives up to this
standard. Human nature has not arrived to this sb.te of perfection in many individuals. When religious sects shall have so far advanced in holiness that they need
no longer to say, "when we would do good evil is present with us," then we will
admit the justice of a criticism which requires of all our members a practical exemplification of all the virtues inculc11ted by Masonry. Any system of morality must
be judged by its teachings and not alone by its teachers.
We claim only for Masonry that its tendency is toward good; that it elevates
the character of men and gives to them better conceptions of their duties and responsibilities before God and man; that the body of the Craft are better men than they
would have been had they not been 1\1.llllons; and that the world is more enlightened,
purer, and freer for the institution. But the effect on the growth of that institution,

produced by such teachings, arises from the ready assent of initiates which they command, and which strengthens with maturer judgment and reflection after their advancment. No philosophical observer can doubt that there is a vast preponderance of
good in the world, and an unfeigned admiration by the great majority of reasonable
beings of that which is right and pure. While there is much of evil there is more of ,
good. Men admire rectitude even if they do not possess it. Even vice pays a tribute
to virtue in its hypocrisy. But the average man, as well as the highly gifted, has
good intentions and loves truth; he recognizes it with pleasure and attaches himself
gladly to its instrumentalities. Hence an element of the success of :Masonry. It
may be mentioned as an accessory, that the truths of :Masonry are illustrated by
symbols of felicitous taste and poetic beauty. Rich in expression, yet limpid in
simplicity, these rare creations of gifted minds exert a strong influence alike on the
imagination and the reason, and give vividness and reality to truths which constant
repetition might otherwise render commonplace or monotonous.
The universality of Masonry has been favored by the same influences which have
caused many secret societies to spring into existence, flourish awhile, and disappear.
These" come like shadows, so depart." Many of them, both social and political, have
been produced and have perished during the present generation. These ephemeral
creations did not take a deep root in human nature, because they either sprang from
superficial causes, were the exponents of a single idea, or were the product of transient,
even if strong, sentiment. Men like mystery. They eagerly seek the unknown;
but there must be intelligence and permanence of purpose to hold the neophyte who
is attracted by curiosity and novelty. No matter how beautiful the symbol, his continued• interest must be secured by something behind and superior to the symbol.
Dramatic work may appeal to the imagination, but if the reason is left unsatisfied, all
soon becomes stale, flat, and unprofitable. Masonry has combined its unsurpassed
poetic imagery with philosophic wisdom and sagacity. It not only allures, it retains.
While consistent, it is many-sided and meets the tastes of all orders of men, from
the humble artisan to the man of abstract science. It numbero in its ranks to-day,
as it has done in all the term of its existence, the brighte•t anrl most progressive intellects of the age. Princes preside over its deliberations in Europe and feel honored by its honors; and the most eminent state>men of this republic have ministered at
its altars. It thus rests on sturdy foundations and is P<>werfullybuttrefsed on every
side. The fiercest persecutions have therefore failed to destroy it. The mark of ancient superstitious vengeance and modern political assault, it has survived unharmed. It can count itll martyrs ruthlessly done to death by thousands; bot its
hist.ory may be almost vainly 8Cann~d for a traitor.
The conflict of ideas between :Masonry and a prominent religions organization is ·a
relic of the past, and is as inveterate as are all of that class of antagonisms which have
a traditiooary basis. The excitements which are periodically worked up between the
descendants of those who fought on opposite sides at t)le Boyne, excite the wonder
of those who do not shara the emotions of the actors therein. So we may marvel
that time and demonstration have not allayed this antipathy to Masonry. The spirit
of the age does not tolerate the forcible•modes of repression of ancient days. Undoubt·
edly the higher humanity which now pervades all government of Church and State,
banishes the barbarous expedients of the past. But Masonry is still discountenanced.
Roman Episcopal letters of late date have defined as dangerous dnd heretical the
teachings of the Craft. By this authority the Lodge room yet conceals the mystery
of iniquity. But the progress of science has justified the right of free inquiry
claimed and exercised by Masons, and has t~ught the world that which they early
asserted, that the path to troth i~ through doubt aud investigation. While we may
notice that an unnecessary barrier stands between us and the numerous followers of
this ancient creed, and that out-worn traditions and past prejudices exclude Masonry
trom the knowledge and symp11.thies of millions of men, we accept the situation which

at the last Annual Communication :I. An Inspector inquired whether or not he should give ii cerllficate of qualification to a Master elect whom he found well qualified in the matters of which it was his
duty to inquire, but who was thought to be unfit for the office by reason of continued

The Grand Master held that the Inspector's duties in that regard were fixed
by the Regulation1-to inquire only as to the ability of the applicant to give
the work and leotures of the three degrees-and that they had not imposed on him
the dnty of canvaaslng or determining the moral fitness of the Master elect for the
responsible duties of that office,
In this the Grand Master was clearly right.. First of all, it behooves a Lodge to
see that the brother whom it elects as Master is a man of good repute and of proper
habits; and next, it behooves the brother elected to see that he not only possesses
the qnaliflcatlon of knowing and being able to give the work and lectures to the
acceptance of the Inspector, but that his moral conduct be without olfens~. The
Lodge which elects a Master, known to be intemperate in his habits, ought to be BUB·
pended; and the Master, against whom the.charge of continued dissipation could be
justly made, ought to be tried and expelled. If he has been elected. and is protlcien~
In the work and lectures, he is entitled to the certificate of the Inspector and to be
inshlled. If, for any reason, he is unworthy to occupy the position, our Constitution
provides the remedy; and it is the duty of the members of his Lodge to avail them·
selves of it.
II. Can the Senior Warden preside at a .trial when the Master desires to become
the proeecutor or is a material witness?
The Grand Master decided that he could not. This was plainly correct. It is the
duty of the Master· to preside at all tria!s, but if he Is the prosecutor, or a material
witness in the case, he ought not to preside; and in such case he should report
the facts to the Grand Master, who alone can depute another to preside, and who
would, in a proper case, appoint some disinterested Master to conduct the trial.
III. Cao charges ·be amended by adding specifications after a commission has

The Grand Master decided that such amendments might be made under sanction

or the Master, provided that a copy of the amendments be served upon the accused

This decision was right in the case in which it was made, but does not go far

IV. When a member of a Lodge has been suspended for non-payment of dues, is
there any limit to the time for which he must pay in order to be restored?
The Grand Master decided that there was no statute of limitations in respect to
Masonic dues and duties.
The party suspended may restore hi~self at any time by payment, but his Lodge
must remit or he must pay as a condition for restoration. The presumption is that
his Lodge will remit if he ought not to pay, and the Constitution has very wisely left
the determination of the matter to the discretion of the Lodge.
V. When does withdrawa,I from a Lodge become comple~; and when does its
jurisdiction cease?
In the one case the Grand Master decided that when the Lodge had, at tbe request
of one of its members, voted him a recommendatory cer~iflcate, it could not, at a sub·
seqnent meeting, by a reconsideration of its action, restore him to membership; and in
the other case that, when a member of a Lodge had withdrawn and removed to the
jurisdiction of another Lodge, the fi:st named Lodge could not entertain ch~rges
against him.
Our Constitution recognizes the right of every Mason to withdraw fl'Om member·
ship in a Lodge. All he has t.o do is to pay his dues and notify his Lodge, at a stated
meeting, that be withdraws from its ·membership. The very moment that he makes
such paymeut and gives such notice he ceases to be a member. Whether the Lodge
will recommend him by certifi~ate to the Fraternity as a worthy brother, is a matter
for the Lodgo to determine; and when membership has been severed, it can be
restored only by petition and election in the way provided for affiliation.
A Lodge has jurisdiction to hear and detel'mine charges against its own mem'bera
wherever they may reside, and against all Masons residing within its territorial
limits.
VI. If a Lodge consents that another Lodge may receive a petition from an
applicant residing within ite territorial jurisdiction, to which Lodge do the proper
fees belong?
The Grand Master decided that the Lodge granting the permission had the right to
the fees, and might, at its pleasure, relinquish or insist upon them. This commends
itself as just. The Lodge, having the exclusive right to receive the petition nnd the
fees, may surrender ih right as to one or both, or may refuse as to either or both,

The Constitution gives t.o a non-affiliate th~ right to preserve his standing as a

X. In r espect to physical qul\lltlcations, the Grand Master decided that the
deformity or dismemberment, which would exclude, must be such as would prevent
a literal conformity to the requirements of the several degreea, and that an applicant
who was bump-backed, but was, "In all other respects of natural physical conformation," was not for that reason·lnelfgible.
·
The 11th of our General Regulations declares that the person who desires to be
made a Mason, must not bl' "deformed or dismembered, but bale and sound in his
physical conformation, having his right l imbs as a man ought to have, and able to
conform litemlly to what the several degrees require of him."
In 1872, the Committee on Jarisprudence said in respect to this r egulation: "In
the judgment of your committee, a fair construction of the regulation requires not
only that the applicant shall not be deformed or dismembered, and shall be hale and
sound in his physical conformation, having his right limbs as a man onght to have,
but that he must also be able to conform literally to what the several degrees

The present committee folly concur in what was then said. They are aware that
very many of the best informed brethren think now, as they then thought, that the
111&t clause was the controlling one, and that the only inquiry to he made should be
as to the ability to conform literally to the requirements of' the degrees; and that, if

XI. Can a witness, for or against a brother on trial, act as one of the trial-com·
missioners?
The Grand Master decid~d that he might so act. He says: "I answere<i that tli.e
statntes do not inhibit a triel-commissioner from giving evidence in the case in which
be acts as such; and, although it would be preferable for a commisgioner not to be a
witness, yet when the evidence is Important and the witness not interested in the
result of' the trial, competency pert~lns; and, as the great object of every trial is to
elicit truth, and in the spirit of truth to administer justice, I could see no objection to
following the custom of military and other courts, and allowing the double office to
be performed."
Your committee think that it would be extremely dangerous to al~ow a witness..
whose evidence is important to th~ prosecution or the defence, to act as a trial-commissioner. We know that witnesses not unfrequently become more or Jess partisana
of the side for which they appear. In some cases an important witnesR might he
willing and able to do exact justice between the parties, but be would be an extraordi·
narily good man if he conldjudge of the character and ~lfect of his own evidence with
the same impartiality as he would of that of a stranger. The Constitution does not, in
express terms, declare tl111t a witness shall not 11ct as one of the judges, but we think
that, by a Fair interpretation of the provisions of that instrument with respect to trial1,
it was the purpose that only unbiased and impartial men ~hould be allowed to act as
commissioners. In our civil courts a witness cannot be a juror, and in a Masonic
court he ought not to be.
If it were known at the time of the election of qommi~sioners that any individual
would be, or ought, from bis knowledge of the facts of the case, to be a witness, the
Master should not allow him to be elected, or, if elected, sbo.uld declare him ineligible
to the position; and if, when the commission has aSllembled to hear the case, or, during the pr.ogress of the trial, either party should call one of the commissioners as a
witness and he testify to the merits of the case, be should cease to act as a member
of the board; and it should be good cause for reversing the judgment or determlna'tlon
of the board that one of the parties p11rticipating in its final action had been 11 witneRs
and testified to the material facts of the case.
SECOND. As to an amendment to Section 1, Article V, Part I, of the Constitution,
proposed by Bro. WILLIAM H. HILL, at tbe last Annual Communication , for the purpose of having the election for Gr11ncl Officers held on the third, instead of t h9' fourth

on the third day. thereof," etc.
In the judgment of your committee, the amendment ought not to he adopted.
The business of the Grand Lodge ought to be finished before the election.takes place,
and it must be apparent to all who have a1tended its meetings that the whole of the
third day is absolutely necessary for the disposition of business, and that , ordinarily,
It is the busiest day of the whole Communication. We recommend that the amendment be not adopted.

SEVENTH. Relative to I\ memorial from Bro. HENRY CLAY DOW!f!NG, of Occide11tal

Bro. DOWNING states in his memorial that he was made a Mason in Occidental

From Bro. SAllUEL. W. BACIUB, the Master of that Lodge, who, with others,
appeared before your committee in this matter, thi:r learn- ·
let. That Bro. DowXING was thrown, .o r. fe11, from a boggy in June last, and
received such injnries that the lower portion of his body became, a nd still continues
to be, partially p11ralyzed; thllt he has been una\Jle since to move himself, and has
been, and still continues to be, under care of a physician; and that he is in necessitous circumstances:
2d. That application ln his behalf was made to the charity committee of his
Lodge, consisting of the Master and Wardens, nod that relief was refused by thP
Master and Senior .Warden, (who acted in the matter without the Junior Warden,) on
the ground that the applicant had been dissipated and had done sundry things which,
in their jndgment, rendered him unworthy of the charities of the Order, and that they

3d. That subsequently, at a stated meeting of the Lodge, a member moved that
the Lodge give one hundred dollars for the relief of that brother; and that this motion

4th. That, at the next stated meeting, a full attendance was secured by summons,
and that then the motion to grant relief to Bro. DOWNING was renewed , but that the

5th. That Bro. Dow111NG resides at San Rafael, and that the Master and Wardens
and two Past Masters of Marin Lodge, No. 191, at. that plao~, indorse upon the petition their certificate that Bro. DowNIXG is "In a condition of helplessneHB, unable
even to move from Ms bed without anfstance, and that he and his family are without
the common aeccssaries of life, except as they are furnished by friends and charities:"
And 6th. That Occidental Lodge is abundantly able, ont of Its proper charity

Under these circnmstances the following questions are brought to the notice of
your commltlee : '
l. Has a Lodge the right to question the worthiness of one of its members, asking for relief, in any way except by the preferring of charges and a trial?
2. Has the charity committee of a Lodge the right to inquire , in such a case,
further than to determine whether there is actual need of help!
S. When a member of a Lodge, at one of its regular meetings, moves that the
Lodge grant relief to one of its members in distress, is it within the discretion of the
Master to refuse to entertain the motion? and

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 12,

'· Was Occidental Lodge, No. 22, guilty of a Masonic offense when, having the
ability, it refused to aid Bro. DowNING?
The case presents some remarkable features. It is certainly remarkable that a
Mason should continue in full membership with a Lodge for fifteen years, and that no
inquiry shouid be made as to his moral fitness until, by a sudden misfortune, he is
rendered helriless and compelled to call for assistance. The common instincts of human·
ity should then impel us to forget his faults and delinquenoes and to tender such aid as
his necessities r.equire. If we can afford to overlook his offenses against the moral
law when he is hale and strong and amply able to provide for himself, it certainly is
not the part of ~anhood to begin to speer out his faults when misfortune has over·
taken him and he is helplese. It is a good maxim, which has come down tons from
the generous and brave old Saxons, that every man is to be deemed innocent until he
be proven guilty, and until his guilt bas been established by the judgment of some
proper tribunal,
·
When Bro. DowNING applied to his Lodgo for relief, his 'name was on its roll as a
member in good standing, and the only inquiry then to be made by the Lodge, or by
its charity committee, was whether he was in actual distress; .and, if found so to be,
the duty to relieve him was plain and imperative, and it was a duty for the neglect
of which it is hard to conceive a plausible excuse. It is no excuse for the Lodge, in
this ~eglect of its first duty, to say that the applicant \iad been dissipated, had squandered his estate, and, through his own folly, reduced himself to penury. That is a
specious pretext-not an excuse.
Your committee think that the time when one of its members needs and applies
for relief is not the time when the Lodge may stop to inquire·whether he has, in something or in many-things, offended, and that he must be presumed to be worthy until
his unworthiness has been judicially determined; and, further, that it is not the prov·
ince of the charity committee of a Lodge, at any time, to canvass or determine the
question whether or not a member of their Lodge is worthy of Masonic consideration.
Their only duty is to ascertain if the member is in actual need, and if they find that, he i~,
they are to relieve him. Your committee are of the opinion that it is the right of every
member of a Louge to move, at any one of its meetings, that the Lodge relieve the
distress of any one of its own members, and that it is not within the discretion of the
Master to refuse to entertain such a motion; and they are also of the opinion that Occi·
dental Lodge was guilty of a flagrant offense when, under the circumstances, it refused
to render any assistance to Bro. DOWNING, and that that Lodge should be required to
make prompt amends, so far as it may, for the wrong done 'and for its wanton disre·
gard of one of its plainest and most imperative Masonic duties.
To the end that justice may be done, your committee propose and recommend the
adoption of the following resolution:Resolved, That the matter of Occidental Lodge, No; 22, in its relations with Bro.
HENRY CLAY DowNING, be referred to the Grand Master, with instructions to require
that Lodge to take promptly such action in the case of Bro. DOWNING as he shall
deem proper in the premises.
EIGHTH. Relative to a communication from the Grand Orient of Egypt concerning
certain action of the Grand Orient of !!'ranee.
The Grand Orient of Egypt informs us that the Grand Orient of F'!'ance, at it>
general meeting in September, 1876, struck out from its Constitution the declaration
of a belief in God and the immortality of the soul, and declares its own belief in
these essential doctrines.
Our own Grand Lodge having several years since refused to maintain friendly
relations or hold any intercourse with the Grand Orient of France, it would be hardly
proper that'we should criticise its action, even in a matter which strikes at the very
foundation of the Masonic edifice.

NINTH. Relative to a communication from the Hon. Secretary of the Masonic
Union of New South Wales, concerning the establishment of an independent Grand
Lodge in that Province 1In the Province of New South Wales there are, as appears from the papers nccom·
panying the communication of Bro. E. H. WILLIAMS, Honorary Secretary of the
Masonic Union, forty-five Lodges, of which twenty-three have charters from the
Grand Lodge of England, sixtee~ have charters from the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
and six have charters from the Grand Lodge of Ireland, with a Provincial Grand
Lodge holding under each or said Grand Lodges. The Masonic Union was established
to promote the for\nation of a Grand Lodge for the Province·, and the communication
of Bro. WILLIAMS asks forinformstion as to what is necessary to be done to accomplish their purpose and to obtain recognition by other Grand Lodge~.
It woald seem that there is abundant materiAI in the Province of New South Wales
for the establishment of a Grand Lodge, and that the necessities or the Craft would
require one. The method of forming and organizing such a body is evidently well
understood by the Masonic Union, and we may assure them that we shall be very
happy to recognize and enter into friendly relations with a just Grand Lodge established there, 'vhenever it shall ha ye first obtained recognition from the Grand Lodge or
Grand Lodges under which its constituent Lodges hold their charters. The reoogni·
tion extended by the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland, and Ireland to the Gr11nd
Lodges of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, within the pal!t,
few years, shows that those Grap.d Lodges are willing to surrender their claim tQ
allegiance from all those Lodges which desire to seek a new allegiance- only
it1sisting that such Lodges as choose to retain their charters shall not be molested.
There is a seeming propriety in that, though we much prefer the American doctrine
of exclusive jurisdiction. ,

of thirteen hundred and eighteen shares of the stock of the "Masonic Hall Aasociation of the City of San Francisco "-the shares being ten dollars each. The Grand

presented the following reports :Your committee, to whom was referred the petition for restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry of MIOHAEI. BOROWSKI, who was expelled by Truckee.
Lodge, No. 200, on the twenty-fourth day of January, l b7l, report that the petitioner
has complied with all the requirements of our Constitution, and that the Lodge by
which he was expelled has recommended his restoration.
The petitioner was expelled for fomenting discord In his Lodge by stating that the
Senior Warden had been guilty of gross Masonic offenses, and that he intended to
bring charges against him. Within a few years the said Warden was tried by his
Lodge for the very same offenses of which Bro. BOROWSKI had accused him, and was
suspended. Under these circumstances your committee are of the opinion that the
prayer of tlte petitioner should be granted, and they therefore oiler the following
resolution and recom1D.end its adoption:Resolved, 1ltat MICHAEL BoROWSKI be and ia ·hereby restored to nll the rights
aud privileges of Masonry.
Your committee, to whom was rererred the petition for restoration to the rights
and privileges of Masonry of CHARLES HOWARD GORDON, whi> was expelled by
Wooduridge Lodge, No. 131, on the sixteenth day of January, 1875, and the protest
of said Lodge against granting the prayer of the petitioner, have bad the same under
consideration, and, after a full and very exhaustive examination into all the facts of
the case as exhibited in the transcripts of the various trials, and a careful hearing or
the state:uents of a number of brethren for and against the petitioner, report as follows:/
.
This case is very familiar to a portion of your committee, inasmuch as it has reg·
ularly come before this Grand Lodie at every Communication since 1873. In that
year the p etitioner was accused in his Lodge of gross unmasonic conduct in that he
did" on or about the twentieth day of May, in effect, say that Bro. JAMES FoLa.r;R, a
Master Mason in good standing and a member of Woodbridge· Lodge, No. 131, did

1877.J

Grand Lodge of Oaliforr1ia.

191

feloniously participate in burning his (the petitioner's) property in Lodi." On this
charge the petitioner was brought to trial, convicted, and expelled. He appealed to
the Grand Lodge, nnd the action of the Lodge was r eversed for the reason that the
accused had been refused a reasonable extei:ision of time in which to prepare his
defense. The case was remanded to the Lodge for further action. A new trial was
had with the same result. Again an appeal was taken, and again the Grand Lodge
reversed the decision, for the reason that the members of the Lodge had not been
legally notified of the special meeting held to elect commissioners. The case was
again •ent back. A third trial took place and the accused was once more expelled.
He appealed, put when the subject came before your committee in 1875., it was found
that the appeal had not been filed within the time prescribed in our Constitution, and·
consequently no action was had. In 1876 he applied for a re!1earing of his case, but
as our law does not recognize any such remedy, nothing could be done. This year
he has, in accordance with our regulations, applied in due form to be restored.
Woodbridge Lodge was properly notified, and has protested against his restoration ;
and thus, tor the firRt time in five years, the case comes up before us in such a shape
that it can be decided on its merits.
This long continued litigation, in connection with personal ond business antagonisms, has engendered such an intense bitterness of feeling between the parties that
it would seem to be impossible for the Lodge, on one side, to impartially weigh and
decide upon the evidence in the case, or, on the other hand, for the accused to l ook
. on most of the members of the Lodge in any other light than as personal enemies.
This condition of affairs is certainly much to be regretted, but that it does exist is a
most unhappy fac.t.
Your committee feel that the utmost consideration should be showri to the protest
of any Lodge against the restoration of a brother by it expelled, but in this particular
case, after careful examination of all the evidence presented in each of the three
trials, they are unanimously of the opinion that no Masonic offense has been proved
against the accused, and that justice rnquires them to report that his request should
~e granted. They therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Res~lved, That the petition of CDARLES HOWARD GORDON be granted, and that he
be and is hereby,restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS,}

VIII. If one, who has received the first, or the first and second degrees of
Masonry in Missouri, desires to receive the remaining degrees or deg1•ee in, and

upon as other petitions are, 1md that Sec. 6, Art. III, Part III, had no reference to
ench a case. His decision was pl11inly right.

Part Ill, of the Constitution. The" dropping from the roll ," so called, as men tinned

ot the writer by the generous courtesy of Past Grand Ma•ter GEORGE C. PERKINS,
l1aving safely taken on board the joyous crowd, cast otr her lines. The captain rang
the "go-a-head bell," the m1m at the wheel put the helm "hard-&-starboard," and
lbe noble steamer, gracefully yielding to the sll.ilor's guiding hand; gently veered to
'11e east-nor'·wllllt, until the smoke-stack and foremast came in range, when
"They steered away, across the bay, to Saucelito'e shore."

REPORT
Of Past Master GEORGE T. BROMLEY, G. C. B.,

RELATIVE TO THE GRAND CLAM-BAKE CELEBRATED AT OLD SAUCELITO
On the Tenth day of October, 7877.

BROTHER GRAND SECRETARY:! feel highly honored, I do assure you, in being called up_on to. fur~ish a report
of the proceedings connected with the Grand. Cl~m-bake Festival given l~ hon?.r of
the Grand Lodge during its recent Commumcation. I approach the subJect with a
consciousness of my inability to grapple enccessfully with an event of such vast
import.ance to those who participated, as well as of such salutary i_nfiuenoe upon ~he
Fraternity at large; and I shall write, therefore, as one who wnteth for ¥ostenty,
remarking that, although thia report may not prove to be as fiowery or h1gh·to~ed
as some reports, I trust that no person will so trifie with his own life as to question
its truthfulness.
.
If the foregoing "introductory'' should not be considered as fully up to the
standard, please let me know , and I will" raise" it if it takes my last chip. That's
the kind of a Grand Clam-Baker I am.
'
.
I suppose that the right thing to do in preparing this report, would 1'.9 t? c~m~
mence with the speech which I delivered before the Grand Lodge when the mvitat1on
to the Grand Clam-Bake wa.s tendered. But it will have to be omitted for the re11-son
that in all human probability the same speech will. be delivered at the next meeting
of the Grand Lodge; therefore, sufficient be it here to say that, for depth of pathos,
soaring eloquence, and brilliant word-painting, it was one of. t~e m08t .r~marke.ble
productions which the Grand Lodge had ever listened to. This is the op1mon of.the
G and Tyler and as such is entitled to weight, inasmuch as he w&1:1 on the outside.
V:hen the q~estion, "Shall the Grand Lodge accept the proposed invitation?" was
t by the Grand Master, one hearty and united voice of approval responded, thus
;~owing that the speech had struck a chord which vibrated in harmony with the
appetites of every one present. It was indeed a great speech. ·
On the morning of the eventful day of which I write, the "early bird," out look·
ing for worms, might have observed at North :i:oint dock a group of eigh~ 1?en, .who,
except for their lofty and independent bearing, might not. have_ ~n distingm~hed
from the "longshoremen" who congregate in that immediate v1crn1ty. These eight
men were the "working force of Past Masters" who had volunteered for the labors
of the day; and here, under their watchful supervision, were being gathered th~ materials which were to make up the bountiful repast. I would be glad to describe .the
scene as it appeared on that lovely morning; but, as they all had left before the writer
of this arrived, it must be left to the imagination of the reader.

1cenes and incidents which occurred during the delightful voyage; but, in consequence
of my having gone over early in the morning, I find some difficulty in doing
lt, and can only say that all arrived in due time at the place appointed, with more
appetite in proportion to the number of men than was ever before exhibited on the
olassio shores of Old Saucelito. Consequently the first course, consisting of stacks
of corned beef, cords of boiled ham, and no end of roast chicken, soon, " like the
baseless fabric of a vision, left not a wreck behind."
With appetites" conquered but not subdued," and with impatient longings, the
waiting host witnessed the laying down of the Clam-Bake; and 'tis safe to say that no
corner stone wa.s ever laid with ceremonies so impressive and amid surroundings so
awe-inspiring. As no language of mine could faithfully portray that imp08ing scene,
I will pass on to the next act in this drama of Masonic life on the sea shore. This
was the second course, consisting of a Sea-Bass Chowder prepared in the highest style
of art, and served in a manner that gave to tin plates and iron spoons a dignity which
the silver ware of the rich could never reach. And here I may be allowed to say that,
could as ample justice be done to the report of those proceedings, as was bestowed
upon that chowder, this paper would be one of, the most brilliant efforts ever
appended to the transactions of this Grand Lodge.
Then followed an intermission of an hour, which was profitably spent in social
intercourse and discussing the merits of the refreshments at the stand presided over
by Bro. OsOAR LEWIS. Then came the announcement that the time had 'arrived for
the un'llailing of the Olam-Bake. In a moment the excitement became intense, and it
was only by the determined military bearing of Grand Commander BRAVES, promptly
assisted by the pious remonstrances of Past Grand High Priest ABELL, that o. quiet
and extended circle was formed around the steaming and fragrant pyramid.
Order ·having been at last restored, Grand Master BROWNE was invited by the
Master of the Ceremonies to make a few brief and impertinent remarks, in order to
give the thing a tone which it might not otherwise possess; and this is what the
Grand Master said, or should have said:" lllustrious Brother BROMLEY:-! greet you, and, as the Worshipful Master of
'Clam-Bake Lodge,' permit me t() congratulate you upon the complete success of
this, the first meeting of you1• new and nourishing organization. You have covered
yourself with glory as with a garment, and your subordinates have shown themselves
worthy of their chief. I must confes~ tliet I am taken somewhat by surprise in being
called upon to make an opening speech upon this delightful occasion; yet I do most
assuredly appreciate the honor, and I only regret that I am not better prepared to do
jnstice to the subject. I will say, however, thitt those whom you see around you
have known you long and well, and have ever honored your virtues and admired
your heroic deeds. But to'-day has been exhibited the crowning glory of your accomplishments, and we all feel bound to you with links strong as the Iron of which our
spoons are made and fragrant as the sausage link which now steams np from yon
architectural pile, and which admonishes me to close by wishing success to you and
to CLAM BAKE I.00011."
In response to the foregoing, Bro. BROMLEY gave utterance to his pent up emotions in the fo llowing words:-

1877.]

The Grand Olam~Bolce at Old 8atUCelito.
