I

"Brethren, you will bear witness to the becoming modesty with which I have
liRtened to the complimentary remarks of Grand Master BROWNE, and I feel that it
would be doing an injustice to him. as well a• to lllyself, did I not acknowledge that
those remarks are not only truthful j)nt well deserved. I think I can safely say
that no Lodge wit!Jin this jurisdiction was ever instituted under such glorious
auspices as Olam-Bake Lodge. Its future is bright andlbe&utiful, and its success is
beyond a peradventure. It is written that 'he who ronnded St. Peter's dome
builded better ti1an he knew;' and he who called into existence the first ' clambake' gave, unconsciously, to a world lying in wickedness, the germ of Rn humanizing influence which will be felt 'until the la8t syllable of recorded time.' Hh name
should be immortalized. if we only knew what it was; but, being thus in ignorance,
we will drink to his memory as soon as we get the conveniences.
"And now, brethren, where. in a)] this wide world could we look upon another such
a scene as this? 'History repeats itself.' Centuries have passed away since the
building of the Temple, and to-day we have built a 'Clam-Bake'- a coincidence as
remarkable as the resemblance is striking. Here are gathered together the admirers
ct the one and the lovers of the other. Many of these have .quaffed their beer with
the poor and lowly, and a few of us have sipped our Roetlerer at the tables of ~he
great and good. Yet, the tables of a king never bore upon their groaning leaves
such delicious viands as wm soon be revealed to your longing eyes. Beneath this
sea-weed mound lies buried all our present hope~. Here the luscious clam opens to ·
welcome it.i destroyer, and no more will it~ mysterious hydraulics guide the mooneyed Chinee to its hiding place. The high-toned sweet potato, as it nestles in it.e
new sea-weed home, disd~ins :Murphy, the common-tater; while the sweet. green
com reverses the order of things, and communicates from ear to mouth. The fragrant tho' doubtful sausage gives forth no bark if' yon utter no growl. Here the ·
delicious lamb-chop seems to &ay that, 'as the lamb-skia is to labor, so is the lambchop to refreshment;' and here the gay and festive chicken, having laid its last lay,
is laitl away to lay no more forever. All the~e things now lie entombed within this
sea-weed sarcophagus, awaiting the signal of the Grand Master to be resurrected
imd to show to us that, as martyrs in a good cause, they have not lived and died in
vain. And now, brethren. we bide the Master'• bidding."
The expected signal w11S not then given ; but insread thereof. there was a mys~
rious lull in the proceedings, when Father SAMUEL GRAVES advanced to the center of
the expectant circle, and thus delivered him>elf :"Brethren, let us allbe thankful that we have lived to see this day. For more
than sixty years I have been a Mason. I have rejoiced in the prosperity of the Craft,
and when the dark clouds of adversity rolled over it, I have never forsaken ,it •.
Through storm and sunshine I have never lost sight of the' Beacon Light of Hope; '
yet of all the varied ~cenes of my Masonic life, the joyous events of this day will be
among those most happily remembered. I shall ever look back upon this oocaeion·
with feelings of ple11Sure only equalea by the anticipation of ' Clam-Bakes' in the
time to come. It is not now my province to make a speech, and I will only add tha~
I take great pleasure in introdncin~ to you one whose name is as 'familiar to you all
118 household words '-Bro. CHARLES L. WIGGIN, our Deputy Grand Mil.Ster-who I
know has something of interest to impart to you."
Bro. WIGGIN the~ approached the center, heading a procession consisting of himself, and followed by four brethren bearing a table, on which rested an elegant morocco casket containing a full set of ivory-handled cutlery. Addressing himself to
the" Clam-Bake Archirect," he spoke as follows:" Bno. BROMLEY : A very pleasant duty has just been assigned to me, and I hasten
to perform it, as the fragrant odors which fill the air admonish me that no idle words of:
mine should delay the more important matters of which they give u~ notice. Your
fellow-members of the PAsT MASTERS' AssoOIATION, desirous of giving expression to

their feelings of the high esteem in which you are held by them. ask your acceptance
of this testimonial. It is in accordance with the ' eternal fitness of things' that one,
whose •well-earned fame bath spread so far and wide' for building up chowders and
laying down cl~-bakes, should find the reward of merit in this appropriate casket of
outlery. This keen.edged carver, we trust, will enable you to carve your way to a brilliant future, while this splendid fork is significant of that virtue which we hope you
may always possess the wherewith to practice, and thus be enabled to fork over
whatever may be due. This ponderous Rteel will constantly remind you of your many
friends now in the penitentiary, and of the necessity for avoiding such company in
the future. Your well-known temperance principles will of course prevent this cork1crew from being of any service to you; yet you will, no doubt, be pleased sometimes to
Joan it to a friend who may ne&i it; and now sincerely hoping that your dinner and
dessert for all time to come may be eqn&l to the twenty-four knives here provided.
I tender this memento in the name of the PAST MASTERS' ABSOOIATION, and with it
their kindest and best wishes for your prosperity and future happiness.''
It was evident that this very pleasing episode had taken Bro. BROMLEY completely
by surprise. and be seemed for a moment to be somewhat bewildered; but, recovering himself, he gave his hat to the Grand Master, and handing his rake to SAM
HALL, it was thus that he responded:" Bro. WIGGIN and Members of the Past Masters' Association:-.
"I feel tho.t this is one of the most trying moments of my life-time. Had this magnitlcent testimonial been discovered amid the steaming deposits of this Clam-Bake,
my surprise could not have been greater; and now you don't know how proud I feel ,
nor bow powerless I am to do justioe to the occasion. I can on!)' say that I accept
the splendid gift with a heart brim-full to overtlowing with gratitude to the generous
givers, and with the hope that all our future associations in life may be as bright and
untarnished as the glittering content.a of the beautiful casket. Thanking you for
this, your kiqd remembrance, I now invite you all to witness the unveiling of the
Olam-Bake."
The disch&rgeof a cannon on board the yacht J.C. Cous1Ke, Bro. Commodore MENZIES, commanding-moored in the offing-was the signal for the uncovering. To de,
soribe the scene which followed would be a task difficult to accomplish. Sufficient be
it here to say that never was patient waiting more bountifully rewarded; never were
viands more superb-everything "done to a charm;" and the Clam-Bake in all its
appointments was a pronounced success.
An immense Crab and Crawflsh Salad, skillfully and artistically prepared by Bro.
Louis COHN, "rounded oft'" the feast, and blending, as it did, in ono harmonious
whole the vast variety of materials of which it was composed, it was a fitting emblem
of an harmonious masonic gathering which will long be remembered with sincerest
pleasure by all those who participated.
Tho return to the city was ma.de joyous by an abundance of sentiment, songs ,
and speeches. Arriving at the wharf all safe, without tho slightest accident to mar
the day's enjoyment, a hearty and unanimous vote of thanks was tendered to Past
Grand Master GEORGE 0. PEBKJNB, to Commodore STEWART MENZIES. Pe.st Master.
to the Saucelito Ferry Company, and to the" working force, " for their generous and
very valuable assistance in making this, the JJ.rst meeting of Otam-Bake Lodge, an
unqualified and unparalelled succcess.
Thus ended the day. Long may we cherish its pleasant memories and cultivate
the feeling of Masonic Broth&hOOd which such fraternal gatherings are calculated to inspire. Bo mote it be.
Fraternally yours,
GEORGE T. BROMLEY,
Master of Olam·Bake Lodge and G. O. B.

Twenty-ninth Annual Communication.
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California. commenced its twenty-ninth Annual Communication at the Masonic Temple, in the city of San Francisco, on
Tuesday, the eighth day of October, A. L. 5878, at 10 o'clock, A. M.

The Grand Ma.star then delivered his Anntia.I Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows :BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORl!IA : In presenting a third annual message, in which will appear the most important of
my official acts during the year, exhibiting the general condition of Masonry within
the jurisdiction and recommending certain l egislation, I do not propose to deal in
vieWll of impracticable and impossible conditions, but in facts, unpleasant facts
though they may be.

The defense of Masonry may be safely left to itself, while its beauties and attra.otions, either mystica.!, sentimentlll, or social, will have a masterly portrayal in the
impassioned eloquence of our brother, the Grand Orator. He will bring flowera,
whose color and fragrance will enrapture the senses. I give you 'fruit-the halfripened with the mellowed-the savory with the unpalaMible.
Faulta may be found in the best systems, and irregularities exist in tile best
methods. Men do things in opposition to original resolution, and when done are
astonished at the act. Men, however excellent in goodness, have moments of weakness-moments when the clearness of their moral perceptions is clouded. So societies
like individuals, are purer· some days than others. ·
'
Certain Masons have erroneous ideas as to the true intent of practical Masonry,
and these ideas, when entertained by the outer world; become, in its estimation, facts.
Now it is not a fact that it is a system of benefits and endowments, that it is a mem-·
bership to promote business interests, or that in any way its workings recognize its
receipts as loans, from which a proportionate benefit, in manner of a return, may be
derived. It is purely and simply a system of practical charity in its highest sense,
disbursing its funds for tho relief of the poor and suffering, without specill.o amount
or defined allowance, but corresponding in sums to the actual want.
It is not a fa.ct that it is a club or plaoe merely of social gathering, an assemblage
of boon companions for conviviality or selfish gratification. It is a companionship
of brothers, united by mystic bonds, which, while affording gratill.cation to the social
feelings, fh1de new motives and added obligations to rectitude of life, and to the
practice of. the genuineness of benevolence: a aooiety for instruction, for the promotion of public and private virtues; for the encouragement of social improvement r
in every form , for the enhancement and refinement of common life, and for the
advocacy of reformatory eohemee with intent to cope sncoessfully with sociiJ.l
mischief.
It is not a fact that it is co-eqnal with, or takes the place of, religion. It is a perfeot
system of morality, of no rui.tionality, and, as such, is the conservator of religion. It
pr~greeses with the highest civilization, and, by its propagation of human sympathy,
nmtes men of all nations in one common bond of amity. Masonry has no creed but
faith; it cherishes hope and fears not, and employs charity in place of persecution.
~!though discountenanced by suspicion, and excommunicated by jealousy, it con·
tmues to be recognized as a steadfast and powerful instrument for the promotion of
peace and good will among men.
·
There is a popular belief that Masons, when aoting as judges, jurors, or citizens.
frequently permit the guilty members of the Ore.ft to escape such justice as they
would measure to those not members of the Order. An eminent officer of the government addressed me on this subject, and although believing that such conduct was
in .opposition to the law of Masonry, yet he had no·faith that it was adopted by man7
as the rule for their guidance.' Not long since one of the Ore.ft was tried in this
State for murder. The evidence adduced was su~haswould authorize oonviction, yet
the jury failed t.o agree, nine being in favor of a verdict for murder in the first
degree, and three for it in the 'second degree. Of the nine, four were Masone-of the
·thr~, two were MtlBODB ; and the public generally believed that the disagreement was
occasioned by Masonic influence in behalf of the accused, because he was a Mason.
If the brothers who adhered to the lesser finding were controlled by the fact simply
that the accused was a Mason, then it is hardly necessary to inform yon that the;r
failed to do their duty as jurors, and had no precedent for such action in Masonic
law.
. :MBSOn~ acknowledges .the 11Upremacy of the government, enforce11 resi;iect for the
01vil magistrates, and enjoins upon its followers &n obedience to !&w, to be exemplary
in the discharge of civic duties, and to be quiet and peaceable citizens. It does not array itself against law, or seek, however remotely, to shield the guilty from punishment.

It has its ~wn trial.a, and convict.a offenders who have been acquitt.ed in civil couri,,

·
There is a disposition manifested by some Lodges to .~umnlate mon~y, apparently for the sako of 110cumu!&tion, and to avoid, as far llB circumstances will permi.~.
its disbursement in the care of the sick and burial of the dead. If the duty can
be performed by others upon whom the recipient may have no cla~me, ~tis. moHt ~­
tingly acquiesced in ; the motive in such instances being how to avoid do mg 1t. This 18
a.n unpleasant fact, but its truth cannot be truthfully denied. I fail to understand
the object of our institution, if it be only to exhibit its principles in words, rather
than in administering to ea.oh other's necessities unselflehly. The Persians say: "I
) consider him as my friend who takes me by the hand in the season of adversity and
distress." This is Masonry-the other is not. Lodges shoUld care for their own, ~d
see that their burdens be not imposed upon others. Accumulate as much as you deaue,
but make the accumulation for the purpose of doing the most good. If the treasury
be exhausted then have recourse to personal donations ; if this be impraoticahle,
then surrender your charter. The suffering will suffer, and the dead will remain
unburied, if dependent only upon Masonic profel!Sions. The truth ofte~ hur~, ~ut
pain is frequently employed to cure a diseased numbness. Yon who especially dislike
the veneering of Masonry are willing to receive the truth.
The meagre attendance at the funeral 'or a brother, which not unfrequently happens, is another deplorable fact. This remark is applicable mainly to Masons who
reside in large communities. To pay the last sad tribute of respect to a deceased
brother, to evince to his family and friends the estimation had of hie character and
the regret ex}ierienced at his loss, and to exhibit to the public that the brotherhood
performs that which it professes, are duties not t.o be omitted without injury to the
Fraternity. It may necessitate some inconvenience; it requires a little time to accompany the departed brother to hie resting-place, there to cast the evergreen and give
the f&rewe!l; but the inconvenience will soon be forgotten, and the time will not be
regretted, in the consciousness of having done unt.o him that which you would have
done unto you when the ending comes. To honor the dead is commendable; to
ignore the dead is lamentable. Masonry inculcates the first, and condemns the
last.

Mention is made that in three Lodges no minute-book had been kept, and, in
consequence of having a Secretary who did not attend the meetings, an irregularity
occurred in the record of the proceedings and the non-receipt for moneys, which
~bvionsly produ~ .an eml;>arrassment, or rather _
a confusion. The books will be kept
m the future, and it is to be expected that experience will be efficacious in the selection
of a competent and faithful Secretary. When this officer, either from indifference or
inability, doee not perform his duty, he should resign; and if he does not, then he
ought to be displaced, and a suital.Jle successor appointed. .The welfare of a Lodge
depends materially on the kind of Secretary it pos•erses; end if the brethren persist
in electing an incompetent person, then the Master ought to correct the situation
without delay, in which course .he may be assured of receiving your approbation.
Mention is made of the inability to assemble the brethren for the purpose of
instruction, although the officers manifesta desire to perfect themselves in the work.
The brethren say that they aro interested in the Lodge and wish for its prosperity, but
have no time to devote to instruction; consequently, when called upon to fill a
vacancy, they blunder through the work in a manner embarrassing to themselves and
humiliating to the Lodge. A poor encouragement, surely, to zealous officel'll I Is it .
.e:l:traordinary that ability and interest gi~e place to inefficiency and lukewarmness?
The .brethren probably consider that they have discharged their duty in annually
electmg officers whom they regard as responsible for the condition of the Lodgeforgetting that the officel'll elected, in tho execution of duty, need their presence, if
not for counsel, at leaat for the encouragement derived from their exhibition of constancy and zeJl. Is it not evident that officers will be stimulated to acquire proficiency in the work if properly aided by the brethren? Until this have accomplishment, only in exceptional cases will the execution of the ritual have the correctnese
of the original 1tnd authorized text. Unless Lodge meetings are made interesting the
number of non-affiliates will increase. If the subject is dwelt upon, the explanation
is to be had in its importance.
Mention is made that certain Masters did not apply for the certificate of qualification requisite for installation. Had the information been received at the proper
time you would have known the reason for this disobedience of your order. Now the
the fact can only be presented.
Mention is mnde cf a Lodge remaining closed for two months on account of the
absence of the Master. The question naturally arises-wher e was the Senior Warden?
As a Lodge is always supposed to have a presiding officer, the absence of the Master
is no excuse for its inaction.
Mention is made of a Lodge the proceedings of which had not been entered in the
record book since 1868, said records not having been signed by the Master since that
date. Again, the Lodge had no complete roll of members, and a few of the members
had not signed the by-laws. You may well be astonished at this culpable negligence.
Oomment is unnecessary, but the inexcusable carelessness will have immediate cor
rection.

Mention is made of the unmasonic conduct of a Lodge faction, and of the matter
or Lodge incorpora.tion, which will be treated farther on.
Mention is made of the use of proselytism. Surprise can hardly express the effect
or the announcement, and yet the assertion. Masonry, in its sublime independence,
ha.s a principle peculiar to itself. It admits of no proselytes. It rules that its followers must not solicit adherents or seek convel'ts by heralding its virtues ~ its good
deeds, when public property, are a sufficient advertisement. le a brother so misinformed of its principles that he fails to discriminate between right and wrong? Doea
he regard Masonry through a medium so discolored and distorted, not to· know that
the making of converts is a Masonic malpractice? Yet truth, it seems, compels the
admission of the fact. It is prohibitive and admonitory, a denial direct, absolute, and
complete. A brother can find ample work in correcting the errors and developing
the capabilities of his Lodge, ~thout seeking to disturb its foundations.
Mention is made of a caae where an objection by a member having been made to
the 09nferring of the .second and third degrees, the degrees were conferred during
the pendency of the objection. Here the Master, by a summary action, violated the
provisions of Section 6, Article Ill, Part III, of the Constitution. This is inexcusable. Even if the statute was less emphatic in language, whenever an objecLtml ia
made it should be regarded that the benefit of a doubt ought to · be given to the
Lodge. Such action, had it been officially 1·eported at the time, would ha'\'e occasioned discipline.
·

quite enough.

I have now officially visited every one of the thirty-two districts of our large jurisdiction, including that at the Hawaiian Islanda. Some of the districts have been
visited thrice, many twice, but all once. When one considers the extent of the State
of California, which embraces nearly as many square miles 118 a.re .comprised in the
New England and Middle States combined, or, in other words, a territory sufficiently
la.rge to form twenty-four States of the size of Massachusetts, one will better understand the number of mil~ traveled in making these visitations. Jf also it be considered that, to reach many of the looelities, it required not only transit by water, but
over rough and tediously long roads, one will better understand the fatigue endured
and the time required. Fatigue and time, however, are not to be arrayed in opposition to the pleasure enjoyed, the iilstruotion imparted, and .the information obtained,
resulting from an individual llSBOciation with the brethren, listening to their grievances, reconciling di1ferences, establishing closer relations; and having an exact
knowledge of the community, its resources and probable future, in connection with
the fraternity. It is true that the duty performed in making these visitations was
self-imposed, yet it is a duty which I think pertains to the office of the Grand Master,
a.nd I sincerely trust that it may have continuance.
I could well employ the language used in my la.st message, regarding the fraternity throughout the jurisdiction, were it not a reiteration, eo closely does the condition
of the past year approximate to that of the pt·esent. The catises of financie.J, commercial, and industrial depreseiou having been but partly removed, the amount of
work done by the Lodges is not substantially di1ferent, although the indications are

ProPcaed amendments for the establishment of life-membership were presented,
hampered with conditions. It wa.s provided that, in the event of the· death of the
holder of a life-membership, the sum originally paid should be paid to his widow,
heirs, or assigns; in the event of a.withdrawal from the Lodge, one-half of said ~um
should be refunded to the withdrawing life-membei·; and, in the event of an eipuls1on,
the whole amount to be forfeited by himself and heirs. These were not approved,
although it was alleged in · support of them that a neighboring Lodge had e. lifemembership with similar conditions, which had been approved by the Grand Lodge.
I am in favor of life-membership. but, whenever this project is entertained, it
should consist simply of the payment of tne sum determined, without conditions,
save the perpetual ·exemption from dues and the issuing of a suitable certificate.
This is the system adopted by some of our Lodges, and its very simplicity and effectiveness seem to make it unsusceptible of improvement. I am also in favor of the
establishment of new Lodges on the principle of life-membership, the moneys thus
received to be funded, and the interest derived therefrom. together with the fees, to
be available tor ordinary expenses and for che.nty. I invite your attention to the
subject of life-membership, and recommend yuur approval of a. plan which, when. .
ever a.dopted by Lodges, will have unifo~mity in. the Code of By-Laws.

In Los Angei,es Lodge, No. 42, several months ago, charges were preferred against
a member and a trial ensued. It came to my knowledge· that at the trial one of the
commissioners, at the suggestion of another, acted as counsel for the accused and
conducted the defense. An acquittal followed. I was asked by the accuser if an
appeal might not be taken, to which I replied that it was not necessary, as the proceedings were illegal and void, and there need be no delay in instituting a new trial.
Time paased and nothing was done, and again my attention was called to the case, the
record of the trial having been transmitted. On August ninth I informed the Master
that the proceedings of the former trial were set aside, and directed him to cause
charges to be preferred anew, and that a new trial occur as early as practicable.
In my message of last year was reported the question, "Would the 8ecretary ofa
Lodge be justified in refusing the dues of a suspended member from persons who might
be deemed aa having personal interests in collecting and paying the same, even without
the knowledge or consent of the suspended member?" I answered at length, in substance, that the reading of the law necessitated the opinion that the restoration of a
delinquent by the payment of arrearages and dues u by his action, sanction, or
knowledge, although custom authorized the payment to be made without either of
the implied conditions. The question bore relation to my decision of the preceding year, which was reversed by the Committee on Jurisprudence, (and the
reversal agreed to by you,) in the case of a suspended brother dying before the payment of arrearages and dues was made, although the money was raised and sent
before death, etc. I then proposed the question, "Does the law intend that the payment of dues and arrearages shall be the act, directly or indirectly, of the suspended
member, or may it be performed without his knowledge or consent?" This was
referred to the Committee on Jurispmdence, who failed to report. This, in its essential outline, was the question which, as applied in the well-remembered case of the
restoration of a brother after death, influenced my decision, which was not approved
by you. My own belief, with every respectful consideration for your non-concurrence, remains the same. In this belief I am sustained by Masonic jurists in other
jurisdictions; and, as a doubt may reasonably exist in your minds, I have to beg your
indulgence for presenting the matter anew, and to earnestly request that it may
again appear for the decision of the Committee on Jurisprudence.
When a non-affiliate of six months or more applies for membership, he will pay
a sum equivalent to six months' dues and the affiliation fee, if any. If he be rejected, according to my reading of Section 1, Article II, Part V, of the Constitution, he
places himself in good standing for six months; and if he applies again within the said
six months he would be req aired to pay the affiliation fee only. I do not think, however,
that the writer of the section contemplated such interpretation, but expected the nona.ffiliate, after rejection, to be required to pay the six months' dues in addition to the
affiliation fee, as in the first instance. Since several Masters have arrived at a conclusion like mine, the matter is presented for your decision.

I am in favor of life-membership. but, whenever this project 1s entertained, it

save the 'perpetual exemption from dues and the issu_ing of a. sui~~le certificate.
This is the system adopted by some of our Lodges, and its very s1mph?ity and effect- .
iveness seem to make it unsusceptible of improvement. I am also in favor of the
establishment of new Lodges on the principle of life-membership, the moneys thus
received to be funded, and the interest derived therefrom. together with the fees, to
be available tor ordinary expenses and for charity. I invite your atten~on to the
subject of life-membership, and recommend your approval of a plan which, whenever adopted by Lodges, will have uniformity in the Code of By-Laws.

llurprised at the existence of an incorporated Lodge in our jurisdiction, I asked for
the time and particulare of the act of incorporation, and if by the consent of the
Grand Master, and waa informed that the act happened in 1876, during my administration. I replied that the subject of incorporation waa presented to the Grand
Lodge by Paet Grand Master PERXINB, but received no action; that in my la.st annual
mees&ge it was again brought before the Grand Lodge and referred to the Committee
on Jurisprudence, who, owing to the importance of the matter, asked for and obtained
permission to defer their report until the present Communication; and that, under
the circumstances, 1 had to require Lezington Lodge, without unnecessary delay, t-0
take the requisite measm·ee for disincorporation. Subsequently, I was notified that a
committee had been appointed by the Lodge with instructions to proceed to disincorporate, of which, when accomplished, I should be informed.
I am opposed to the incorporation of Lodges, believing the act to be subversive of
the principles of :Masonic government and in opposition to the prosperity of the
Order. By it the State becomes paramount in authority, annihilates the appellate
ju~ction of the Grand Lodge and Grand :Master, and subordinates the :Masonic to
the civil authorities. By it ·a positive antagonism is arrayed against the self-management of the internal affairs, and, in its ultimate, general, and permanent effects, the
Lodge would be lees real, less stable, lees solid. An independent corporation may
be formed for the purpose of holding the title of real estate or investing money,
which would be controlled by the Courts, but no Court ought to control the affa.irs of
a Masonic Lodge.
There may be other incorporated Lodges within our jurisdiction. Consequently
you should determine at this Communication the expediency of having Lodges corporate and politic, the practicability of having a divided allegiance, and whether the act
would be at variance with the essential character of Masonry, for the guidance of
Lodges that may have already Incorporated, and that n9 doubt may exist in the
future ae to the "fill of the Grand Lodge; and, also, to define the manner of election,
and the duties, powers, and succession of trustees in Lodges not incorporated.
I am fully convinced that the Committee on Finances ought to be made a standing committee. At present, being a regular committee appointed at the commencement of each Annual Communication, sufficient time ie not allowed to have its duties
satisfaetorily performed for a report to be made until the last days of the eeesion,
when, usually, a large number of the members &1·e absent. It is highly important
ihat the financial condition and proposed amount of appropriations should be presented at the earliest practicable hour, in order that ample time may be given to deliberate and pronounce upon the report. I therefore recommend that measures be
taken to constitute the Committee on Finances a standing committee, and that when
so constituted, it shall be required to meet at the office of the Grand Seoretaey on the
Saturday preceding the annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, and examine the
books, papers, and accounts of the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary, and report
the result thereof to the Grand Lodge on the second day of the session in each year.

Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary, and for the sum of five thousand dollars each
by the Trustees of the Reserve Fund, in October last, and they received mv approval.
The Grand Treasurer will present a report, in detail, respecting the management
of the Reserve Fund, aa derived from the several reports of its Trustees, and, also,
as exhibiting its actual condition.

A member of Monterey Lodge, No. 217, in good standing, was imprisoned at Auburn, awaiting a secoy.d trial on the charge of murder. I was asked if his. family
and himself were entilled to receive assistance from that l.odge. My reply wa.e that,
if he was still a member of the Lodge, and not under suspension for non·payment
of dues, or for other cause, he must be regarded as in good standing, and, as euch,
entitled to be the recipient of all the rights, privileges, and charities of the Lodge;
that the fact of his incarceration did not remove the good standing, no charges having been preferred against him, since in equity, he might be supposed to be innoceni
. until proven to be guilty; and that he, his wife, and children had a right to receive the
attention of the Lodge. Assistance was afforded the family by ]i}ureka Lodge, No.
16. Montm-ey Lodge 'tas informed of the fact, and was asked for repayment, as well
as for instructions for the future. That Lodge remitted a sma.11 sum, announced its
impecunious condition, and declared the.tit could furnish no further aid. The family
were in distress and had to be relieved, either by the fraternity or by the public.
.FJureka Lodge saved the fraternity from reproach by ministering to the family,
assisted by Granite Lodge, No. 222. Recently, the second trial of the acc1JSed
occurred, resulting in a verdict of guilty of murder in the second degree. The· case
is peculiarly unhappy. A grave charge was made against a member of a LOcl.ge,
which continued to hold him in good standing, and was consequently obliged to .care
for the distreseed family. The Lodge could not or did not supply the neceslJtliq
relief; but, fortunat.ely, the family did not suffer, their wants having been supplied
·by other Lodges. You will probably concur in the opinion that a restitution shouU
be made to these Lodges, and if so, in what manner? Monterey Lodge asserts i1' ·
inability; the Grand Lodge can give relief-will it? The case stands for your disposal.
This is our twenty-ninth Annual Communication, and yet the Grand Lodge has no
fund set apart for charity. True, it has a reserve fund-to what extent? Does not
its history show that it would have been better were it a charity fund? Ought the
Grand Lodge to accumulate money simply for the gratification of having an overflowing treasury? If some of its excess of funds is not to be applied to the relief of
the necessitous, then let the dues of its subordinates be lessened 'in order that their
charities may be enlarged. Is there not a simplicity and directness in this assertion?
Need there be any extended remarks to convince you of its desirability-may I not
say of its feasibility- if you will but act? I can find abundant reasons for, and each
. year affords accumulated evidences of, the propriety of 2stablishing a Relief or Charity
Fund. Certainly it can be done, and assuredly, too, it is of the essence of :Masonry
to do it. For the third time, then,'! make an earnest appeal in its behalf, recognizing always that our deeds are poorer than our wills, yet that what is true will ulti·
mately assert itself; and, as there is a sayinll' in England " that patience and perseverance will make a bishop of his reverence," I feel that patience and perseverance
will soon secure the fulfillment of this long cherished project.
l come now to a subject which, judging from the ;Masonic communities visited in

422

Prooee,dings of the

[Oct. 8,

various parts of the State, is of common agitation-the reduction of the expenses of
the Grand Lodge. " Whether a wind be warm or cold it serves to fan a kindled fire."
It is claimed that our Grand Lodge is more expensive, proportionately, than that of
other jurisdictions, and that the reduction should apply to dues, salaries, and the
lopping off of some ordinary expenditures. Briefly, a general reduction is proposed.
It is certainly a self-evident proposition that no useless expenditure ought to be tolerated, and that the amount of appropriations should be commensurate with the exigencies of the occasion. I am, as formerly expressed, in favor of any retrenchment
that will not conflict with the proper working of the Grand Lodge. Year after year,
to a greater or less extent, the cry of retrenchmem is heard; and year after year you
have sought for the remedy which has always been in your hands, and you have persistingly refused to apply it. Is it because you recognized that there is in every case
a great interval between theory and practice? Is it that you feared that the application
of the remedy might be too experimental for a salutary and corrective effect? Year
after year you approve the appropriations recommended by the Finance Committee,
and, surely, you have no right to complain because the Grand Officers simply perform
their duty in causing the appropriations to be expended in exact conformity with
your instructions. You alone can decide the amount of money to be disbursed, and
you alone are responsible if the expenses of the Grand Lodge are excessive. Here,
you should speak the same as you have spoken to me. Be not deterred because you
are unaccustomed to public discussion; we want facts, not eloquence-acts, not
complaints-in order that we may be able in some degree to estimate the proposed
retrenchment, honestly examine and sufficiently understand the condition, and, with
no other motive than fidelity to honest conviction, deliberate and determine.
At our last session I suggested the propriety of appropriating a sum to be employed
by the Grand Master, in case of any calamity happening to other communities by pestilence, fire, or any other cause, for the relief of distressed brethren in such communities. The suggestion was not approved. A calamity more direful than could have
been anticipated came, and I acted as though the appropriation had been made. For
weeks the accounts daily received from the pestilence-stricken districts in the South
have familiarized you with the desolation, distress, dismay, and death attending the
r!lyilges of that most virulent disease-yellow fever. .But of all this, that which
has jmpressed me, most touchingly is an editorial written by one who, on the folloWmg day fell a victim, and which gave a sad realization to his gloomy forebod:thgs. ,Those of you who, like myself, have witnessed the frightful results of the
fever pl~gue, will fully understand the vivid, unexaggerated description:·{:
"AVALANCHE OFFICE, MEMPHIS, Midnight, August 29th.
We are doomed. It is hard as we write in this dark, dismal night of death, not to
realize the full meaning of that brief sentence. It is ~ard for !1-ny m~ of the few left
in this city of sorrows not to take the sentence to himself with a pamfully personal
application as the sentence of death. Scarcely any are left but those who are cr~w~­
ing down personal care in the noble pnrpose of others' good. To them death? if it
comes will have the sweetening conso1ation that it is brought by as noble a service as
the GOd of heaven; as man on earth, ever looked upon. To die for man is to imitate
the grandest event in the history of our globe. It is to imitate the death of the
Saviour of the world. The rain falls slowly, the storm of the afternoon having sunk
into a dismal, solemnly sad drizzle, as though the heavens themselves were touc!ied
to tears at the sight of so much human misery. The rattle of an occasional vehicle
along the silent street tell_s that a me.mber of some ~en~volent society is hastening. to
minister to the sick or dymg. That is all. All else is silent, deathly, and awful, with
naught but the rattle of the water from the roof into the gutter; and that has the
ominous gurgle of a death rattle in the human throat.
Seventy dead and at least one hundred and twenty-five new cases. God help
us l If hope wer~ not worn to a skeleton-if she had not taken herself to prayer-we
might find a spark to kindle a weak glow of light in this impenetrable darkness, and
expect that the heavy shower of to-day would wash from air, from gutter, and from
bayou, a part of the foul pestilential air which is breeding death.
The horrors of the hour cannot be told, even if the heart did not sicken at the
task. They are horrors such as make a hell on earth ; such as make life almost a

unexpectedly has recently taken from ns two of the honored members of this Grand

For years Bro. WILLUM EDWARD MoODY gave his labors to the fraternity, in the
Lodge, in the Ohapter, ln the Oonricil, and, by virtue of his position as Assistant Grand
Secretary, in the Grand Lodge. How well he execute() his various dntles is known to
the office.rs of these several bodies. Though assailed by an insidious disease,yet with
fai~ing strength and haggard countenance, he faithfully remained at his post until ,
stricken by the fetal band of paralysis, he succumbed, and Jost strength, conscious.
ness , and finally life. His nature was of a gentle, amiable, humane quality, with
frank cordiality of heart, and genial manners. He knew the world, and had expe·
rienced its trials, its temptations, and its disappointments. The mystery of life to him
has been revealed; to us that mystery remains unsolved , and continnes so inexplic·
able ln its tangled mass, that, tolling ever throughout all there may be of Jiffi, with
all our own soul and strength, we cannot unravel its sorely twisted threads.
"As in the autumn time the leaves fall off,
First one and then another, till the branch
Unto the earth surrenders' all its spoils ..,
On the day following. the obsequies of Bro. MooDY, suddenly died Bro. HENRY
~UNTLEY HAIGHT, ex:Governor of the State, and Grand Orator of this Grand Lodge
m 187L Eloquent eulogies have been pronounced In memory of this distinguished
executive, able lawyer, and most estimable citizen, whose administration was cbarac·
terized by honor and purity, whose " great duties were greatly done/' and whose
integrity, which nothing could corrupt, and whose independence, which nothing could
s~ake., secured to him the confidence of the public, and made him trusted 11like by
friend and opponent. We eulogize hi~ as a brother-modest, unselfish, earnest,
and true hearted-with a moral rectitude outllnfng his high character, pure in per·
sonal qualities, with manly force softened by gentleness, pursuing the practical,
active In humanity, sympathetic and charitable. · His habits of life were simple,
temperate, and never snbje9ts of display ; and his excelfencfe• of heart came from a
generous nature. He was a good man, and no tear of bitterness was shed over his
grave.
The certainly of our own mortallty and the uncertainty of earthly affairs are lessons
taught by the death of our brothers, and from these lessons ~e should learn that we
ioo are passing beyond cares, struggles, failures, and snccesses, error and lap'11e, and
even of a certain goodness only divined by each or us In the privacy of our inner·
most, bettermost selves, to the final sleep " iu the windowless palace of rest." As,
in the presence of death, the harsh and bitter features of this or that experie11ce
are gradually obliterated, and memory looks kindly on the past, so in the presence
of life, let us exercise more kindness, more real sympathy, more beneficence, more
forbearance, with a greater desire to help one another, so that, in our " souls' brother·
hood," we may fully renlize that " if Jove is the faith, then friendship is the charity
of life."

20th. A letter from the Grand Secretary General of the Grand Orient of Spain,
dated at Madrid, on the twentieth day of March, 1878, inclosing a communication
from that Grand Body, setting forth the vicissitudes through which it has passed in
consequence of unjustifiable persecutions, and of errors and bad faith on the part of
the clergy and the g.overnment; exhibiting a statement of the prosperity which has
attended it since its reorganization only two years ago ; and soliciting the kindly and
fraternal consideration of our Grand Lodge.
21st. A communication from the Grand Orient of Egypt, dated at Alexandria,
on the fifteenth day of May, 1878, expressive of its horror of wars and of its hope that
the influence of Freemasonry may always hereafter be used for the preservation of
·
peace among the nations.
The Committee on Juri11prudence, in its concluding report r.t the last Annual
Communication, relative to matters presented in the Address of the Grand Master,
stated that ''the subject of the incorporation of Lodges demands more time than the
committee can give at this Communication," and desired that it be referred to the
committee for the present year. It has, therefore, again been plaeed before thatcommittee, as unfinished business, together with the accompanying inquiry as to " the
manner of election' and power of trustees" for the purpose of purchasing and holding property. See pages 22 and 197, proceedings of 1877.
A few other matters, presented in the Address of the Grand Master last year, appear to have escaped the notice of the committee above named ; and they also, as un"
finished business, have ag11.in been thereto referred, as follows:1st. Whether, in a case where a Mason has been duly summoned to appear for
trial, and" remains away,'' but puts in "a plea of guilty through a brother,'' the
· trial should proceed ez parte.
2d. Whether, in a case where a Mason was in prison awaiting trial on a charge
of murder, " the Lodge should at once proceed to have charges preferred against the
prisgner," or should defer action until after trial by the proper criminal court.
Sd. Whether the Secretary of a Lodge "would be justified in refusing the dues
of a suspended member from persons who might be deemed as having personal interests in collecting and paying the same, even without the knowledge or consent of the
suspended member."
4th. Whether a Master should entertain "charges against a brother who had
purchased goods from another brother, and subsequently, although in the possession
of funds, left the country without paying for the articles bought."
5th. Whether Lodges in this State should be permitted to ask for contributions
from Lodges in other jurisdictions for the purpose of organizing relief funds, or for
any other purpose.
6th. Whether, after the reception and approval of a report, a Lodge can expunge
any part thereof?
Since the last Annual Communication, nine special dispensations have been issued
from this office by direction of the Grand Master. Of these, six were to permit reballots upon the petitions of rejected applicants for the degrees, within the period of
prohibition prescribed by the general provisions of our law, sufficient reasons having
been presented therefor; and three were to authorize the elections of officers at times
other than the regular one provided in our Constitution, the necessity for such elections having been made apparent. The action of the several Lodges presenting the
foregoing appears to have been in accordance with the provisions of our laws, and
the petitions, together with such correspondence as relates to them, are herewith
submitted.

o Clinton Lodge, No. 119, to remove its place of meeting from Piety Hill, in the
county of Sh11Bta, to Igo, in the same county.

A communication has been received from Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, at Honolulu,
Hawaiian Islands, praying that the moneys which have been paid into the Grand
Lodge treasury from the funds of the extinct Maui Lodge, No. 223, be donated to
the charity fund of the Lodge first named. The reasons presented for au.ch peti·
tion are that "that money was raised entirely from Masons resident in these
Islands;" that" it would seem only just that it should be expended for charity in
our midst;'' and that the numerous ~alls for assistance to which Hawaiian Lodge is
peculiarly subjected, induces its members to think that this petition is not.unreasonable. The paper is herewith submitted.

The Address of Grand Master PALllER J. PILLANS-& brief but well-written document-was presented and read by the Grand Secretary. He expressed hie regret at
bis inability to attend this Communication of the Grand Lodge, and congratolated
the Fraternity on the" better dawning for Masonry in the State. Though but few
Lodges bad been formed, yet several of those which had become dormant had been
recalled to life and vigor." He bad isaued dispensations for the formation of fivo
new Lodges.
The Grand Master of Wisconsin having complained of the violation of his jurisdiction, in conferring the degrees upon a rejected candidate from that State, the
Grand Master, ou Inquiry, llndin~ the complaint well founded, had made suitable
apologies, and the good feeling b~tween the two jurisdictions continues.
Several of the decisions of the Grand Master are pub:ished, but we find none
calling for special comment.
Past Grand Master JAMES MCCALEB WILEY, a veteran Mason, having died dnring
the year, the Grand Lodge paid suitable tribute to hie memory. A committee thlls
speak of his Masonic life and character :Oar de.c eased brother, for nearly a holf century, exemplified by his upright walk
and blameless character, t~e principles of truth, love, aud charity, as taught in the
aoleJDn ceremonies and obligations of our Order, o.nd by an enthusiastic devotion to
Masonry, not surpassed by any of hi! cotemporaries, gave proof or the sincerity of.
hie profession, and hie unwavering faith In the teachings of Masonry to promote peace
and p:ood will among men; and, for thirty-six years, without · intermission, he faith·
fully attended the ann?~I Commu11lc11ti?11e of this Gran~ Lodge, and during that period,
lilied most of the pos1t1011e of official dignity with credit and honor, and by hie experi·
ence and wise oouneeis contributed largely towards shaping its edicts and promoting
its prosperity, and was twice elected Grand Master, receiving and wearing with
becoming dignity the highest honors which hie brethren could bestow. Full of years
and crowned witl1 honors, loved and venerated, he has passed away, we trust, to a
1eat above the starry-decked heavens, where all true Masone hope at last to arrive.
The Grand Lodge decided that no appeal could be taken from the decl~ion of a
subordinate Lodge by one not a member thereof, unless he himself was the defend·
ant. One Lodge had acquitted an accused brother of the charges brought against
him, but then "censured him for drinking too much." The Lodge unquestionably
deemed itself to be a court of equity as well as of law.
The Committee on Correspondence submitted an elaborate report upon the rival
claims of the "United .Grand Orient" and the "Supreme Council of Brazil in the Valley of Lavradio," to bet.he "genuine, original Jacobs," (masonic ally speaking} of that
Empire. While doubt existed in the minds of the committee, they concluded not to
disturb the present relations, which were with the last named body. They stRte
the following as having been the cause of that recognition, and it certainly shows that
that Orient knows how to do good Masonic work, even if it should be a little irregn·
lar:A few years ago the generous, large, and warm-hearted charity exercised by the
Masons of Brazil toward the family of a brother of this jurisdiction who had died
among them, a stranger, leaving his dear ones in bitter desolation and distress. touched
a chord of responsive and fraternal aympo.tby which filled the hearts of the whole
fraternity in .Alabama. We have never known to which branch or division of our
Brazilian brothers we owe this illustration of tbe irenuine spirit of Masonic charity.
Indeed, it. occurred, If we mistake not, about the time when a nnioo-nufortunateiy
only of brief duration-had been eft'ected between the two parties. It ao happened,
however, that while the emotions excited by the ~xbibitioo of fraternal charity, just
referred to, were still fresh in our minds and memorieP, overtures for official inter·
communion were made by the "Grand Orient of Brazil," of the Valley of Lavradlo.
It is probably ail.fe to asaume that, when these overtures were received, not half a
dozen members of' this Grand Lodge, probably not a member, was aware of the exist·
ence of any conflict in Brazil; nor is it likely that the question of an organic diver·
eity, and perhaps incompatibility, In the composition of both Grand Bodies claiming
jurisdiction in that conntry, aa compa1·ed with our own system, was seriously coosid·
ered. Acting on the impulses of the heart, rather than on the sober conclusions of
a judgment formed al\er due and careful examination, the proposition was at once
accepted in tbe same fraternal spirit in which it was tendered.

We make the following note of several of the decisions rendered by the Gr11.nd
Master:Neither the Worshipful Master or Wardens c.an resign during their term of
office. A Lodge has no right to charge a fee for a dimlt.
A subordinate Lodge cannot suspend or set aside the by-laws enacted by the
Grand Lodge for its use.
We should think not, but we believe that they Lave tried the experiment in other
jurisdictions. Our Grand Masters and Grand Lodge would make short work of snch
Masonic filibusters.
A belief in a Supreme Being is required of all candidates for the mysteries of
Masonry. No Atheist can be made a Mason.
.
So mote it ever be. We want no l''rench novelties in the Freemasonry of the
United States.
A Lodge has the right to raise or reduce the annual or quarterly dues which it
charges against its members, without consultlng the Grand Lodge.
That may he good law in Arkansas, but it Is not in California. · Every change
here must be passed upon by either the Grand Master or Grand Lodge, and in fact
by both.
The reception of the Past Master's degree in a Chapter confers no aut)J.ority
on the bl'other to pre~ide in a Master's Lodge. Symbolic. Masoorv is not dependent
on Ca.pitular Ma•onry to furnish it with qualified officers for the government of the
Cran.
Is it necessary for the Past Master's degree to be conferred on a Worshipful
Master elect priol' to his Installation? We regard the Past Master's degree as a
modern Innovation, accepted by usage, but wholly unsupported by law. The full
and complete installation ceremonies seats the Master elect in the Oriental Chair,
and qua.Wies and empowers him to preside; and no degree conferred in an Irregular
manner, unknown aud unrecognized by Symbolic Masonry, can do more.
We will note here the fact that the Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence nonconcurred in part as to the last ijecision. They say, and the Grand Lodge agreed
therewith, thatWe concur in so much of the foregoing decisiQn as holds that it is not necessary
for the Past Master's degree to be conferred on a Worshipful Master elect prior to
his installation ; and that the full and complete installation ceremonies seat the Mas·
ter elect in tile Oriental Chair, and qualify and empower him to preside.
The Master elect may preside over the Lodge al'ter he is installed in the ordinary
open form, but his installation is not full and complete, and he is not seated in the
Oriental Chair, in the tl'ne Masonic sense, until the order of Past Master is conferred
upon him in a convocation of Past Mastel's duly assembled.
We do not concur in the remark of the M.-. W.-. Grand Master, that "the Past
Master's degree is a modern innovation, accepted by usage, but wholly unsupported
by law."
The order of Past Master, as conferred in convocations upon Masters elect, is as
old and as constitutional as any .degree in Masonry.
As a Chapter degree it is American, adopted as a part of onr capitular system
nearly a bun.Ired years ago, as above observed, and is made by the Constitution of
the Genera.I Grand Chapter of the United States and the Constitutions of the State
Grand Chapters a regular degree. · .
•
As an order, conferred in oonvocatlons, or as a degree of the Chapter series, it is
supported by law, and, when properly conferred, like all the orders and degrees of

The past year had been one' of Masonic prosperity to the Lodges, notwithstanding

object were through, the Grand Master solemnly turned over all the jewels, property,
and records of the old Lodge to the new, and caused the proper records to that end
to be me.de on the minutes.
Thoe, in this case, I have discharged this duty, and believe that "peace and bar·
mony" have been restored to the Ore.ft in that ple.oe, and hope for good results to
follow.
Upon this very extraordinary proceeding, Bro. ROBERTSON comments as follows :
The "certain brethren" who were requested to retire, must have been consider·
ably astonished at what took place after they left. They suddenly found themselves
"oat in the cold, "-the Lodge going on as usual, with all the property and books of
the old Lodge, and all the old members, except them, and they not able to enter as
heretofore. We can fancy them asking each other, "Why is this thusly?" "How iR
this so?" They muat have come to the conclusion that they were not exactly posted
on the work, that there was a way of doing things that they never heard of, and that
the powers of the Grand Master were not to be sneezed at. Seriously, however, we
de.re say that these brethren had rendered themselves obnoxious to the rest, but we
cannot approve of this method of exclusion. It is possible that peace and harmony,
obtained at the sacrifice of principle, may be purchased too dearly.
We find many other good things in this excellent report, but lack of time oompels
us to leave it here.

Bro. BYRON L. CARR delivered an oration which we like exceedio11ly. Here are
one or two common-sense paragraphs which it will hurt nobody to "read, mark, and
inwardly digest":Whether any direct connection can be traced between the Masonic institution of
to-day and those societies of the most ancient times is a matter of doubt and uncertainty, but, to the intelligent Freemason, the striking similarity of the legend of Osiris,
and others that might be mentioned, tci one of the legends of our society, is strongly
sugl{estive of such a connection.
Were we to give such an account of Freemasonry as should contain all that we
actually know of its origin and original purposes, and onl,y that, we would say that it
is a moral institution, established sometime in the past; but exactly, or even approximately, when, we are unable to say. It was probably instituted by men, but who
they were who first perfected an Institution like ours, of what race or nation or Ian·
guage, the record is silent. It was probably instituted for the improvement and protection of Its members; but we learn this more from analogy, and from the traditions
and work of the order, than from any actual record now extant. It has flourished
from the time of Hs institution down to the present, with vary.iog prosperity-at
times prospering in the light of the protection of State and the patronage of Church,
and at other times oppressed by the one and anathematized by the other. • '" •
Of what consequence is it to us to know whether we are descended from the
Roman Colleges of Constructors, instituted by NuMA PollPILIUS twenty-six centuries
ago, or from the guilds of workingmen of Gaul or Britain? Or suppose we could
extend our gaze into the remoter shadowR of the past, and demonstrate that the
rites and ceremonies of the Lodge are descended to ns from the Greek, or Hebrew,
or Egyptian, or Syrian, or Hindoo mysteries?
·
These are matters of interest to the antiquarian, but it la of no practical Importance to us as Masons whether we are sprang from one or all these sources. To the
thirsty traveler journeying across the trackless plains under the scorching rays of a
noonday sun, what matters it whether the sparkling rivulet which appears to him in
the distance derives its source from the eternal snows of the distant mountains or
from perennial springs. a lesser distance away, or from showers of rain.which, but
recently, perhaps, have fallen npon the plains higher op? His only concern Is to
know whether the stream itself is '{!'Ure, and will satisfy the barning thirst which is
consuming him, and sustain the life which is languishing within him. He stops not
to inquire whether it has fiowed for hundreds or thousands of miles, bot he laves hie
body in the cooling wat,er, and, with a heart thankful to the giver of all good, he
applies it to the uses for which nature Intended it, and draws life and physioal com·
fort therefrom.
To the members of our Masonic institution it is a matter of little concern who
were its founders or what was its original purpose. It is with the institution itilelf.
as we see it at the present time, that we as Masons ate most concerned. The
question is not, What were its objects and purposes centuries ago! bot, w1.... t are ite

Answer -No it is no a11ouchment al all. No diploma, cert1ficau, or any other

The Grand Master devotes two pages to the discussion of the subject of Masonic
prayers, and comes to this conclusion:The moment a brother assumes that the Supreme can be approached only through
some one name-be that name Brahma, Jesus, Buddha, or Allah, that moment he
enters upon tbeological definition and interpretation, the very root of sectarianis!JI,
which, with its twin evil, political partisanship, Masonry seeks above all others to
exclude.
Our.Grand Lodge, mindful of Its obligation to the landmark, bas by statute pro·
hibited the introduction of either np on any Masonic occasion ; and no one who will
pause to reflect upon the essential nature of a brotherhood claiming to be universal,
can doubt the wisdom or Its action.
It is flain, tllen, that a brother cannot use distinctively Christian prayere in the
name o Masonry, without dlsregardinir our local re~ulations, nor witbout doing
.
violence to that catholic spirit wliich breathes through its immemorial law.
Our only comment thereon is the question, Oui bono any such discussion or decls·
i<in? It Is a two-edged knife and dangerous to handle. The Grand Master publishes
thirty-two of his decisions. We copy a few of the most important, without comment:·IC a Lodge accepts a n0te of hand from a brother, In Uquidatlon of arrearage•
for dues, it thereby places his obligation for such arrearages on a purely busines1
basis, and cannot make tile non-payment or such note tile basis of charges with a
view to penal 4iscipllue. .
.
When a brother Is on trial before his Lodge for an alleged Masonic offense,
the record of his conviction or the same offense in a civil court is not sufficient to
warrant the Lodge in finding a verdict of guilt. The case is now to be tried before
an entirely different jury, and must be conducted according to the rules laid down
by the Grand Lodge, which require the jury to hear the evidence before voting on
· the question of guilt or innocence.
·
The application of a colored Mason to visit may be entertained, if he be Jaw·
fully made. Masonry knows no distinction of color. The question is not one of
race or complexion, but of legitimacy. The right of visit is possessed equally by
all, white or black, who, having been made In a constitutional Lodge in this .Jurisdic•tion, or in a Lodge subordinate to any Grand Lodge recognized as legitimate by the
"Grand Lodge of Illinois, still remains in good standing. None, black or white, pos·
sess the right who lack these qualifications . .

Our ideal of Masonic aspiration Is In seeing better husbands, fathers, sons, and
citizens. lf we did not believe In the elevating power of the Craft, we should fail to
find anything in it worthy of much consideration. 'f hat which should most concern
man in this llfe is manhood ; and any organization resting In this central thought that
Is unable or unw!lling to exert its powers In that direotion oannot long retain itself
In the. friendly regard of the benevolent and beneficent activities of thE'. age. It la
for this reason, brethren, that we give you the best sentiment of our distinguished
fraters of other jurisdictions, rather than devote the entire labor of the rear to jurls·
prudence and oontroversy. We do not wish to be understood as depreciating either,
except when they are held np for the exclusive contemplation of the Craft.
We take great plee.sure in saying that the Masonry of 1876 and '77 Is in advance
of the Masonry of 1875 and '76. Grand Masters are more trenchant in the adminis·
tration of rebuke, less active in the production of homilies, and more active in the
enforcement of healthy discipline_and in conserving fraternal welfare.
If Masonry was fully aware of its possibilities, there is not an institution of
human origin now making an impress upon society that otfers to the weary pilgrim
on life 's dusty path-way so much of hope, so much of consolation and encouragement
as this manhood necessity. All along the track of ages its temples have opened thei:
portals to the rich ·and the poor, the man of renown and the more humble factor of
destiny. Some enter to plant a fresh flower that is to gladden the hearts of the
countless throng that is unceasingly wending its way towards the mysterious empire
of eternity; wliile others, thoughtless and unconcerned, enter only to appropriate
the perfume, pluck the blossom even to the roots, leaving foot-prints that chm the
tender, retiring tendrils of Faith, Rope, and Charity. Thus will it always be · but
instead of promoting apathy, distrust, or discouragement, the fact that these' are
mort~l, and, like all mankind, liable to disregard the claims of humanity, should
s~imolate the thoughtful Me.son to more exalted conceptions of his fraternal mis·
s1on.
Bro. GURNEY devotes nearly twenty pages of his report to a full and elaborate con•
sideration of the vexed question involved in the rival claims of the two Grand Lodges
in the Island of Cuba. He pnblishes at length the documents reoelved, which we
believe were the same reported upon by our own Committee on Masonic J.urispr11•
dence last year, but not published in our journal. The conclusion reached by him
is, that "the Grand Lodge of Colon and constituent bodies were extinct, and as
completely lost"to symbolic Masonry e.s if incorporated in like manner into an organ·

commenced in the city of Topeka on the seventeenth day ofOctober, 1877,-the M.·.
w.·. J.1.cos D. Ruse, Grand Master, presiding, and the B.·. w.-. JoeN H. BROWN
being Grand Secretary. Ninety-four Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in his Address, congratnlated the fraternity on the prosperous
state of Masonry, generally, in the jurisdiction; alluded to the important business to
come before the Grand Lodge, and expressed the earnest wish that " no member of
the Grand Lodge would return to his home until all the busin.ess of the Communica'
tion waR thoroughly and completely finished. I believe," he added, "that more injury
is done t-0 Masonry through hasty legislation in our Masonic Grand Bodies than by
all other causes combined.'' Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California will please
make a note of this, and govern themselves accordingly,
Dispensations had been granted for the formation of five new Lodges. In
alluding to the fact that he had refused applications for many other dispensations,
and thereby offended many of the brethren, the Grand Master gives vent to his
feelings in the following plain, truthful, and common-sense words :The true object and intent of our noble Order[is, in many instances, I fear, being
perverted into uses ent.irely foreign to the original designs laid down npon our trestleboard; too many are applying for our mysteries, and too many are gaining admis·
aion everywhere, for the well being of the Order; too many rough unfinished ashlers
are being placed in the edifice. They not only mar its outward beauty and finish,
but also its internal strength and utility. We should pay more attenlion to the character of the applicant for Masonic honors, and not so much to our numerical strength.
'l'. on may say tf1at it is much easier to criticise than to correct the evils referred to.
That is very true ; yet we cannot expect to ever get complete control of our
work, and get a perfect building, unless we employ only skillful and careful work·
men, who will see to it that no rough or unfinished stone e ver finds a place in our
noble edifice.
It would be very pleasant, no doubt, ir we could delnde ourselves Into the belief
that by a rapid establishment of new Lodges, and the consequent opening of numerous new avenues of entrance for the anxious seekers after light, we were by so
doing conferring a lasting benefit upon the fraternity. But fortunately all cannot
think or believe in that way, If a.Ii who seek an entrance at our doors did so through
pure motivea, and a sincere desire to be of benefit to mankind, or if the black ball
was more freely used, then the danger of a too rapid increase of membershi1> would
be very greatly modified. But, unfortunately, for the good of the Craft, such is not
the case.
F ew, comparatively, of the vast numbers who yearly gain admission Into our
Lodges, ever make genuine, true Masons, and labor for the good of the Order and of
mankind. Many seek admission through purely mercenary motives, having a vague
Idea that, by becoming a member of such an ancient, honorable, and powerful iastitutlon as ours, they will, in some manner through its influence, be financially beaeftted, Others, 11gain, are attracted to our Lodges through sheer curiosity, and a
desire to kaow of what those ceremonies consist which have stood the test of so
many ages. It is needleRS for me to say that neither of these classes either benefit or
adorn our Order; but, on the contrary, they hang to us like an incnbus, and, if not
shaken off, wlll, in time, alm'lst destr(Jy our entire intluence for good. We can best
remedy those evils by strictly guarding the doors of entrance already created, and
in forming as few more only as absolute necessity would seem to require.
He had in every case refused to grant dispensations to " confer degrees in less
than the constitutional timA ;" and wisely, too. '.l'he Grand Master is no lover of
non-affiliates, as witness thi~ decision of his :Every Master Mason should belong to some Lodge and be a contributing member
to its charities. One who voluntarily takes his dimit and severs his connection with
the fraternity, not for the purpose of becoming affiliated with another Lodge, thereby
relinquishes his claim upon the fraternity tor all those beneH.ts which he ac<Juired by
becoming a member of it. Therefore, in the absence of an'{ local regulat10n upon
the subject, I hold this to be the correct and just status o that class of Masonic
vagrants, viz.: any non-affiliated Master Mason in this jurisdiction who does not,
within six months from the date of bis dimit, become a member of some Lodge. shall
not be permitted to visit any J,odge (after that time) more than once, nor be permitted to walk in any Masonic procession, or participate in any M88onic ceremony;
neither shall they be entitled to receive Masonic bnrial, nor to r eceive relief from the
charity funds of the Lodge.

Will we encroach too much upon our allotted space if we copy Grand Master

Ee.oh in their turn have had one or more committees ohasmg after these good (?}

·
.
Fortunately we have no existing legislation upon the subject to trammel u_s, and
we are consequently in a good position to begin the a~tack ·~pon thl1 formidable
portion of our Order. In answer to each query opnn this subject, I have given my
decision No. 7 believing that If It is adopted by this Grand Lodge It will do more
towards correcting this evil than any other law which we could enact.
We have run after the non-affiliated Masons long enough, to the detriment of the
faithful and true Masons who have held fast to their faith and Masonic homes at the
same time. Let us try a different kind of tactics upon t hem by changing our course,
and instead of chasing after them. let us turn and face them 1 and establi~h our laws,
saying, thus far you can go, and no farther, only at you~ peril. Let us give them au
opportunity to run after us for awhile, and see which. IS. the most successful plan.
Believing the latter would be, I made my decision a:coordmgly.
Non-affiliation separates those who are Masons m name only from those who are
Masons at heart. Let them go if they wish to, but not upon full pay and honors.

not concur. But it will come in due time, Bro. BaowN, so hop.e on.

.
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge fully sustains Alp ha Lodge, No. 122, loc~ted at

erected within the territory of the Cherokee Nation.
We hope that this war-cloud on the border will not increase or burst, but, now
that Arkansas has extended the right hand of fellowship to the Grand Lodge of Indian
Territory, that Kansas will do the same.

The Grand Master gives good and sound reasons for withholding his assent to the
request of a Lodge that it might appeal to others for aid in the erection of a suitable
Hall. He .disapproves of this resort to raise money. The result proved that such
applications· were unnecessary, for he had been called . upon to dedicate the hall
which the brethren had erected, unassisted from abroad.
Another Lodge was about to become a stockholder in an ontside "Building Association," hoping thus to secure means for a hall of its own. To this the Grand Master
could not assent, and gives these good ~easons for his opinion:~
Stock companies do not bear the best repntation. The,r are generally regarded
as games of chance and speculation, and their ultimate failure is almost a foregone
concluaiou. I think that Masonry should keep itself free from all entangling alli·
ances witn such associations.
i::lpeculative Masonry does not mean Masonic speculation. Lodges should not
engage in business transaction~ w~~re t~ere is a probability or a possibility of failure,
and thereby become mvolved m lt!tp;atton, and perhaps Involve the Grand Lodge in
its complications. I Intend no reflection on the assooiation referred to, or on those
who compose it; but I speak of stock companies in general, and only reiterate what
I conceive to be the settled policy of this Order-not to engage in a!Jy enterprise with
the outside world, whose failure is possible and business comphcations may be the
result.
The Deputy Grand Master found that the Past Grand Master's Jewel of a deceased
Grand Master had been disposed of by his widow, and was in danger of finding its
way to a pawn-broker's shop; he therefore purchased it for $100, and the Grand
Lodge took it off his hands at that price, with thanks for his timely action.
One Lodge had been instituted during the year. The Grand Master had made
three decisions on the "physical qualifications" question, all which were approved
by the Grand Lodge. They were as follows:That an Entered Apprentice with one eye was not ineligible to receive the two
remaining degrees in this jurisdiction by means of said defect.
That an applicant with a defect in the right hip that makes it impossible to put
the right heel to the ground is ineligible.
That an applicant who has lost the first three fingers on the right hand is ineligible.
The nnfriendly relations which had existed for several years between the Grand
Lodges of ·Louisiana and Canada had been amicably settled and full fraternal relations again restored.
Upon the recent action of the Grand Orient of France, the Grand Master ut~era
these few, bnt very plain spoken words, in which every true-hearted Mason will fully
concur:A re-eshblishment of fraternal relations with the Grand J,odge of Hamburg is
possible, as she is already giving ·evidences of disquietude in her present false position. Not so with the Grand Orient of France. Between us there 1s now a great gulf
fixed, whiuh no Maso11 can ~ass. By a solemn decree they have expunged" God and
the immortality of the soul ' from their constitution and ritual.
In view of our unfriendly relations, it would, perhaps, be in bad taste to snbject
this action of the Grand Orient of France to severe criticism or denunciation, but I
cannot allow this occasion to pass without expressing an emphatic and indignant con·
demnation of this innovation upon the body of Masonry.
The paternity of God, and the fraternity of man, are the inseparable tenets of
Masonry. Eliminate the one, and the other is a shadow without a substance; the
ritual is stripped of its beauty and impressive solemnity; the great moral design is

The Grand Secretary submitted an elaborate report, full of statistics and sound
advice to the Craft. He takes occasion, as the result of his observations and experi·
ence, to read the Lodges a lecture on the subject of adequate dues. . In some they
amounted to only one dollar per year, and in others to two, with ten dollars as the
fee for a degree. Of even the small amount of one dollar, one Lodge remitted fifty
per cent. to its members. How Lodges could keep alive and be furnished with necessary tools for work on such a meagre sum, was an enigma to the Grand Secretary, 011
it is to us. He hits the nail square on the head in this manner:Does a farmer believe that he would make a good crop with poor stock and poor
tools? No; his experience would teach him that a wooden plough or hoe, or a stone
ax, would prove dear at any or no price at all ; and how much better will It prove
with a Lodge that has a wooden Worshipful Master or Secretary. In Masonry, as in
farming, the best tool is the cheapest in the end. A Lodge whose members have too
little pride in it to induce them to spend money for what is essential and necessary,
will never raise a good crop of Mason•. Take a more liberal view, brethren, and ask
yourselves-what should my Lodge be, and what should it be able to do, and how
much will it require to make it fulfil the expectation?

On another case we find these comments. Bro. DRUMMOND has always been
opposed to "compulsory charity," bellevfog that the qualifying w~rd is wholly inconsistent with the other:One singula.r. case came before the Grand Lodge: A brother, who had been a

be was paralyzed. The Lodge was able to assist him, but refused, althougb he was

decided that he must be presumed worthy until the contrary had been established

need? " The matter was referred to the Grand Master, witll instructions to require
the Lodge to do what he might deem proper in the premises.
But can a Lodge be required to give in charity unless it sees fit to do so? Can
compulsion be used in such a case, any more than with an individual? These are
new qoestiens; bot we think that the ohligation to releive the destitute is as binding
as any otller; and if a Lodge, or an Individual Mason, of admitted abUity, refuses to
a.BBlst a distressed brother they are liable to Masonic discipline. We say "admuted
ability," because if the refusal should be placed on the ground of inability, the ques·
tion is a very different one, as each Mason is the j udge, upon tb.at point, for himself,
and it would require a very strong case to override this rule-a cas& in which it is
manifest that the brother is acting in bad faith and alleging his want of ability a~ a.
pretense.
