We thank Thee that Thou didst keep fresh in the heart of this grateful city tile
memory of Its heroes, and that, therefore, it would build Into stone, so that all mea
might see their honor for the dead.
·
We bless Thee that Thou didst give this pictured beauty to the artist's thonght
and this wondrous ~kill to the artist's hllnd. Gladly do we remember before Thee
that these foundation s were laid in no spirit to perpetuate rememb~nce of fratricidal
strife or of triumph over men, but were laid to honor the memory of patriotic devotion to the flag of our whole conntry, and, to that end, of brave self-sacrifice, even
nnto death.
We praise Thee that by the achievements of such men Thou didst re-establish onr
National Union; didst proclah1 liberty throughout the land; didst confirm the Constitution which our fathers wrote.
And now, 0 God, to remembdr these things, and these men, and for those who
builded this Monument, In honor of the men who bu!lded anew a nation, have we
come to consecrate this stone.
Well made, well proved, builded according to Thine eternal laws, Great Architect
of the Universe, approve it, we beseech Thee.
Bless this stone, 0 heavenly FatherIn honor of mothers who bade their sons do brave deeds:
In honor of wives who wept for the husbands who should never come home again ;
In honor of children whose heritage is their fallen father's heroic name :
In honor of men and women who ministered to the hurt and the dying :
But chiefly, 0 God, In honor of men who counted not their lives dear when their
country needed them; of those alike who sleep beside the dust of their kindred, or
under the salt sea, or in nameless graves where only Thine angels stand sentinels till
the reveille of the resurrection morning.
Preserve it, we pray, in the years to come; in heat and cold, In snows and rains,
in seed-times and harvests. Let it endure, that the men who 1ee it, In the coming
generations, may be inspired to know that honor jij more than wealth, right is more
than peace, and heroic death more than life.
These praises do we render Thee, and these petitions do we olfer Thee, in the
name of Him who passed through his Gethsemane and snlfered upon Oalvary. Amen.

1800, by the Hon. TrnOTBY BIGELOW. The oration ls printed in the proceedings
before us, and we feel strongly disposed to copy liberally therefrom. We will cull
one or two paragraphs-thl1 from the beginning:Though silence be justly considered the langu11ge of grief, yet It is equivocal.
Hypocrisy or indifference may assume It. On great 00011slons, therefore, It becomes
a duty to vindicate ou·r feelings, though it be Impossible fully to express them. Highly
laudable then is the conduct of our generous nation, at the present meurnful crisis. While all classes of oor fellow-citizens, obedient to the lnjonctioos and imitating the exBmple of Coogres11. are pouring forth their sorrows and recounting the ·
virtues of the deceased W .lBHINOTON; whife the great and good of other nations are
miogllog _their regrets with the lamentations of his affiicted countrymen-shall the

Proce,edings of the

[Oct. 8,

Masonic Fraternity be silent? Suppress their grief they cannot, and shall they
attempt to conceal it? No, my brethren, he had a double claim to our attachment,
and we will dwell on his memory with peculiar affection. If our departed brother
yet takes an interest in what passes npon earth, if his bl"est shade still hovers over
the country which he protected and loved, may we not hope that our tribute of respect
will be acceptable: that our united plaudit may even touch his immortal soul
with pleasure? A hope like this would soften our pangs, and dart a ray of comfort
through the gloom of affiiction which surrounds us. But ah, how unlike are our
present emotion•, at best, to those we have been wont to indulge on the returns of
this anniversary! Long have we been accustomed to hail it with joy, and regard it
as the era of Heaven's peculiar favor to our country. Blind to futurity, we have
fondly hoped that he would yet continue many years : that he would long defend us
with his sword, and bless us with his counsels ; that he would glide gently down the
declivity of life, majestic as some mighty river, and late, very late, sink in the ocean
of eternity. Bo long shall we deplore his apparently untimely departure.· So long
will this returning day call forth the mingled emotions of joy and mourning. But
future times will again regard it as auspicious. Our remotest posterity, inheriting
our freedom and independence, and that happy Oonstitution which alone can secure
them, will never be unmindful of the MASTER, who presided at the building of the
fair fabric of political glory, or forget that on this day WASHINGTON was born.
And this as to the Masonic character of the illustrious patriot:Having already contemplated such a variety of distinguishing features in this great
and amiable character, does it still admit ofadditlon? Is there room in the portrait for
another trace of the faithful pencil, that will increase its beauty? Yes, my brethren,
to us another and no less interesting view remains. Animated with a generous philanthropy, our deceased brother early sought admission into our Ancient and Honorable Fraternity, at once to enable him to cherish with advantage this heavenly prin·
ciple, and enlarge the sphere of its operation. He cultivated our art with sedulous
attention, and never lost an opportunity of advancing the interest or promoting the
honor of the Graft. While Commander in Chief of the American revolutionary army,
he countenanced the establishment and encouraged the labors of a traveling Lodge
among the military. He wisely considered it as a school of urbanity, well calculated
to disseminate those mild virtues of the heart, so ornamental to the human character,
and so peculiarly useful to correct the ferocity of soldiers and alleviate the miseries
of war. The cares of hie high office engrossed too much of his time to admit of his
engaging in the duties of the chair; yet he found frequent opportunities to visit the
Lodge, and thonght it no derogation from his dignity there to stand on a level with
the brethren. True to our principles on all ocoas1ons, an incident once occurrecl
which enabled him to display their influenc(e to bis foes. A body of American troops,
in some successful rencounter with the 1lnemy, possessed themselves, among other
booty, of the jewels and furniture of a. British traveling Lodge of Masons. Thia
property was directed by the Commander in Chief to be returned u'nder a flag of
truce to its former proprietors, accompanied with a message, purporting that the
Americans did not make war upon institutions of benevolence.
Of his attachment to our Order in general you, my respected brethren of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of this Commonwealth, have had personal knowledge.
His answers to your repeated addresses breathe throughout the spirit -0f brotherly
. lov1l; and his affectionate return of thanks for the Rook of Constitutions, which you·
presented him, and for the honor, as he was pleased to con•ider it, which you did
him in· the dedication, must be evidence highly satisfactory of the respectful estima·
tion In which he held you. The information received from our brethren, who had
the ha.ppiness to be members of the Lodge over which he presided many years, and
of which he died the Master, furnishes abundant proof of his persevering zeal for the
prosperity of the Institution. Constant and punctual in his attendance, scrupulous
in his observance of the regulations ofth1l Lodge, and solicitous at all times to communicate light and instruction, he discharged the duties of the Chair with uncommon
dignity and intelligence in all the mysteries of our art. Nothing can more highly
conduce to the prosperity and honor of Masonry, than a successful imitation of this
bright example. It cannot fail of its effect upon our brethren in its immediate neigh·
borhood in the South; they will beautify their column. And shall we be outdone
in zeal? Placed geographically in the east, in a. quarter of the Union from which
the nation has been accustomed to learn wisdom, it should be our peculiar care to
diffuse light through the temple of Masonry. As it is known that we shared largely
in the esteem and affection of our deceased brother, it is easy to perceive that our
good conduct will itself be an encomium on his memory. We see before us, among
the sad emblems of mortality, not only the sword which in this neighborhood he
drew In defeooe of his country, but also the very attire which he has often worn as a
Mason. How devoutly Is it to be wished that these striking memorials may stimn·
late us to a noble emulation; that, like the mantle of Elijah, they may inspire us
with a.n unalterable attachment to virtue and benevolence ! This day witnesses to

At the Annual Communication of 1877, a resolution on the subject of temperance
was introduced and referred to a committee, to report at this session. Bro. JOHN W.
. OllAHPLill, Past Grand Master, from that committee, submitted the following report
which was adopted by the Grand Lodge :Your committee beg leave to report that they have had the subject under consideration, and have arrived at the following conclusions:lat. No general legislation is needed to maintain a proper respect for and observance of the Masonic virtue of Temperance. The observance and practice of
this virtue is inculcated in a most impressive manner on our first admission into a
Lodge of Masons. It is there enjoined npon us as the constant practice of every
Ma~on. It stands at the head of the four cardinal virtues as the faithful guardian of
the secrets of the Order. To violate this virtue subjects the offender to the contempt
and deteetation of all good M11.sons, and to the iufiiction of Masonic penalt!es. 'fhe
law as.it.exists is olear and the penalties adequate. No additional legislation can
add to the heinonsness of the offense of intemperance, and no additional penalties
known to Masonic law can be imposed.
It is not in new legislation that f.he remedy for intemperance is to be found, but
in the enforcement of existing laws. Your committee are satisfied that much of the
cause of complaint in this behalf arises from the neglect of observiug those reciprocal duties and obligations which rest upon us as Masons towards one another.
Intemperance does not burst forth suddenly Into the enormity of an offense. It is a
plant of slow gr11wth, having Its roots nurtured from frequent indulgence until it
forms a habit. It ls a falling away from that high plane of temperance upon
which all upright Masons stand. The downwal'd steps are plainly to be perceived
by all the brethren, But do the brethren, animated by that fraternal regud for a
brother Mason's welfare whic!J we are taught to exercise and which we profess to
have, stretch forth their hiinds to assist and save the falling brother? l>o they whisper In his ear words of caution? Do they give good counsel, not by chiding public·
Jy, but by private admonition! Or rather do they turn away from him, or pass by
on the other side, giving hilD no due and timely notice that he may ward off impending danger!
Your committee are speaking now of that form of intemperance which is mani·fested ·by habitual drunkenness; and they are of the opinion that in a Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons, the members of which discharge towards each other the
duties and obligations of Masons, it is generally impossible that there should be an
habitual drunkard. Of all the vices to which weak human nature is ad<licted, it is
one most easily detected. 1t is known and seen of all men, and it is also a vice which
Is most easily eradicated by the timely interposition of brotherly love. No man can
withstand the kindly influence of all the members of a Lodge if put forth to succor
and to save. If, having discharged toward one who is contracting the vice of intemperance these good. offices, he will not give heed and forsake the error of his ways,
cast him out as an unworthy member, who Is not entitled to our sympathy, favor or
protection.
2d. Special legislation is not needed upon the subject, either to enjoin temper-·
ance or to Inculcate brotherly love. For if the initiate will not respect the cardinal
virtues, nor the brethren fulfill their obligations, without special injunctions so to do,
both will be alike unavailing. There is no life in the letter of the law, bot in the
spirit.
Therefore we say to those brethren w.ho complain of the evil of intemperance
among the fraternity, that the blame does not rest upon the intemperate alone, nor
with the law-givers, bot with the brother In that he has himself so degraded, disgraced and fallen ; and with the Lodge in that they did not save him from falling ;
or failing in this, that they did not wipe out the degradation and disgrace to the
fraternity by suspending or expelling him from all the rights and benefits of Ma•
sonry.
On this subject of temperance, the Grand Lodge, after much discnseion, adopted
the following as one of its standing resolutions:Resolv_ed, That t.he manufacture or sale of intoxicati~g liquor.a as a beverage-by
Masoos-1s a Masomc oft'ense ; and that, 1f a brother persists therem as a business after
being duly admonished, it is the duty of the Lodge of which he is a member to suspend or expel him, in its discretion.

.After penning the foregoing, we received from our Grand Secretary the proceedings for 1877, which had come to him out of season. The Communication was held In
Grand Rapids, on the twenty-third day of Jannary,-the M.·. w.·. MATT~RW H. MAYNARD, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·.
ELLERY I. GARFillLD being Grand
Secretary. Two hundred and nineteen Lodges were repre11ented.
The Address of the Grand Master was mainly devoted to the business of that
Jurisdiction. He had issued dispensations for the formation of five new Lodges, and
had arrested the charter of one for very nnmasonic conduct. The Grand Master
complains of the remissness of the officers of Lodges in not attending the Be.hoofs of
Instruction held by the District Deputies. As to a proposition to abolish this system,
he writes strongly in favor of its continuance,· and pays a well-merited tribute to the
judicious work of the Deputies. One of hie decisions relates to the granting of dimits
when no reasons for the application are given-that being a pre-requisite in that jurisdiction. He holds that the whole matter rests in the sound discretion of the Lodge.
As to the policy of granting or withholding, under the circumstances alleged, the
Grand Master makes these timely suggestions:. So much for the law. On the question of policy, I will only say a word, which
will not be law, but a suggestion. lf you have got a mail who has a substantial
grievance against your Lodge, or againlit any brother, don't let him go until you
endeavor to reconcile him. If r,ou ~ucceed, "thou hast saved thy brother·" If yon
fail, "pot yourself in his place,' and do as you would be done by. If you 'have got .
a man who has lost his mterest in Masonry, who, perhaps, is disappointed in his
e'.Cpectatione of finding it to benefit bis trade or business, who is too stingy to pay
bis dues or who pays them grudgingly, who le always finding fau lt, who is mad
because he has not had some office, and in a "hundred and one " ways makes himself disagree_l'ole and all about him unhappy; don't you think yon had better Jet
him go? Why do yon want to keep him? !<'or the sake of what he pays annually
into your treasury? Harmony and peace are worth more than one two, three or
four dollars per year. Yoo had better let him go. In fine, my brother, act cha;itably and honestly toward your brother an(j, toward your Lodge, and you will have ilo
trouble in deciding what are good and sufficient reBBons for granting a dimit.
Here is one of his decisons, out of which ultimately grew the "temperance"
question, on which the report of the committee is noticed in the foregoing review:It is not ground for objection to the installation of a duly elected Worshipful
Master that he keeps a billiard saloon. If, however, connected with such business he
has a bar at which intoxicating drinks are retailed to his patrons, his business is
essentially immoral and demoralizing in all its effects upon the community. .Any
Lodge that will elect such a man 88 Its Worshipful Master is unworthy to hold its
charter.

I am glad to say that Bro. BRADEN during his last sickness was the recipient of
that loving care of his Masonic brethren that baa so long made the order memorable for its deeds of love and kindnesa. Our brethren of San Antonio, with loving
hands performed the last sad offices due from the Jiving to the dead, and the widow
and the fatherless, though in a strange land, found In the fraternity true and affectionate friends in the dark hour of their aftllotfon. Bro. n. H. NEAL, Worshipful
M&Ster of Anchor Lodge , No 424, of San Antonio, Texaa, with Bro. C. E. F1SHEB,
were with the family of our Grand Master during bis laat hour•, rendering every
attention that could alleviate the sorrows of thoae who stood by the bedside of him
who was so soon to enter the gloomy portals of the world bo1ond. When the spirit
of our brother had taken its flight, and but his unconscious form remained, Masonic
hands, actuated by the same brotherly love, performed the laat Rad duties due to our
dead brother, and, with kind words and deeds, did all that In their power lay to lighten the grief of his widow and little ones. The same ~ood oftlce1 to the dead and
widowed were bestowed by the brethren of Houston, 'lexas, St. Louis, Mo., and a'
St. Paul.
Bro. BRADEN'S remains were followed to their last restlng·plaoe by a large and
imposing cortege of our brethren, and as tbe sun sank slowly below the horizon on
Sunday, December sixteenth, we tenderly and sadly placed all that was mortal or our
late Grand Master in the sil~nt tomb.
Brethren, the character of our Grand Master was such as merits onr warmeat
commendation. His character was of that rare type that men delight to honor, and
my brethren, the honors that we have paid, and on this day pay, to the memory of
our deceased brother, are not mere offerings to the dead or mere consolation to the
living, for honors paid to the memory of such a man go be1ond, and become lncen·
tives to those who, witnessing such scenes, cannot remain rnsensible to the fact that
men's lives live after them in the memori of their fellow men. As a citizen, Bro.
BaADSN was strictly moral and of rare al11llty; as a soldier, our State and country
can testify of his worth, recorded as it is, In the history of hard fought battles; aa a.
husband, devoted and affectionate, and solicitous always for the happiness and welfare
of her who in early life he had chosen to walk with him life's pathway hand in hand.
And now, my brethren, you have again, like the craft of old, assembled to re·
ceive lnatructions for your work. You examine the trestle board, and behold there
are no plans upon it; you look to the East, and the Grand Master is not there; in·
stantly there flashes upon your mind the beautiful , aye, the grand story upon which
our noble order Is founded, and in quick review pass before yon the quarries and
the Fellow Crafts at work-the mountains of Lebanon, with their tall and stately
cedars, solemn sentinels of that sombre land, and there is Joppa where the timber
for the building of' the temple was brought by the sea, there she sits on the high bills,
overlooking the waves, while far away to the west shines the Mediterranean, blue
and lustrous, as a silken tunic; and there too Is Jerusalem, the city of the children
of (fod. , and in the minds of us they are building the second Temple; silently, stone
bf stone, rises the magnificent fabric, the temple of a nation, the poetry and religion
o a whole people, grand and lofty, as was found expression in that one temple, built
and dedicated to the one God.
But a shadow falls across the brightness ofthe·scene. No~lans are found npon the trestle board, and the workmen, looking each into the fa.ce of his brother,
say," Our Grand Ma~ter Is dead.'' So I come to you, my brethren, this day, and
say, our Grand Master Is dead.
The acting Grand Master had but few items In bis Address in addition to those
which refer to the great loss the Craft in the jurisdiction had sustained. The scour.11e
of grass·hoppers, which had devastated the fertile plains of Minnesota In years past,
had passed away, and " the places that were laid waste and desolate are now the
homes of plenty, peace, and happiness."
The defalcation of the late Grand Secretary, E. D. B. PORTER, he having' appropriated to his own nse one thousand dollars of the Grand Lodge funds, was brought
before the Grand Lodge, and the brother, making no defense, was expelled from the
fraternity.
Dispensations for four new Lodges were IBBned and two other applloatlona were
referred to the Grand Lod~e.
. Bro. AHIBA RICHARDSON, the Grand Tyler, had also passed away daring the year,
and the Grand Master pays a suitable tribute to his memory.

Bro. 1Bv1NG ToDD, and one thonsand copies were ordered to be printed a.nd 1old to
the subordinate Lodges. When will some zealous and ca.pable brot.her do the same

The Grand Master publishes fifteen of his deol1lon1, the 1econd of which was that
" the loss of two fingers of the left hand constitutes no phyeical disqualification under
the laws of Masonry." On this :decision, the committee en Masonic Jurisprudence
and the Grand Lodge reported and decided favorably, 1u1talnlog the same by thi1
train of reasoolng :The subject of" physical qaaliflcations" comes up lo some quarter of the juri&diction regularly every year. It is here the loss of an eye, there or a linger or two,
and somewhere else a thumb, or even an arm or leg. It also happens that those
persons who have been so unfortunate as to lose a member or a limb are good men,
and their friends think it unjust that they should be deprived of the privileges and
benefits of Masonry through an accident for which their moral character Is in no way
respoosible, 'f his is a question which mast be met and adjusted OD a basis Of common sense, to be either ju•t or generally satisfactory; and our forms and rituals
furnish the key to such a solution. The original object of many of our forms of initiation was to place a bar agaiost the admission of any ooe who had not the free and
unhampered ase of all bis limbs. Ability to conform to our ceremonies implied that
he was also able to make his own living, and not be a burden on the Order; and, if
need be, to render bodlly assistance to a brother in distress. These conditions were
exemplified in the rule:. " We should make no man a Mason who is not upright in
body, or who is deformed or dismembered at the time of making, but he must be of
hale and entire limbs, as a man OU{2'ht to be,"-which was affirmed by oar Grand
Lodge, in 1850. It has been necessary to construe and apJlly this rule to individual
oases from year to year, and men hl\ve been ruled out for the lack of an eye, and admitted when their defect was the loss of one or two lingers of the left hand. A strict
conatructien of the old regulations would, doubtless, exclude all physical or
mental defects that are apparent. Let us construe the law and usage, at once
and for all, according to the forms and ceremonies of initiation, making them the
infallible test of bodily and mental qualifications, by re-affirming the rule of 1871 :
".Ability to conform literally to the ceremonies of initiation into the several degrees
meets the ancient qualifications of 'sound in mind and member.' " This rule can
work oo unjust ostracism, and it is understood by all M.isoos. Let it be adopted.
On the eighth decision-which relates to a perplexing qnestion,-the Grand Mas·
ter thus reasons and decides rCan a Lodge of Masons, when requested ·to conrluot the funeral ceremonies of a
deceased brother, who was also·a member of non-M:asonic associations, share with
such associations the right of a.ppointing pall-bearers, or allow them to participate
in the ceremonies at the grave? '
The difficulties surrounding this question are recognized. Ir no reqnest Is made,
we have no right whatever to appear in procession with other associations which
have been requested to perform the last sad rites of burial over the remains of a de·
ceased brother. This Is a rock of offense to such associations. If the request ls lejirally and properly made to a Masonic Lodge, then, In performing these ceremonies:
1t must have ·absolate control ; and in those jurisdictions permitting other associations
to a•sist at the grave, the Lodge performs Its ceremonies last. This gives offense.
We cannot aft'ord to apologize to other assooiations for our laws. They have
been haoded down to as Crom generation to generation, and we can suffer no infringement upon them. The Lodge on such occasions ls at labor, and no one not a Mason
can participate therein. Non·afliiiated Masons cannot appear In our processions.
Why exclude them, as well as our Entered AppNntices and Fellow Crafts, if profanes are to a•sist in this labor ! There is no question of courtesy here. It ls a
question of Masonic law and Is not rightly viewed In any other light.
There is no prohibition against any other associations following the Lodge In procession to the grave, thus testifying their respect to the dead, but they are excluded
from Bil further participation.
This is the only rule that will prevent conflicts on each mournfal occasions, and
Is in strict accordance with our priooipleB.
Decision.-That a Masonic Lodge is Bt labor when conducting funeral services,
and in the performance of this or other Jllasonic labor in public it mnRt have absolute
control; and, while exercising this control, no noo-M:asonlo associations shall be
permitted to participate. This, of coarse, does not extend to religions exercises.
We have had our say on this question, In previous reports, and add no further
comments at present. Dispensations had been issued for .the formation of four new
Lodges.

It ha_s been said that a famous light-house off the coast of Cornwall, England, was
first bntlt by an ecoentric genius, who, proud of its structure, from its balcony
defied the storm. The. night came when the sea swallowed up the tower and builder.
It was built a second time of wood and atone by another, who perished in the flames
that destroyed it. Yet the third time it lifted np Its head under the skill of the
~uilder, who from the rock of the foundation took the stones of supel'l!trncture. Upon
its lower course was Inscribed, "Except the Lord build the bonse, they labor in
vain that build It." And on its keystone, above the lantern, the simple tribute
"Lana Deo." And the structure still standP, holding Its beacon light to the storm'.
tossed mariner.
The temple we are erecting has for its foundation stone, "Trost in God." In faith
hope and charity, we draw _from this foundatfo~ material for our superstructure, and
so long as we shall labor with terpperance,fort1tnde, prudence, and justice onr build·
ing shall riKe in wisdom, strength, and beauty.
'
·
In the performance of our work, let us hold aloft the Great Light which enables us
to separate the good from the evil, and may we lead onr fellow men to the trne
knowledge and worship of Him who alone can "cause onr feet to stand in an even
place." Then shall there he said of it : " The snn will no more be thy light by day
neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee ; but the Lord sball b~
unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory." In the study of our ritnal let
us not forget that our work and influence must be felt beyond onr Masonic halls. He
alone earns for himself the title of a workman that needeth not to be ashamed who
uses his light and knowledge not only to restrain bot to call back his brother' from
error's way, and to alleviate the woes ~nd misfortu!les of his fellow men. High upon
the Rocky Mountams thPre blooms a httle flower, hght and graceful in form. ~hough
the storms hover around it, oome early and linger late, it refreshes the air with its
perfume and fragrance. There Is no place so bleak and barren, pressed by the foot
of man, bnt there he may leave evidence of his kinship to the Great Creator, if he
will only imitate the Divine example. Here aud"there he may scatter words of kindness, love, and sympathy, and, by acts of mercy, refresh with perfume even the last
darkness that must come to the tired and worn spirit. If we would always be on the
alert in the dark _and by-ways of earth throngh which we most travel, we may discover hearts bendmg before the cold winds and storms of adversity, into which we
may drop the seed" whose bloom the world shall see." Our laws may be without a
flaw; the truths we teach and principles we hold be perfect in their adaptation to the
wants of man; but without we put them to practical nee, our tenets of Brotherly Love
Relief, and Truth are meaningless words.

Here is another absurd case on which the committee and Grand Lodge sat down
rather heavily:The specifications in this case charge the accused with insulting the Lodge publicly i11 the presence of" profanes." The evidence shows that there was a celebration and dinner by the Lodge, which the accused refused to attend, and, when asked
for his reason, he said that he did not want to eat dinner with two men who bad
swindled him out of $1,100 or $1,200; that it was hard at his age, when too old to
work, to lose that money by these men. This answer was made to a Mason, but in
the presence of some parties who were not Masons.
We do not know any law in Masonry that compels a man to eat dinner with a party
when he don't want to; nor do we know of any law that prevents a man from answering a question when It is propounded. We regard this trial, and the expulsion of the
brother by a vote of only eight members, as a farce. The record does not show that
the members were notified, according to law, of the meeting of the Lodge for the
trial, and, there being b11t eleven members present, we cannot presume that notice
was given.

The Grand Lodge of Montana commenced Its thirteenth Annual Communication In

Nineteen Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master submitted an Address, well written and full of exoellent suggestions for the benefit of the Craft. We cull a paragraph or two from the opening, as
Chey speak onr sentiments to a dot:It is often said that we make religion of Masonry. " Religion Ia the golden cord
that unites man to God; Masonry the silver line which rune from man to man."
We do not pretend to place Masonry on a par with religion ; bnt !ta mission is one
of peace ; 1t unites men of every country, sect and opinion, and brings them to one
com':llon altar. And while it does not compel a behef in any r.articular creed or
rebg1on, It does require of each Initiate that he profess a belief n the ex'.tence of

500

Proce,edings of the

· [Oct. 8,

God, the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe. It teaches reverence to God-that
there is a life beyond the grave-a hope in immortality.
Masonry is condemned by its enemies because it is a secret society. While it is
true that Masonry does its work in secret, it cannot be said that we conceal our
principles or designs. No society or sect in the world carries out the duties of reli'evmg the distressed, of comforting the widow and the fatherless, as faithfully and in VII·
riably as the Masonic Fraternity. Masonry advocates and upholds everything that
is calculated to promote the happiness and best interests of mankind ; and, while
pursuing its mission on earth, opens its doors and invites the good men of' everr
nation to enlist under its banner. It asks no one to go beyond his means or capact·
ties-requires ef us no more than we can perform; only our duty to God, our neigh·
bor. aud ourselves.
.
The world is full of men with little or no principle ; and, unfortunately for ns, too
many of them have got into our Lodges. There are Masons who seem unable to speak
well of any one: who are always ready and only too willing to circulate a slander
against a brother. Any slanderer is detestable, but more especially a Masonic slanderer. We cannot be too guarded in our words and actions. Masonry teaches us
to regard a brother's honor as our own. and to protect his good name whenever unjustly assailed. Masonry does not teach us to expose and perhaps magnify a .brother's faults, but to be charitable toward one who errs; to hide hie faults from the
world, while we admonish him privately; and by precept and example assist him in
regaining the position he has lost through folly or error.
The Grand Master alludes to the complaint made by Eureka Lodge, No, 16, of
Oalifornla, against Silver Star Lodge, No. 17, of Montana, for not refunding moneys
expended at Its request upon Bro. T. W. N1xoN, a member of the last named Lodge.

nnlimited expenditures of mone7s for the benefit of indigent members in a. foreign

The Grand Master apeaks these plain words relative to vices too prevalent among
Masons "who kuow the right and yet the wrong pursue:-"
I am of the opinion that the standing resolution .adopted at onr Sixth Annual
Communication, A. L. 5872, declaring that •'indulgence in the vices of In temperance,
gambling, licentiousness, and profanity, is virtual high treason to the most vital and

1878.]

Grand Lodge of California.

501

eHential tenets of Masonry," has not been as strictly enforced as it should have been.
If we desire to maintain the honor and advance the prosperity of the fraternity, we
should not, in our intercourse with the world, disregard its principles or neglect the
duties which it teaches. Indulgence In those vices not only injures the individual
Mason, but it brings disgrace upon the entire fraternity. Masonry is not a temper·
ance organization ; yet temperance Is one of the cardinal virtues of the Order.
.Masonry is not a religious Order; but it advocates a high standard of morality, and
teaches us to square our actions by the no erring rule of God's sacred word. Masonry
Is nllt a school for reformation; therefore those who Indulge In those vices should
not be permitted to enter our door. We are responsible for the character, and are
judged by the acts of our individual members; and when a brother wilfully violates
that resolution, and persistently refuses to listen to words of admonition, it is not
charity for his Lodge to tolerate such continued wrong-doing. It Is only self-preservation that such punishment as the nature of the case demands should be promptly
inflicted.
The Grand Lodge responded by adopting the following as a subatltute for the
standing resolutions then in force :Resol1Jed, That it is the determined sense of this Grand Lodge that the Indulgence
in the vices of intemperance, gambling, licentiousness, profanity, or either of them,
by Masons in this jurisdiction, should be promptly suppressed by the subordinate
Lodges; and it is enjoined as a constant and special duty of all Masters to counsel,
caution, and admonish the Craft in this respect; and in case of willful persistence,
the Lodge shall punish those foand guilty of such indulgence, by the infliction of
adequate penalties.

An elaborate oration was delivered by Bro. LEONARD W. COLBY, and published
in the proceedings. We make no apology for several liberal quotations therefrom.
They convey items of information to us, and we doubt not that they will to many or
our readers. The orator explores the dark ages of the past, and gives data relative to the Egyptian, Eleusinian, and Odinio mysteries. We give the substance of
what he says relative to their respective ceremonies of initiation, from which every
Mason can see how ridioulous is the belief of many that our rites were derived therefrom or have any connection therewith. First, as to the Egyptian:The. character of thi~ an~ient order, a.sit h~ been partially preserved in its initiatory r.ites and ceren_io!l~es, is a subject full of .mterest and instruction to the scholars
of our Craft. The mit1a.tory rite was a. mystic drama., i·epresenting the progress of
man from barbarism to civilization, and his oonll.icts, through darkness and toil,

Proceeaings of the

[Oct. 8,

to light and perfection. The ancient historian, PLUTARCH, describes the candidate
as a seeker of light and purity. At first he wanders in winding ways, with his mind
filled with uncertainty, perplexity, and doubt. Painfully and with great labor he
advances over rugged mountains and yawning chasms, plunged from time to time in
profound darkness. Again he sees everything under aspects the most terrible and
awful. Next he is a suppliant in the presence of the divine Osiris, who holds in his
hands the emblems of Justice and Benevolence. A miraculous light blazes upon
him. He is closely questioned, all the acts of his life severely scrutinized, and, if
worthy, he is allowed to pass to higher mysteries. Forward he moves, guided by an
initiate disguised as a dog, through mysterious labyrinths, till he comes to a stream
of water, where he is stol!ped by three terrible beings, who present him with liquid
from the dark stream which he must soon cross, and bid him drink, addressing him
in these words:" Aspirant to the honor of a divine companionshiI?, seeker after celestial truth,
this is the water of forgetfulness I Drink to the obliv10n of all your imperfections,
and thus be prepared for the reception of the new revelations of virtue, truth, and
goodness with wnich you are soon to be honored."
'l'he trembling neophyte drinks; the dark river is passed; the spectacles of terror
disappear; a divine light breaks on his vision; new scenes appear, and smiling fields,
flower-decked meadows, and enchanting visions of beauty, laden with the richest
perfumes of "Araby the Blest," environ him. Sacred songs and choruses of triumph, jo7, and love charm his ears. The sublime doctrines of sRcred science, art,
ancf religion are given him, and visions of holiness and profound beauty delight his
wondering eyes. He is baptized into a new life, and instructed in a divine science.
He is now free and perfect. He is crowned and triumphant, and goes henceforth to
commune with those pure spirits to whose companionsnip he has just been raised.
But the Greek or Eleusinian mysteries appear to have far exceeded these, if we
may judge from the following :The candid11te was first prepared for the solemn rite by days of abstinence, fasting, penitence, and prayer. He was then received into the Sacred Temple, into the
Provmce of the Hierophant, the Torch Bearer, the Sacred Herald, the Priest, and
Archer. The Hierophant sat upon a throne brilliant with gold and precious stones,
as the representative of the Creator. A robe of regal splendor graced his shoulders.
From his neck suspended a golden globe, the symbol of absolute powei;. On either
hand were twenty-four attendants, in snowy robes and crowns of gold. Seven
torches, refiected and multiplied by a thousand mirrors, dazzled the candidate. And
over all arched a rainbow, in whose mystic circle were seen the moon and seven
stars. After being blindfolded, the neophyte makes a long and painful pilgrimage.
He is led through dark and winding passages, up rough, sharp, and ragged ledges,
where jagged rocks tear his feet and limbs; through dense forests and miasmic valleys where he hears the fierce roar and snarling of savage beasts and the hissing of
serPents, and feels the clammy touch of bats and reptiles. The bandage is now taken
from his eyes, and he finds himself in a wild and strange region, whose gloom the
sun has never penetrated, whose horrors are seen only by pale spectral lights.
Fierce tigers and hyenas, and poisonous reptiles are on every hand. Thunder and
lightning, sulphurous fumes, fire and water, earthquake and tempest, threaten his
immediate destruction. Trembling with terror, he sees before him a huge iron
door, on wliich is emblazoned these words:.. He who would attain to the highest and most perfect state, and rise to the
sphere of absolute bliss, must be purified by fire and air and water."
The massive door swings on us hinges, and he is suddenly plunged into a vast
gloomy space which resounds with horrible groans and shrieks, loud wails of sorrow,
and penetrating cries of pain and anguish. On his right hand open the terrible gates
to grim and dread Tartarus, a fathomless gulf of fire, in which, passing and repassing,
ar11 seen the spirits of those who were false to truth, and life, and virtue, pursued by
avenging furies, with all the appalling incidents to the ancient doctrines of purification by lire. Behind him yawned the dark and dismal region or purgatorial air,
where burning winds carried wails of suffering and woe to his ears, and where the
mighty wheel of expiation rolled its endless circuit with ceaseless regularity. On the
left hand appeared the gloomy lake of Purification, half concealed by mists and
showers, into whoBI> murky, sulphurous waters were plunged the spirits of those less
guilty than their fellows.
After these and other awful visions of the great truth~ of religion and the eternal
principles of retribution, the candidate is led to another iron door, and thus addressed, in a deep and solemn voice, by his guide :" Consicfer the Divine Nature, the Supreme One. Contemplate Him without
ceasing; rule thy spirit and purify thy heart; and, walking in the way of justice and
the safe path of truth, admire Him who is alone the Master of the world. He is one.
He is self-existent. To Him &11 beings are indebted for life."

A voice of ho:r. is heard from within. The massive iron door slowly opens, and

"Odinic" Masonry, as the Orator calls It, prevailed In the north of Europe. Its
ceremonies of initiation were as follows:The neophyte personated & pilgrim who is weary with travel and desires rest.
Having wandered far and wide, he finally arrives at A1gard, tho City of God,
whose many mansions, with roofs covered with golden shlelds, have greeted the
longing eyes of the wanderer for many leagues distant. The guard leads him into a
lofty palace, whose huge doors close behind him with the nol1e or thunder. He is
taken from room to room, through varying scenes of life, tlll he come& to three
thrones, raised one above the other, on which are seated The High, the Eq11al to The
High, and The Hi~hest.
The pilgrim ism search of light and knowledge of the Sapreme One, and the following questions and reponses ensue :Pilgrim-" Tell me, 0 Lofty One I who is the first of the gods? Where doe1 He
dwell? What is His power? And what has He done to display Hie glory T"
The High-" He liveth from all ages; He governeth all realms, and 1wayeth all
things, great and small."
Equally High-" He hath formed heaven, and earth, and air, and all things."
The Highest-" And what is more, He hath made man, and given him & soal
which will live and never die, though the body sh11ll have mouldered away or have
turned to ashes."
Pilgrim-" What was the beginning of things? "
The High-(Ia the words of the Edda)
"'Twas Time's first dawn, when naught yet was,
Nor sand nor sea, nor cooling wave;
Earth was not there, nor heaven above;
Naught save a void and yawning gulf;
But verdure none."
Pil.grlm-" What is the end? "
The High-" There will be a new heaven ; and there will arise out of the sea a
new earth, most lovely and verdant, with pleas11nt fields where grain shall grow
unsown. A dwelling place shall be there more radiant than the sun. There the
sons of earth shall dwell together in peace and concord. Evil shall disappear from
the empire of Odin, and happiness and virtue shall be universal and perpetual."
The novitiate is then instructed by the Three in the science of life, and is given
the whole cosmogony of that ancient people who deified the forces of nature and
converted natural science into theology. The creation of the heavens and the earth,
of gods and men, is explained. He is taught the mysteries of life and the world.
They discourse to him of the son, moon, anil stars, of day and night, and the seasons; of the Destinies, of the Golden Age, of the way to heaven, of the Twilight of
the Gods, and of the final conflagration of the universe, of the great Ygdrasil-the
ash tree of life and death-of the Giant Ymer, whose flesh made the earth, whose
bones are the rocks, whose blood is the pulsing ocean, and whose skull is the great
blue vault of heaven.
The initiatory rite closed with a sublime representation of the world and humanity in its perfected er ideal state, where purity, love and peace shall reign eternal.

The report of the Committee on Grievances In one case presents a new point in
Masonic jurisprudence, and we copy its substance. A brother bad refused to plead
either guilty or not guilty, but simply nolo contendere, and had thrown himself
upon the mercy of the Lodge. The Lodge accepted tbe plea, and voted an indefinite
suspension. The committee thus reason, and, as we. think, corre.ctly :Masonic jurisprudence recognizes but two pleas in Masonic trials, guilty and not
guilty. The accused may plead guilty as to a part of the charp:es and not gftilty as
to the rest, or be may plead p;nilty and set up certain facts in justification or extenuation, but his plea must be either guilty or not guilty. Should the accused fail to
plead, it becomes the duty of the Lodge to tile a plea of not guilty. Our own Grand·
Regulations are In accordance with these principles of Masonic law. No such plea
. as nolo contendere is known in Masonry, and it would be establishing a dangerous
precedent to allow snch a plea to be received. When a brother is accused of crime
and put upon trial, the object is to prove his guilt or innocence. If guilty, then to
administer the proper punishment; if innocent, that he ebould be so declared. It is
entirely foreign to the purposes of the <Jraft to inflict a punishment until the guilt of
the accused Is clearly established. In this case, after the counsel for the accused
filed the plea signed by the accused, in which he said he neither admitted or denied
the allegations, be asked the Lodge to consider the accused guilty, and the Lodge
seems to have put that constrnction upon the plea, for they voted unanimously to
suspend him from all the privileges of Masonry. The record does not show that any
vote was taken upon the question or expulsion. .
In this case there are two very serious objections to the proceedings, viz.: the
plea of nolo oontendere, and the omission of the Lodge to vote upon the question of
expulsion. The Grand Constitution has wisely provided how the Lodge shall proceed to determine the degree of punishment to be inflicted. There are good and sufficient reasons, too apparent to need mention , why its provisions should be followed.
No departure from this role ehonld be allowed by this Grand Lodge. In our opinion,
the objection taken by the counsel for the Lodge to the plea or the accused was well
grounded; it should hRve been set &Ride , and if the accused failed to plead anew. a
plea of not guilty shonld,have been filed for him, and the trial proceeded with in the
regnla.r way.

adopted unanimously:Resol»ed, That this Grand Lodge views with deep sorrow the late action of the
Grand Orient of France, in. striking from its constitution that great fundamenta

principle and landmark of Freemasonry, the belief in the. existe!1ce. of God as the

We are here not only for legislative purposes, but to guard the trust lei\ to ns by
the Masonic fathers. That trust is a system animated by the spirit of universal
benevolence, on marred by the strife of sect or party ; its watchword is human brotherhood; its mission , peace and love. While claiming no divine origin, it builds op
the foundation truth that the " Lord reigneth: " atheism t.nd unbelief are therefore
alien to its system. The book of the law of God-the Holy Bible-is set forth as its
only rule of faith and practice, and is lifted up as a beacon light for humanity. No
other "book of the law" could have any other signification in Masonry, for all the
teaching, symbolism and lectures of the degrees of ancient Craft Masonry are drawn
directly from Holy Scripture. That sacred Word of God is reverently opened upon
our altars as a silent witness to the unseen presence of Deity. It Is borne forth in
ceremonial procession, that the world may know that the "light" by which true
Masons work is from the throne of Hix who Is "God over all, bfessed forever."

The Address of the Grand Master is able, and one of the best we have perused.
He congratulates the brethren on the fact that they " meet in a season of partially
recovered prosperity, when the incubus which, resting so long on all industrial
pursuits, has, In a measure, been removed ; when peace and plenty crown our
labors ; and the song of a happy people once again fills the land."
Here Is the Grand Master's view of the objects aod intents of Masonry, which
we could wish were "graven upon the fleshly tablets of the heart" of every brother,
and made the rule and guide of his conduct :·
Onr Masonry teaches a meek and quiet spirit ; charity for all unenlightened
brethren; a mode8t seeking to overcome, it may be, honest error; an exemplification
in our own walk and conversation of that friendship, love, and troth, so beautifully
taught in our rituals; an earnes~, hearty, continued elfort, without ostentation, to
benefit the human race; a looking after and alleviating di•tresa; a thoughtful care
of orphan children ; a diligence in onr respective callings; a liberal benevolence :
all these go to make up an nnselll•h , true, and beautiful Masonic character. Let us
emulate that pattern, so conspicuous in Masonry, whose virtnons conduct, unfeigned
piety, and inflexible fidelity to his trusts, made his life-work not only a ble,;sing to
those by whom he was surrounded, but a guide for us and countless generations yet
to come.

One of the Past Grand Masters , M. ·. w.·. WILLIAM G. HILL, had been called
away by death, and suitable tribute was paid to his memory by the Grand Master and
Grand Lodge. We copy two or three of the six and twenty decisions published :Illicit distilling is sufficient ground upon which to base charges against a brother,
and no hesitancy should be had in acting accordingly.
Financial difficulties between Masons should, if possible, be adjusted amicably,
but it Is not unmasonic, when other mean s fail, to bring an action at law.
Two persons, one a Mason, the other a profane, having dilferences of a private
character antecedent to the initiation of the latter, remain unreconciled , when it
comes to the knowledge of tbe initiate that the brother proposes to use the black·
ball when he applies for advancement. The initiate being a man of irreproachable
character and good citizen, the . Lodge generally being exceedingly desirous for his
advancement, ask what to do. A brother has tbe right to object.without a question,
and such objection, till removed , acts as a barrier to such advancement. Though
unwise, it is not unmasonic to declare what he will do in certain cases proposed.
The criminality lies in declaring the act performed; for instance, yon cannot try a
Mason for saying he will blackball a caudidate : bnt if, after he is blackballed, he
makes the declaration that he has done so, he violates an edict of the Grand Lodge,
and is liable to prosecution.
The Grand Master strongly and justly reprobates the act of the French Grand
Orient in striking from the faith of the Mason the belief in a God. On this faith,
which he deems the "foundation stone" of the Masonic building, the Grand Lodge

But the Committee on Jurisprudence thus reported, and the Grand Lodge concurred in the repon :The loss of an eye does not disqualify a candidate for the degrees of Masonry.

quota.lion; but our allotted space will only permit of one or or two. They are
Mr.sonic gems :Such persons appear to think that if the ancient traditions concerning the origin of
111.asonry are swept away, the whole super~tructure must fall; but the institution of
Masonry, whatever its age, exists not by so frail a tenure: It derives not its value as
an institution by reason of itB antiquity. It is no sacred outgrowth of the past, which
neither the experience of ages nor the changes of human society must be permitted
to affect. On the contrary, its value to-day is because it la a live, active institution,
adapted to the wants of man ; to help the unfortunate ; to redeem the erring; to rescue the lost; and whatever may be its origin, it has undoubtedly outlived many con·
temporary institutions. It has survived fierce opposition, true to ltB Ancient La.ndmarks and the high purposes of its institution among men, and has wielded a
mighty influence for the alleviation of human misery, and in bringing the human
family into more intimate relations with each other. A strictly historical address,
r eachmg back te the infancy of the order, tracing its rise and growth, describing its
struggle with civil a.nd ecclesiastical powers, and itB triumphant progreBB to its
present po•ition against all opposition, would not only be profitable to the craft at
large, but intensely interesting to the student of Masonic literature. I have neither
the ability nor material for such an address, and it is not my design, upon the present
occasion, to underta.ke;such a task. A more pertinent question is, what is the present
claim of Masonry, and what shall be its future infiuence in the world?
We need more light as to the great principles upon which our institution is
founded, because, if Masonry is to endure, those grca.t principles must remain , in the
future as in the past, the. basis upon which the whole superstructure stands.
The proposition of the Atheists and Materia!istB to strike out of the French Oon·
Rtitution the clause which declares that "Freemasonry is based upon the existence of
God and the immorta.lit)'.' of the soul," is portentous with danger to our ancient
Order. Whenever from its foundation these principles are wrested, the total demo!·
ition of the structure is not far distant. It is sincerely to be hOJ?ed that such a
departure from the Ancient Landmarks of the institution, if made, will at once sever
French Masonry from the great Masonic fraternity.
A great trust has been placeit in our hands . . A grand institution, hoary with the
lapse of centuries, but vigorous as in youth, appealing to the best and noblest feelings
o( the human heart, adapted to the wants of man as a social dependent being, bas
been bequeathed to us. Upon us restB the responsibility of preserving it and transmitting it to the generations to come.

The Address of Grand Master MoTT is long, but well written, and mainly occupied with the aft'airs of this large and important jnrisdiction. We are pleased t-0 read
these good words, which form part of the opening p&ragraphs. We wish the same
could be said of every jurisdiction and Lodge:From all the information I have been able to gather, I am satisfied that the moral
tone of Masonry in Texas was never better than now. There has been less comparative increase of membership than at some former periods of ita history, whieh of
itaelf is an auspicious omen. Lodges have given more attention to the exclusion of
unworthy material. The portals have been more closely guarded, and the moral
qualifications of candidates more strict!)' inquired into. Gambling, intemperance,
and kindred vices have been warred agamst, discipline enforced, and the laws and
regulations of this Grand Lodge generally observed and respected. The spirit, philosophy, and teachings of t .1e Order are being better understood, and its great moral
design more ap.Preciated. Still, much remains to be done in this direction. There is
yet much gropmg in the darkness by those who have been accustomed to consider
the ritual and lectures as the sum and substance of Masonry, though I am happy to
say that inqmry is awakening, and the moral beauties and sublime truths of the Order
are being daily more and more unfolded in the light of earnest investigation. When
every Mason m this jurisdiction comes t.o understand that Masonry means something more than lectures, attendance upon Lodge meetings, and the payment of
Lodge dues-that it is something higher, nobler, and better then a mere mutual aid
a8sociation, 11 brighter future will take the place of the already bright present. The
Fatherhood of GOd and the Brotherhood of Man find ample exposition in the spirit
of our institution. It reaches into and touches the hearts and homes of men, their
happiness and their moral welfare. It guides them into the sweet paths of virtue,
and holds out the hope of a glorious immortality. " Her ways are ways of pleasant.

There is something peculiarly touching and interesting in this record. Those
noble men, standing upon the confines of civilization, seeking to establish an Empire
in the almost untrodden .wilds of Texas, and looking forward with prophetic ken to
the time when the" wilderness would blossom as a rose," and" tower'd cities and the
busy hum of men " usurp the resort of the Indian and the home of the wild beastseemed to feel that Masonry was a necessary incident to the civilization of the AngloAmerican. They Haught to invoke its. beneficent teachings and humanizing influences
in aid of their grand undertaking. No higher tribute was ever paid to our Order.
No nobler estimate of its wisdom and truth was ever imprint.ad upon the records of
time.

adopted without dissent. We ·hope to see every Grand Lodge taking the ground of
the second resolution :~solved, That the Grand Lodge of New Mexico is hereby recognized as an independent Grand .Lodge, and welcomed to correspondence and the interchange of such
courtesies as are u•ual among Grand Lodges.
Resoi1Jed, That the Grand Orient of France, in abolishing from the foundation of
its Constitution the assertion of the exist.ence of God and the immortality of the soul,
and so opening its doors to atheism , bas made a fundamental change in its character,
and .we ca.n no longer recognize it as a pa.rt of the Masonic body.
We always look over the reports of the Committee on Grievances' in this Grand
Lodge, for we a.re sure to find something spicy and to the point. Here ls the way
they disposed of one case that came before them:• The question m11.y well be asked whether the specification contains any Masonic
offense. It is in these words:" 1. In that the accused, Bro. HODGES, is a member of a. club organized at Little
River Academy, who call themselves Free Thinkers, but better known as Infidels,
whose leading principles are a denial of the divine authenticity of the Holy Bible."
The most that this plea finds him · guilty of is belouging to a certain club whose
leading principles are found in the denial of the divine authenticity of the Holy
Bible. It does not necll!'sarily follow that he adopts all its t.enets, or promulgates
such doctrines. He may have joined from curiosity, a .desire to learn the reasons
held out by its members, or from social influences. Take the contrary proposition:
He belongs to the Masonic Fraternity; a society which takes the Bible for the rule
and guide of its faith, declaring it to he "the inestimable gift of God to man ."
Yet it would seem from the findings of the Lodge that he ignores the doctrines of
that society. Taking the two together, it would seem as if one was a set-off against
the other.
And here is a little touoh of waggery :There was one circumstance developed in the record which may tend to show
want of fairness, viz.: the 1lote was eight to seven, and it may occur to some that those
particular numbers smell loud to heaven.

our plan of commissioners than to have such .b urlesque " trials by the Lodge." And

UTAH.
The sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Utah was held in Salt
Lake City on the thirteenth day of November, 1877,- tbe M.·. W.·. JOSEPH MILTON
ORR, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.'. CHRISTOPHER DIEHL being Grand

The Address of Grand Master ORR does credit to his heart and pen. He congratulated his brethren that the "Angel of Death" had not visited them, and that "peace,
comfort, and happiness had attended their homes.'' He had visited nearly a.II the
Lodges in the jurisdiction, and speaks highly of those in Salt Lake City. But we
were sorry to read what he wrote of the Lodge in Corinne, the only Gentile city in
the Territory. If this plain history of what he saw doeA not arouse the brethren to
better and more decent conduot in the future, then they should be punished by the
arrest of their charter :After visiting the bl'ethren at Oirden, we took the train for Corinne. a bright little
city on the banks of Bear River. On arriving, our party desired to visit the Lodge
room, and requested different brothers resident there to accompany us. They could
not; all were "too busy." This seemed strange tons at first ; however, we passed
it by as the rel(nlar meeting was to be held that evenluir, at which time we visited
the Lodge room. We found a pleasant hall, we~! furnished, and would be attr~ ctive
if properly cared for. The reason was soon plain to me why the brethren hesitated
to visit their Lodge room durinll' the day. The Tyler's room had the appearance of
an old store honse, in which was deposited all the traps collected hy them ever since
the whistle of the locomotive was heard in the valley of the Wasatch, while the
Lodge room seemed to be the repository of the surplus alkali dust of that beautiful
city. The brethren doubtle•s regard the bl'oom, brush, and feather du_ster as profane, and will not admit them in their Lodge room . The records and minutes of the
Lodge "lay around loose," mixed up with those of the Odd Fellows, who occup.i: ~he
same ball. We met at the Lodge the Master, Tyler , two members, and three v1s1t111g
brothers: that was all. I was mortified, and my traveling companions blu•hPd for
shame. I speak in plain terms, and .mean ju~t ~hat I say. Th_e memb_e!shiJ? of this
Lodge is large-second to none outside of this city. Its financial cond1t1on 1s good,
and there can be no reason for the carelessness and negligence of the officers and
membere. .Additional words are not necessary.
Here ls one of the decisions of the Grand Master. It appears that the " one·eyed"
question, like BANQuo's ghost, will not down at the bidding. Grand Master Ona thus
met the vexed topic :Q. At an explosion of a mine in Little Cottonwood a man lost his let't eye. The

being a very moral and intelligent man would make a good brother. Can we receive
his petition?
· ..t. Yes, you can. But I say this Is the Masonic rule: No candidate can receive
the degrees who Is not of lawful age (21 years); nor can one who is in his dotage; nor
can any one who le lncapablll of supporting himself and family, .or of rec~iving and
communicating the mysteries of Freemasonry. The. old regulations relatmg to the
deformity of applicants Is greatly relaxed, and very justly so too.

Another of the Grand Master's decisions was as follow1 :Q. Has a member of a Lodge the right .to object to the advancement of a
brotner who has been elected for the degrees and duly Initiated an Entered .Apprentice, without giving his reasons for so doing?
·
...t. He bas such a right. No person can be initiated Into a Lodge without the
unanimous consent of the members present, Nor can he be advanced without a !Ike
consent, and the brother can not be required to give any reason for objecting. This
is a well seUled principle of Masonic law.
This decision i1 not in accordance with the law and practice In Oalifornla, nor do
we belien it harmonizes either with the principles of Masonio usage or oommon
sense. As against profanes we admit this rule in its widest extent, and any
Master or Lodge that disregards it should be summarily dealt with. But an
Entered .Apprentice 11 a Mason, and, as such, has rights, though not to the full
extent of a Master Mason. If unworthy, he should not be advanced, but he should
know what ha.a been objected to him, and should have the right to meet and explain
the charge. If not, what are the "rights" to which he has been admitted? We
have argued this question in former reports and will not enlarge. We think the
Grand Master and Grand Lodge of Utah wrong in their position.
We heartily concur in what is here said of the atheistic course of the Grand Orient
of France. Had no other sin been committed by it, this a.lone should break the bond
of friendship between it and all other Masonic Bodies. Belief in God is an essential
which admits of no liberty or cavil in Masonry :'I'hc Grand Lodges of America have for many years past had difficulties and misunderstandings with French Mason17, and now arises a new source of trouble
which we exceedingly regret. In charity we say that some erratic leader of French
Masonry has caused the name ot' God to be stricken from their Constitution. and profess a belief only in that old French adage, "Equality of man and Universe.! Brotherhood." We behave and feel that there is a God who will love and oherish us "after
shufHing off this mortal coil." It is a J?leasing thought, and one we can not and do
not surrender. A belief in Divinity is impressed upon our hearts. It grew with us
from infancy, and we carr1 it with us to the grave. When the Lodges of France
struck from their Constitution the name of the "Great I Am," they violated one of
the most auoient and revered landmarks of our Institution. France ought to learn
something from hiHtory, and remember that when infidelity wrote over the church·
yards of France," Death is an eterna.l sleep," their nation suffered, and that Order of
Brotherhood whioh teaches man" to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly before
his God," received a wound from which France never recovered.
We were pleased to read the following plain-spoken words of the Grand Master,
in relation to the fool blot upon Utah'e otherwise fair escutcheon:In concludinir my remarks, I have only a few words to say. Twelve years ago
there were no MaRonic Lodges in .this Territory, and now, with a population i>f
about 150,QOO inhabitants, we have only six subordinate Lodges; but that Is not discouraging to the brother who studies our history as .Masons, and who understands the
embarrassments with wblch we are mrround.ed. Our prospects, however, for the
future are every day growing brighter. I ha~ seen, during my residence in Utah,
many bad men acquire power, and fall because of their evil act&. I have seen good
men driven t'rom tlie Territory by the Intolerant rule of a fanatical priesthood, while
others fell beneath the stroke of the assassin's dagger from which the bravest men
recoil. It is not so now; the time has passed when men are compelled to cbev the

Let your thoughts wander backward, back to a period that will measure almost e.
century, back to a time when the thundering of' artillery was heard, and the smoke
from the battle fields of the revolution, slowly lifting, disclosed to view the powder
stained face of many a brave man who laid down his life that we of this day might
live, think, speak, and act as freemen; back beyond the days of steam and telegraphy;
back to a time when two great thoroughfares ran through the State from North to
South, one on the west side, the other on the east side of the mountains; back to a
time when the city of Burlington had less than three hundred inhabitants; back to a
time when the freemen of Vermont were struggling with the New York tories for
their homes, and Massachusetts was stretching forth her hand for a share of the
tight little State; and, with all these internal troubles, furnishing their share of men
to fight the battles of a Congress that would not give them a voice in her councils; and,
to the honor and glory e>f their wise leaders, they did it all without taxing the people
& dollar: back, I say, to 1781, the year ETHAN ALLEN, who is sleeping just. above us at
Winooski, wrote to Congre~s that he was re,olutely determined to defend the independence of Vermont, and rather than fa.ii, he would "retire with the hardy Green
Mountain Boys into the desolate caverns of the mountains, and wage war with humau
nature at large," Back, in fact, to the month Governor CmTTENDEN wrote his
famous letter to General WASHINGTON, detailing Vermont's situation, and ma.king" an

independence."

head in old Virginia, as well as in some jurisdictions further west:Being informed by a District Deputy Grand Mll8ter that a member of one of our
most flourishing Lodges, consisting of Christians and Jews, had publicl.v and seriouslv avowed that no Jew should be admitted within the Lodge-thereby causing great
detriment to it, and exciting one cla.as of its members 11211inst the otlier, each threatening to exclude by their ballots every candidate of the opposite religious persuasion! held such conduct to be so grossly unmasonic that it should not be overlooked ;
that no one had a right to set up hie narrow opinions against one of the fundamental
principles of Mll8onry. All it requires on this subject from 11 candidate for initiation
mto its mysteries, is that he have a sincere belief and trust in God. Beyond this,
it is not lawful for any Ma.eon, or body of Masone, to impose any religious test upon
11 candidate for admission. If he have the necessary moral and physical quali£ca.tions, 118 prescribed in our Book of Constitutions, the doors of our -Lodges should be
118 wide open to a J ew as a Christian. - Moreover, a. Lodge fa not compelled to submit
to its destruction, in deference to the wilfulness or prejudice of any of its members.
Whilst the secrecy of the ballot is not to be int1>rfered with, and no enquiry is permitted as to how 11 member has voted, even though such vote be injurious to the
welfare of the Lodge, it is wholly different when one seriously avows his purpose to
use the ballot in order to violate one of the great principles on which our mst1tution
is founded. Such an avowal, deliberately made, proves the offender to be wanting
in that charity which a Mason must have and practice. I therefore instructed the
District Dopu{y Grand Mll8ter to warn the offending brother that unleBB he wholly
abandoned this erroneous principle and would heartily conform his conduct to what
llfasonry requires, he would be subjected to a trial ; and required, u nless he did so
abandon it, that the District Deputy Grand Master should see tha.t cha.rges, with
proper specifications, were preferred. And 118 other members had threatened reta.liation, (which though natural, was very unmasonic,) I instructed him to administer 11
sharp rebuke to them.

Grand Master COTTRILL presented an AddreBS which is all excellent and timely
those which had already emanated from the same pen. He had granted dispensations for four new Lodges. He had visited many of the Lodges during the year,
and found them generally prosperous and harmonious. Among other things he had
decided that" an Entered Apprentice who had not applied for advancement for nine
yea.rs, and had in the mean time lost his right hll!ld, was ineligible for advancement."
This decision is somewhat ambiguous in its language. If the Grand Master meant
that the prolonged delay had disqualified the Entered Apprentice for advancement,
we should be inclined to say, "served him right;" but if for the other reason, we do
not believe the decision is either sound law or justice. An analogous oaee was very
generally discussed several years since In Grand Lodges, and, although diversity of
opinion and decisions prevailed, the preponderance, and as we believe rightly, was
in f"vor of 'advancing the maimed Mason-because he was a Maaon. Tho principle
underlying this decision would prevent a Master Mason who had lost hi~ right arm
from visiting a Lodge, for reasons palpable to every Mason. Would Grll!ld M1111ter
COTI'BILL go that length?

In reference to the adoption of the new amendment to the Constitution, Bro.
SIMONS, of New York, has these few well expressed sentences:At the annual assembly in September last, the amendment was adopted by a decisive majority, (for its terms see Ante, under England,) and a committee was named
to revise the rituals, to the end of making them conform to th11 new Constitution.
It was claimed in the debat.e that the 'object of the amendment was not to denv the
existence of God, but to place French Masonry on the plane of the .widest toleration,
refusing admission to no man for his opinions. It is only necessary for us to remark
that, so far as Masonry is concerned, there is a limit to toleration-a distinction
between liberty and license. The very corner-stone of the institution, as it has come
down to us from the fathers, is the belief in the existence of one ever-living and true
God , not as a theory of sectarianism, but as a universal principle of all religion and
all.morality. Given a ~elief in .the existence ?f God, .the qrea~r and Ruler of the
umverse, Masonry neither desnes nor permits any mqmry mto the creed of its
adherents. They may be J ews or Moslems or Christians; they may accept Mahomet
or Confucius•or Jesus Christ, and there is nothing to be said; but certain it is that one
who denies the existence of God cannot be made a Mason. ]'reemasonrv is neither
a form of worship nor a sect, for it respects the opinions of all men; 'but having
adopted in the beginning the belief to which we have alluded, it can permit no toler-

We do not deem it necessary to ma.ke any apeolal recommendation. Our official

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 8,

The question coming from the hearhl of the younger brothers sounds loudly and
audibly before my eus: "It shall be practiced, that we know; but is it really practiced? that we should like to know," my brothers I I give you an unequivocal, precise answer: "Freemasonry is a human institution, and as such not perfect; its
members are human beings, who, when tried and initiated, are neither omniscient,
nor exempt from weakness. Therefore not every Freemason is an ideal, a perfect
brother; but generally and wholly brotherly love is practiced with great willingness.
resignation, and sacrifice. I refrain from recounting the examples of energetic and
unremitting brotherly love, which have passed ID\Y spiritual eye from the time when
the Master's gavel made me a Freemason. I am unable to say how often I have seen
that relief was granted before it was asked for. And for that reason my confidence
is not diminished, if I should even once see that brotherly love is comprehended less
ideally. The thirty years, which I have passed as a Freemason, preach audibly:
'There is such a thing as brotherly love I It is net a.n empty word, it is a tangible
fact.'"
lt stands the test, not only in ·trllles, coined metal, or favors, but also in the most
serious situations of life. A brother Apprentice puts the question to me, "We are
instructed in the sign for assistance, is that ever used?" I a.newer it in a few examples.
.
You all know how renowned the powerful, indefatigable Bavarian troops have
been in the late German-French war. When the first French captives were sent to
the homes·of the !blue devils (di.ables bleu), the;i: were in great fear that t.hey would
be ill-treated, for they had only seen this terrible people in deathly conllict. The
train stopped at the depot in Munich, which was filled by one thousand curious people; one of the captives, an officer, made a certain sign and half a dozen spectators
ran to the window of the car, shook hands with the brother, assisted hiru m alighting, and during his whole stay the officer resided with a Mason, and found happy
days where he only feared to find dread and horror. At that time the news came
from Munich. A new proof of the kindliness of the inhabitants of our city was given
Iat.ely at the railroad depot. When the first Frencli prisoners arrived, an officer,
who expected to find in the home of the feared Bavarians only " devils," tried to
awaken the sympathy of the crowd by stating that he was the son of a poor widow.
Immediately citizens of this city stepped to hi• car, stretched out their hands, and
one of theni took him to his residence, etc. We, my brothers, know what the prisoner said; the profane, indeed, did not understand it.
He continued to relate similar occurrences in the year 1866, 1813, and he even
traveled over to this continent, and speaks of such deeds performed in 1860, in Texas,
and on July fourth, 1873, in New Haven, and concludes as follows:Brotherly love proves itself in the hour of danger; it duplicates joy, alleviates
grief; it i s the sun that spreads happiness over the whole univel'l!ll, wherever brothers meet.
And why have I to-day unfolded before your eyes all these facts? Because to-day
all the brotbers of the four Eclectic Lodges of this Orient, and a great multitude of
visiting brethren, are assembled here, and I wish to close with the admonition, "Go
and do likewise !''
CONCLUSION.
Here again we lay a.side our pen. Our work has been pleasant, rather than tedious, though taking up much of our time. If our present report shall prove acceptable and profitable to our Masonic readers, we shall have no regrets, as certainly we
have no apologies to offer. We have done what we could, and submit this specimen
of our skill for inspection. We have not tabulated the various items of Grand Lodge
information, but in each review have given the number of Lodges and members.
We think the total will not vary substantially from that of last year. Some jurisdictions have increased, some stood still, and others have decreased. But we
believe we can say that the cause of Freemasonry moves onward. The internal,
rather than the external, improves. And may that good work go on, until practical
Masonry in the lives of its professors, shall be all that the theoretical is in the manna.ls and work. We are glad to see such uniformity of expression from Grand Masters and Grand Lodges, in reprobation of the action of the Grand Orient of France
in relation to a belief in God and the Immortality of the Soul. These are, indeed,
fundamentals, and if the corner-stone be displaced, the superstructure will totter
and fall. We have proposed no formal action thereon on the part of our own Grand
Lodge, but would suggest a concurrence in the almost unanimously expressed ver
diet of American and British Grand Lodges.
All which is respectfully submitted, for the committee, by
'
WILLIAM H. HILL, Chairman.
