Bro. THOMAS H. CASWELL, from the special committee to whom had
been referred the Address of the Grand Master and the Report of the
Grand Secretary, presented the following reports:To the M." W." G1·and Lodge of California:Your committee, to whom was .referred the third Annual Message of our M. ·• W.·.
Grand M:aster,have read with great care and much profit ihat admirable paper; and,
in submitting their report, desire particularly to call the attention of the Grand
Lodge, and of the fraternity generally, to the extelleat exposition of what Masonry
really Is, and of the duties incumbent on as ·as Masone, in all the relations of lifecivil, religious, and social-a set forth in the introductory part thereof.
The custom too commonly prevails, in papers of this kind, to leave everything like
wholesome admonition in the backgroiind, and to portray the grandeur and enbliroity
of the teachings of Masonry, rather than to hold the. mirror of truth before us, as our
Grand Master has done, so that our short-comings may be realized and the opportunity for amendment given. The enemies of Masonry are ever watchful and are quick
to detect the least remissness in its professed votaries; but the victory is surely ours
if we tut keep the faith we have plighted and practice what we teach. With
appreciative gratitude then to the M.·. w.·. brother who has BO skillfully withdrawn
the vail, however thin it may have been, which obscured our moral viHion, let us
resolve to be henceforth truer men, more faithful MasonR, and better citizens-with
more of love in olir hearts, and a charity for all that shall be both warm and effective.
Your committee would particularly commend another portion of the message to
the thoughtful consideration of the Grand Lodge-that in which he so feelingly and
ably refer~ to "the meagre attendance at the funeral of a brother." Would that it
were possible for us to believe the reference unwarranted, and that a dereliction so
sad and flagrant could not be chargeable to Masons, anywhere. The fact, however,
exists; and it is rightly characterized as "deplorable." Caaµot some means be
devised by which the evffmay be remedied and the reproach it occasions be removed?
At least, Jet the closing words of the Grand Master upon this subject Rink deep into
the hearts and minds of all-" to honor the dead is commendable; to ignore .the dead
is l11mentable. · Masonry inculcates the first, and condemns the last."
The good resulting from tbe regulation requiring Inspectors to report to the Grand
Master the condition of' tbe Lodges In their several districts, is manifest from the
information so clearly, though briefly stated by him, and derived from that source
alone. Iu no other way could the Irregularities weatioaed be brought to your notice,
or the means of correction be afforded. Your committee unite with ·the Grand Master
in expressions of regret that thirteen of these conservators of Masonry were so
unmindful of its welfare as to neglect so paramount a duty; and, fully concurring in
his suggestions, would recommend that so much of the message as relates to the subject of Inspectors be reforred to a special committee.
·
The thanks of the Grand Lodge are again due to the Grand Master for the con·
tinuance of the system of visitations so successfully pursued by him. The time spent
and fatigue endured in this self-imposed duty, are aptly illustrated in the comparison
instituted· but the amount of good accomplished is beyond calculation or illustration.
The seed bas been sown-may t.he harvest be early and abundant, and the fruitage
perfection.
·
Your committee, contrary to their intention and desire, are reminded that they

Yonr committee, to whom was referred the transcript of the record of the second
trial of G1waox M. PINNEY, by Oakland Lodge, No. 188, resulting in his acquittal,
have examined the same and report-That the accused was convicted by the above named Lodge on the first trial and
sentenced to be expelled ; that the case was sent back to the J,odge for a new trial
for the technical reason that " no summons was actually served on the accused as is
required by law ; " and that at the same time your committee reported that " the
evidence produced on the trial was amply eufficient to warrant the sentence of expulsion which was adjudged by the comml~eioners." (See Proc., 1877, page 192.)
Now, the evidence presented at this second trial was identical with that offered at
the first, it being a certified copy from the reoords of the Nineteenth District Court
of tlie divorce of the accused from his wife for repeated acts of adultery, together
with the cumulative evidence that the accused had llpplied for a new trial in the said
Court, and that his application had been denied. Under these cii;-cumatances your
committee are at a loss to understand how the commissioners could have rendered a
verdict of acquittal, and they therefor offer the following resolution and 'recommend
its adoption :-.
Resolved, That the action of Oakland Lodge, No. 188, in acquitting GEORGE M.
PINNEY, be reveraed and set aside, and that he be and is hereby expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.

578

· [Oct. 9,

An examination or the evidence introdnced at the trial shows that the offence was
clearly proven, and that the accused was properly convicted. It only remains then
to consider whether or not a simple reprimand was an adequate punishment. Had
the acCtDsed confined himself to mere abuse, yoor committee might po811ibly, though
most unwillingly, have allowed the verdict to stand without interference ; but when
he so far forgot himself and his Masonic obligations as to threaten to kill a brother
Mason, and that, too, within the walls of his own Lodge, they are of the opinion that
the commissioners erred in awarding so light a penalty. No possible circumstances
can justify the use of snch language, and your committee offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:Re1olved, That the action of Pactfic Lodge, No. 136, in sentencing JACOB DEUTSCH
to be reprimanded, be reversed and set aside,·and that the said accused be and is
hereby suspended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Yonr committee, to whom was referred the appeal of ELISHA HENBY HALL from
the action of .E'uening Star Lodge, No. 186, in expelling him from all !he rights and
privileges of Masonry, have had the same under consideration and report that the
accused was charged with striking a brother of his Lodge, an<! also of using vile and
obscene language toward~ him, both In the Lodge-room and upon a public street.
Both of •se charges are fully established by the evidence. The accused, as it
appears from the trial-record, endeavored to Introduce certain testimony apparently
intended to show that he had reason to think that the brother aBSaulted by him had
injure<!, or endeavored to Injure, him in some way at some former time. The Master
very properly rnled this out as Irrelevant and having uo bearing on the matter in
hand. It Is folly time that Masons should understand that this Grand Lodge has
again and again decided that no previous provocation will warrant personal violence
or the use of indecent or threatening language to a brother Mason. The notice of
appeal sent to the Lodge by the accused Is a most remarkable specimen of verbal
pyrotechnics; and, if words could annihilate, your committee are quite sure that
there would be nothing left by this time either of the :Master of the Lodge or the
commissioners thereof. Fortunately they have escaped this threatened disaster and
are still borne npon our rolls as very live men, willing to brave any amount of further
danger in the good cause.
Yoor committee offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption by the
Grand Lodge:.;...
Reaolved, That the action of Evening Star Lodge, No. 186, in expelling ELISHA
HENBY HALL from all the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is hereby
&ftirmed.

ere, In rendering a verdict of suspension rather than one of expulsion, went fully as fa

Bro. WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, from the Committee on Grievances,
presented the following report :To the M. ·• W. •• Grand Lodge of Oal!forn1a 1Your committee have had before them the appeal of JAKES HOWARD from the
action of Ferndale Lodge, No.198, in et.palling him from l\Jl the rights and privileges
of Masonry, have carefully euminEd the ao-calle4 evidence upon which he wa&
~xpelled, and report as follows : -

586

Proceedirl{JB of the

[Oct. 10,

The a.ccused was charged with misappropriation of a portion of the funds of the
Lodge, he being at the time its Secretary. When the commissioners met, the a.ccused
was absent. He excuses himself for this on the ground that he came to Ferndale
from a distance for the express purpose of being present and presenting his defense,
which he claims would have fully exonerated him; that he supposed the meeting was
called at seven and a half o'clock in the evening, whereas it appears that the time
appointed was ten o'clock in the morning; and that, in his ignorance of this, he
retired to a hotel a.nd, having had no sleep for several nights, went to bed, and con·
sequently was not aware that the trial was in progress until after its termination.
These facts alone, if trne, would seem to warrant your committee in sending back
the case for a new trial; but apart from this, they should be compelled to take that
course, for the reason that the transcript of the trial-record fails to show a.ny evidence
whatever to support the verdict.
.
The accused seems to think that a prejudice exists in the minds of some of the
members of Ferndale Lodge, which might militate against him in a new trial, and
asks that his case be transferred to some other Lodge in its vicinity; but your com·
mittee are confident that there is no necessity for this. They have too high an opin·
ion of the average Masonic character to believe that commissioners chosen by any
Lodge in this jurisdiction would decide age.inst a. brother when he we.a able to show
that he was guiltless of the offense charged; and, in any event, should he deem himself to have been wronged, he has recourse to this Grand Lodge, in which he is sure
to obtain full and ample justice. They therefore recommend the adoption of tho
following reBOlutlon : Re1olvFd, That the action of Fernc:laleLodge, No.193, In expelling JAMES How.um
from a.II the right.a a.nd privileges of Me.sonry, be reversed e.nd set aside, e.nd the.t the
case be reme.nded to the ea.id Lodge for a. n ew trial.
All which i' respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM T. REYii!OLDB,}
JORN c. PARTBIDOJi:,
Committee.

AND BRETHREN OF THE GRAND LODGE:Jam but a novice in Masonry, for "I am but of yesterday" as to my membership,
eompared with many of the sage and venerable brethren before me. This will plead

our honorable fraternity. But, what I lack in age of membership, msy be made up

and in me there burns all the enthusiasm of a first love. From the freshness of m7
ns i give utterance to thoughts of the honr.
0
Onr system· has many elements ef attraction, and seems to me to have incorpor·
ated not 11 few principles fitted to impart stability and guarantee a noble immortality.
I. It potently appeals tons by its antiqnity. We are so constituted by our Crea·
tor as to be susceptible of such an appeal. Vastness or duration gratifies our sense
of the sublime, inspires us with awe, lirte us into a mo.od of reverence, chastens and
subdues the spirit. Thus the ocean touches us, for it is old. Navies have swept its
waters and commerce ploweli its billows; but it is older than the white·winged ships
of Tarshish or the men of war that roamed amidst the Isles of Greece, at once repellen
of the Persian tyrant and defenders of their own most sacred liberties. Old .1 Who
knows when it lay in the hollow of God's hand, even as a dew-drop within a rose-bud,
until He had carved for it 11 tlwelling·plaoe in earth's deep bosom, and there set it to
be the everlasting mirror of His own infinitude ? Its age overpowers and spell-binds
us. But even this aged thing is as nothing compared with His age who is the Supreme
Architect of the Universe, and in whom we place our trust. He is the Ancient of days.
When not a billow heaved, not a wild bird sang, not an ancient hill kissed the heavens ;
when not a ra_li of light had traveled, not a planet wheeled, not a snn burned; when
not 11 seraph had wa~ed his pinion, or, with the wing wherewith he swept into the
presence of His Maker, vailed his face-then was He, the All·Snfficient, the I·Am;
and, in His Nature, t.he very principles which form the essen.ce and strength of onr
ancient Order-truth, justice, lo•e, dwelt; having neither beginning of day, nor end
of life. · Our principles are as old as God.
And, going back to the distinguished persons of whom we speak e.s the historic found·
ers of our Order, through what centuries are we borne; on wh'at ruins of empires look
we down. DJmasties blotted out; seats of kingdoms transferred from ori:mtel to

name and a memory. But in us there glows the fire of an unwasted yonth. We,
after the rush of centuries, renew our youth like the eagle! We, despite the perils
and trials and slanders of foes, secular and spiritual, ask our enemies to trace a
wrinkle npon our brow, or pluck a gray hair from our exuberant locks. We, like
Israel's great leader, after the lapse of near three thousand years, move forth, bathed
In the dew of the morning, with eye undimmed, with form erect, with natural
strength unabated, destined to run a race with time, and prove, in our principles,
heirs of a radiant and rapturous immortality.
rr. It appeals te ns by the element of the mysterious. This susceptibility of onr

III. Would the Secrehryof a Lodge be justified In rel'uslog to receive the dnes of

The Grand Master answered that the Lodge has a right to expect that every member In arrears will, if he cannot pay, either directly or indirectly make known his
condition and ask remission or Rn extension of time for payment, and that a failure
1o do so would be calpe.ble. The presumption is, and should bl!, that each payments
a.re when made by others than the party himself, me.de with the knowledge and co•··
sen~ of tbe party, bnt that the Secretary would be warranted in refusing to receive
nch payment when tendered by parties who are induced to make it by their own
personal interests, and when the receiving of it might be in contlict with the good of
the Lodge.
As the case was put to the Grand.Master, his decision was right. As a rule, however, It should not be left to the discretion of the Secreta.ry to determine whether a
brother off'ering to pay the dues of another was doing it to subserve his own personal
Interests or not, or whether the good of his Lodge would be best promoted by receiving or refusing the payment. The presumption is, and should be, that the brother
making such payment does it from pure motives, and that it will meet the approval
of the party for whom it is made. If a brother is in arrears for does and Is about to
be or has been, snspended for non-payment thereof, ordinarily another may properly 1
co:Ue to his relief and make the payment for him, without his knowledge ; and the
olrcnmstances must be pecnliar that would make it proper for the Secretary to lnqnire as to the motive. The consent 'of tbe party for whom tbe .payme.nt ~ made
must be presamed, because it is for his good. If, liowever, havmg the ablhty, he,
himself, had refused to make the payment, then no other ~hould off'er or should be
allowed to make it for him. We do not want unwilling members.
A Lodge must exact the payment of dues to en&ble It to meetltR necessary expendlditurea and a member ls bound te pay his dues as he ls to pay every other debt. If
he negiectB to pay without excuse rendered, the law suspends him and cuts him off
from his Masonic privileges so long as his neglect continues. He may reiieve himself at any time by making the payment, and no good reason occurs to y?ur committee why he should not be relieved if another makes the payment for him. If a
case should occur in which a brother, from improper motives, should pay, or offer to
pay the arrearages of another, he may be dealt with for his actual or attempted
wro~g. No Lodge ought to have any me.mber whose dues, if ~n arrears, i.t wonld
not be willing to receive from any oue oft'errng to pay them; .and,if any one of its members, suspended for non-payment of dues, i~ unworthy. of restoration, he should be
dealt with in the manner prescribed by our laws.

·
Your committee most heartily indorse the decision. There is an old law maxim

men for off'ences against the m<1ral law, but does not attempt to enforce the payment
of debts.

v. When charges have been preferred by one Mason against another, is it competent for the accused to adjust the diifereoces and then withdraw the charge1?
In the particular case brought to the attention of the Grand Master, his dec!Bir .i
may ha.ve been right, but would It be a safe rule to adopt to allow the accuser to
settle and dismiss the case? Your committee think not. Whenever charges have been
preferre,d,which ought to be entertained at all ,tbe Lodge and the whole body of Masons
are interested in the result; and It ought never to be permitted that any Mason should
make use of the procedure of the Lodge for the adjustment of his private business
affairs. That procedure Is criminal and ls intended to punish olfenses. When
offenses have been committed we are all Interested to see that the olfender is punished, and it should never be left to the accuser to determine whether or not the
trial should proceed. The Master of the Lodge should, In the exercise of a proper
discretion, determine whether the oll'ense charged .is of such a chuacter as to
demand investigation, and In that he will look to the Interest of the Craft and not to
the private interests of the acoueer.

question of authorizing auoh l11oorporatloae la before the Grand Lodge for consideration and determination , no Lodge should attempt to forestall Its action.
VII. Your committee fully concur In the following decisions of the Grand
Master:let. That, when charges have been preferred and oommlssloners have been
elected, a trial must be had, and that the fact• that a grand jury had ignored a bill
against the party for th-e olfense charged, could not relieve the commissioners from

2d. That a Lodge may dispose of real estate or other property as any other
owner might:
3d. That a non-affiliate may apply to any Lodge in this jurisdiction for membership:
4th. That the members of a Lodge are not entitled to know or to inquire the
nauie of the brother who interposes an objection to the initiation of a candidate any
more than they would the name or motives of the party casting a black ball :
5th. That, in elections, blanks found in the ballotrbox ought not to be counted as
v otes cast:
.
6th. That persona who have lost one or more fingers of the right hand, and all
persons who have not their right limbs as men ought to have, cannot lawfully be
made Masons in California.

Bro. WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, from a majority of the same committee, presented the following report :To the M.'. W.·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :In the matter of the petition for restoration of CHARLES. How ARD GORDON, who
was expelled by Woodbridge Lodge, No. 131, on the sixteenth day of January, 1875,
your committee have again carefully examined into t~e merits of the case, and feel
that they can add nothing to the very full and exhaustive report presented at the last
Oommunication of this Grand Lodge.
Though still holding to the opinions expressed by your previous committee, in
regard to the injustice of his expulsion, yet, after having t~ke~ the advice of. many
prominent Masons residing in that section of the State, and m view of the c~ntmuous
and bitter opposition to his restoration evinced by all the members of his former
Lodge, a majority of your committee feel compelled to report that it will be for the
best interests of .Masonry that the prayer of your petitioner should not be granted.
They therefore recommend the adoption of the following resolution :Resolved, Th~t the petition of CHARLES How ARD GORDON, for restoration to all the
rights aud privileges of Masonry, be.11nd is hereby denied.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM T. REYNOLDS, l Of the Committee.

Bro. JoN.A.TRA.N D. HINES, from the Committee on Finances, presented the following reports:To the M. ·• W.·, Grand Lodqe of California : Your committee report th11;t the claims, for necessary expenses In attending the
Grand Lodge, presented by Bro. JOHN MILLS BROWNE, Grand Master, for $26 00, and
by Bro. WILLU.H HENRY CRANE; Junior Grand Warden, for $61 00, amounting in all
to $87 00, are correct, and It le recommended that they be p1id.
Your committee, to whom was referred the report of the Grand Secretary relative to Masonic contributions for the yellow-fever sufferers in Louisiana, Miesiseippi,
and Tennessee, report that they have examined that paper, with its accompanying
vouchers, and find that, as usual, all has been done thoroughly and well ; and they
would do Jess than their duty were they to dismiss, without proper commeudatio11.
the excellent manner In which that officer has conducted that business and the
promptitude with which he has acted·In forwarding the contributions to our brethren
in those a1!1.icted States. ·
Volumes would be inadequate to properly express the admiration which all must
feel for the generous donors who so promptly and liberally responded to the cry
of anguish and sorrow which arose from these fever-stricken districts, and it speaks
to the credit of humanity and Masonry, that 11 brotherhood, at this time poor and
struggling with its own necessities, should, almost lo 11 moment, imbued with the
grandest sentiments of love and charity, rise as one man in response to the wail of
woe, suffering, and sorrow in our sister States.
.
Your committee r ecommend that the report be printed with the proceedings, and
that, so soon as all reasonable apprehension ot' a necessity for further need shall have
passed away, the Grand Secretary distribute the amount remaining In his bands to
the aeveral donors, In the proportions paid by each, and that he report hie action
thereupon at the next Annual Communication.
And your committee further desire to have perpetuated their remembrance of
the aid which this Grand Lodge bas received in its charit11ble efforts, by recommend·

PART II.

ARTICLE VIII.
OF ITS REVENUES AND THEIR SOURCES.
SECTION 1. The revenue of the Grand Lodge shall be derived from the following
sources:1st: From fees charged for dispensations, charters, diplomas, and other documents
issued 'under its authority:
2d. From contributions levied upon the Lodges, which shall always be equal and
. .
uniform, in proportion to their membership and degrees conferred: and
Sd. From the funds, dues, a.nd prooeeds of all property of dissolved Lodges w1tl11n
its jurisdiction;
SEC. 2. The following shall be the fees charged as above, exclusive of those
provided in Seo. S, Art. IV, Part II, to be paid to the Grand Secretary:1st. For a dispensation to form a new Lodge, the sum of seventy-five dollars:
2d. For a charter to perpetuate a Lodge, the sum of fifty dollars:
Sd. For a dispensation to hold an election of an officer or officers at a time other
than that presoribecl in Seo. 1, Art. I, Part IV, the sum of ten dollars:
.
4th. For a dispensation to ballot for a candidate for the degrees, without the reference to a committee prescribed in Sec. 3, Art. III, Part III, the sum of ten dollars:
5th. For a dispensation to receive and act upon the petition of,a re.)ected candidate for the degrees, within a iess period than the twelve months prescribed in Sec. 2,
.&.rt. Ill, Pe.rt III, the sum of ten dollars :
6th. For a dispensation to receive and act upon the petition for degrees of a person belonging to the army or navy of the United States, who may not possess the
qualification of residence prescribed in Bee. 2, Art. III, Part III, the sum of ten dollars: and
7th. For a diploma of any kind, the sum of one dollar, except when issued for
the widow or children of a deceased Mason, in which case there shall be no charge;
but no diploma shall issue except upon the presentation to the Grand Secretary of a
.certificate from the Secretary of a Lodge, in one of the forms prescribed in Art. III,
Part VII.
SEO. 3. In no case shall either of the foregoing documents be issued until the
fees therefor shall have been paid to the Grand Secretary.
BEo. 4. The following contributions shall be paid as annual dues by each of the
Lodges, whether chartered or under dispensation, at the time and in the manner provided in Bee. 4, Art. II, Part III:.
Jet. For ea.ch degree it she.II have conferred during the year, the sum of one
dollar:
2d. For each Master Mason borne upon its roll at the date of its annual report, the
sum of one dollar :
And the Grand Lodge may levy, in addition to the above, such other contribiltionB
IM in its judgment may be required.
BEo. 5. In case of the dissolution 'of a Lodge, the Grand Secretary, or some
brother by him duly authorized, shall at once prooeed to receive its funds on hand,
collect its outstanding dues, and dispose of its jewels, furniture, and other property
of every kind, in such manner as shall seem to him most judiciou1; and he she.II
place the proceeds thereof, after the payment of all just debts and necessary expenses,
among the funds of the Grand Lodge.

8. At the close of each Annual Communication, a committee, to be known as the
"Committee on Pay of Members" and to consist of ftve, shall be appointed by the
Grand Master, whose duty it shall be to ascertain, during the year succeeding, the
exact cost of transportation for one person from the location of each Lodge in the
State to the place of meeting of the Grand Lodge and back again; and, at the fol·
lowing Annual Communication, to report such cost of transportation as the sum due
to the officers or representative in attendance from euch chartered Lodge, which sum
shall be paid by the Grand Treasurer, 11nch report being his voucher therefor. But
no payment shall be allowed for the officers or representative of any Lodge, the dues
of·which Rhall not have been paid in full.
9. .The appointed Grand Ollloers and the chairmen of standing comlllittees shall
receive paymeut for their neoes~ary expenditures for transportation to and from each
Annual Communication of the Gr&nd Lodge, in the same manner· as ordered for the
officers or representatives of Lodges; but no Grand Officer, chairman, or officer or
representative of a Lodge, shall receive 11uch p11yment in more .than one of those
capacities, nor shall he receive It unless he shall have been in attendance at such
Communication from tile ftrat to the last day thereof, inclusive, unleBS excused by the
Grand Lodge.
.
10. The work and lectures pre1ented by the committee appointed for their exam·
ination and revision, are approved, adopted , and made obligatory upon all Lodges
within this Jurl11dlotion; and any Lodge which shall have had opportunity to ob bin
instruction therein, and shall neglect or refuse to learn and use the same, shall, upon
representation of that fact to the Grand Maeter, be liable to the arrest of its charter,
it, in his discretion, he shall think it proper.
11. T!l.e person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor
eunuch; free born, being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in
God and a future existence; of moral conduct; capable of reading and writing; not
deformed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation, having
his right limbs as a man ought to' have; and able to conform literally to what the
several degrees respectively require of him.

12. No Lodge under this jurisdiction, located beyond the limits of .this State, shall
receive any allowance for the expenses of a representative to this Grand Lodge ; nor
&hall any such Lodge be chargeable with dues on account of the Representative
Fund.
13. All Masonic intercourse between 1his Grand Lodge and the Grand Orient of
France ls. hereby suspended, and the Lodges and Masons of this jurisdiction are tor·
bidden to recognize or hold communication with any brother w\lo hails from or
acknowledges allegiance te the Grand Orient of France, so 1011g · as that body continues its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of the jurisdictional rights of the Grand
Lodge of Louisiana.
·
14.. Each Lodge within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, so far as It is able so
to do, shall see that the needy of its own membership and neighborho.od are not made
11 burden to others.
15. The Grand Master shall appoint for each district an officer, to be called
Inspector, who shall be a resident of the district tor which he is appointed, and whose
duty it shall be to visit annually (and oftener if desired by any Lodge,) each Lodge
in his district; to inspect the work and, if neceSBBry, correct the same in accordance
with the work as adopted by this Grand Lodge; and to report the working condition
of each Lodge in his district to the Grand Lecturer, on or before the first day of September.in each year: and further, to examine the records and all tire books of each
Lodge and the manner of transacting its business with reference to its conformity to
our Constitution and Regulations, e,nd report thereon to the Grand Master at the same
time. Each Lodge shall pay such necessary expenses of the Inspector as may be
incurred in performing the duties of the visitation herein required.

16. No Master of a Lodge shall be Installed until he shall have produced to the
installing officer the certiftcate or the Grand Lecturer, or of the Inspector of the
district in which such Lodge is situated, that he 11 qnallfted to give the work and lectures entire in the three degrees; and such oertlftcate, lndorsed by the inetalllng
officer, shall be f11rwarded by him to the Grand Lecturer, to be kept on file in his
office.
17. Whenever an appeal shall be taken from tho ~udgment of a subordinate
Lodge upon the report of trial-commiBB!onera, any and nil addlttonal evidence, which
either the· accuser or accused shall desire to have heard on the appeal, shall be taken
and reduced to writing within sixty days from the day on whluh the announcement

and representations which it is desired t11 have oonlldered on the appeal shall also be
